# Brainstorming **Core concept directions:** - Literal-comedic: gods living in the modern world, decked out in sneakers as part of contemporary fashion — Hermes in limited-edition runners, Ares in tactical boots-adjacent high-tops, Artemis in trail shoes. Fish-out-of-water divine comedy. - Romantic-lyric: gods' power is tied to their footwear. Sneakers are modern artifacts of belief — the way mortals move through the world reflects how they worship. Worn soles mean fading divinity. - Noir/mystery: someone is stealing divine sneakers, and each stolen pair "kills" or diminishes a god. A mortal detective or cobbler must track them down. - Sports/competition: a marathon where gods and mortals race together; the outcome decides the pantheon's fate. - Kid-facing fable tone: a child finds a dead god's sneakers at a thrift store and gains fragments of divine power with each step. - Sincerity-first: a small cobbler shop that repairs gods' shoes; through the protagonist's eyes we see the quiet decline of the pantheon. **Character ideas:** - Protagonist: a cobbler or shoe-repair apprentice. Cobblers occupy rich mythic space (the Fates spinning thread, elves and the shoemaker, Hermes' sandals). Could inherit the trade from a grandparent who secretly served the gods. - Alternates: a teenage sneakerhead who can identify any shoe at a glance; a marathon runner; a thrift-store employee; a god living incognito as a mall shoe salesman. - Supporting gods: Hermes (the natural entry point — messenger, fleet-footed, shop liaison), Artemis (wilderness atrophying, threadbare soles), Athena (immaculate, tactical, chess-player), Hades (wearing down at the heels from endless standing), Ares (confrontational antagonist — scuffs everything he touches). - Antagonist candidates: Ares as a brute force of opposition; a forgotten, nameless god who eats other gods' footwear to survive; the protagonist's own doubt/burnout; modernity itself — the gods fading because no one walks anywhere anymore. - The Fates as divine cobblers who spin, measure, and cut the laces. Very strong image. **Worldbuilding / imagery bank:** - The Fates spinning, measuring, and cutting the laces. Powerful image. - Sole wear as a measure of belief: a god with no followers has no tread left. - Sidewalks as sacred ground — every street a potential pilgrimage. - "Walk with me" as the ritual form of divine conversation; gods do business on foot. - Scuffed shoes as battle scars; pristine box-fresh shoes as vanity/emptiness. - A god's true name stitched on the inside tag. - Marathons as the last mass rituals where mortals unknowingly worship. - The shop itself: an ancient storefront wedged between modern buildings, older than the street. **Tone options:** - Whimsical and wry (Gaiman-flavored Americana/urban fantasy with wry humor and melancholy). - Bittersweet literary: the slow death of things walked past. - Broad comedy: pantheon office comedy, sneaker culture jokes. - Fable-like, quiet and precise. **8-chapter shape, cobbler version:** 1. Ordinary day at the repair shop; first hint that the clientele isn't mortal. 2. Establish rules: shoes = faith, wear = decline. Hermes as recurring customer/teacher. 3. A god arrives in crisis — Artemis's soles nearly gone, the wilderness thinning with her. 4. Midpoint reversal: the "wear" isn't natural. Someone is cutting the laces — the Fates' work being undone, or a forgotten god devouring tread. 5. Protagonist begins a craft project: re-soling a god, learning what mortal-made repair can and can't do. 6. Deeper into the underworld or the forgotten god's lair; stakes become personal — protagonist's own connection to the old belief. 7. Climax: a public walk — gods take to the streets in their shoes and mortals run alongside them; belief flows back through shared movement. 8. Quiet resolution: the shop's new role, the protagonist's place in a small, living mythology. **8-chapter shape, race version:** Marathon as climax instead; protagonist trains with Hermes; Ares sabotages the course; the finish line is a temple threshold; final chapter the gods walk home in their worn shoes, content for once. **Pacing considerations:** - ~1000 words per chapter means tight scenes: one setting, one or two gods, one revelation or escalation per chapter. - Chapters should alternate small-intimate (shop scenes) and big-mythic (underworld, streets, ritual) to keep rhythm. - Antagonist needs a face by chapter 4 at the latest; mystery can't sustain 8 chapters of ambiguity. - Final chapter should resolve both the external plot and the thematic question: why sneakers, why walking, why now. # Reflection The prompt "Gods wore sneakers" is past tense — an observation. That strongly suggests a mortal witness perspective, someone positioned to *see* the gods' footwear up close. The cobbler angle is the strongest fit: it gives the protagonist a legitimate, intimate reason to look at gods' shoes, and it taps into deep mythic material (Hermes' winged sandals, the Fates spinning thread, the shoemaker and the elves). A thrift store or sneakerhead angle is fun but stays at the level of concept-joke; the cobbler shop lets the shoes carry actual narrative weight. The comedy direction is tempting but risky — broad sneaker-culture humor would exhaust itself well before 8,000 words, and leaning on real brand names (the Nike problem, when Nike is literally a goddess) would create tonal tangles and read as either lawsuit-adjacent or as a one-note gag. Better to invent original divine footwear: shoes named for their domains, laces spun by the Fates, tread made of belief. The prompt's charm comes from treating the whimsy *seriously*, not winking at it. The strongest thematic engine is the fading-belief premise: worn soles as dying divinity. It converts a whimsical image into real stakes and gives every chapter a measurable, visible progression — we can literally see gods getting better or worse. The Artemis example is potent because it links a god's condition to something readers care about (wilderness, disappearing places). The bittersweet tone serves this well: melancholy undercurrent with warmth and humor in the dialogue and details, Gaiman-like. Pure tragedy would be a slog over 8 chapters; pure comedy would hollow out the stakes. The midpoint reversal ("the wear isn't natural — someone is cutting laces") is necessary structure: without it, the story is just a sequence of sad god portraits. It converts observation into plot. The forgotten-god antagonist is thematically tidy — the pantheon's decline embodied in one starving creature — and allows a resolution more interesting than a fight: recognition, remembrance, maybe even the protagonist re-shoeing the antagonist. That said, a purely redemptive ending may be too soft; there should be a real cost somewhere. The two 8-chapter shapes can probably merge: the shop-first structure with the climactic public walk/race in chapter 7. A mass mortal event — a marathon, or simply gods walking openly down a city street with people joining — is the right visual and emotional climax because it answers the theme: belief restored not through worship but through *walking together*. That's the image the prompt has been building toward. Pacing-wise, 1000-word chapters demand economy: each chapter needs one god encounter or one plot movement, no scene that exists only for flavor. Hermes as the recurring customer/mentor gives continuity; Artemis as the god in decline gives urgency; the forgotten god gives menace. The protagonist needs a small personal arc too — likely inheriting the shop, or learning why their grandparent took the job — so the ending lands for them and not just for the pantheon. Concerns to keep in mind: the ensemble could sprawl (limit on-stage gods to four or five); the magic rules must stay consistent (shoes = belief, repair = intervention, new soles = new worship); and the final chapter must explain, explicitly or implicitly, why the gods wear *sneakers* specifically and not dress shoes or boots — the answer is probably about modern mortals, modern walking, and what kind of faith still fits today.

# Intention **Premise and protagonist.** The story will center on Marisol "Mari" Vega, a young cobbler who inherits her grandfather's shoe repair shop in a mid-sized American city and discovers his true clientele: the old gods, whose divinity lives in their footwear. The cobbler angle is the firm choice — it gives the protagonist a legitimate, intimate reason to observe gods' shoes up close, it echoes real mythic material (Hermes' winged sandals, the Fates spinning thread, the shoemaker fable), and it keeps the story grounded in craft and hands and tools rather than abstract spectacle. **The central conceit.** A god's shoes are their divinity made visible. The soles are made of belief; tread wears as worship fades. Laces are spun by the Fates. New shoes cannot be manufactured — they can only be earned through new belief. Repair, therefore, is an act of theological intervention, and a cobbler is closer to a priest than a tradesman. This gives every chapter a visible, measurable stake: we can watch gods improve or decline through their shoes. **Tone and style.** Bittersweet urban fantasy with wry warmth — Gaiman-like, melancholy undercurrent but generous with humor in dialogue and small details. Whimsy taken seriously, never winked at. No real brand names; gods wear original, purpose-made divine footwear (Artemis in woven-ivy trail shoes, Ares in steel-shanked high-tops, Hermes in something that never touches the ground quite fully). The prose should be sensory and craft-focused: leather, wax, thread, the smell of the shop. Voice is close third person on Mari, plainspoken with occasional lyric lifts. **What to avoid.** Broad sneaker-culture comedy (it would exhaust itself by chapter 3 and gut the stakes). A rigid tragic register (unsustainable over 8,000 words). A sprawling ensemble (no more than five gods on stage: Hermes, Artemis, Ares, the Fates, and the antagonist). Ambiguity past chapter 4 (the mystery must resolve into a face by the midpoint). A purely redemptive ending (something must be lost or paid). **Thematic throughline.** Belief isn't restored through worship but through *walking together* — shared movement, attention, presence. The final image answers why the gods wear sneakers: sneakers are what mortals walk in now, and gods dress for the company they want to keep. **Protagonist arc.** Mari begins ambivalent — she inherited the shop out of obligation and is quietly planning to sell it. Through the story she learns why her grandfather kept the ledger, takes up the trade in earnest, and ends as the pantheon's keeper. Her arc runs parallel to the gods': both must decide whether old things deserve their feet. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — "Walk-Ins."** Ordinary day at Vega & Sons Shoe Repair, three weeks after the funeral. Mari is cataloguing the shop to sell it. A last customer arrives at closing: a man in immaculate, impossible shoes who speaks of her grandfather by name, leaves shoes that are "tired, not broken," and pays with a coin that becomes a live bee by morning. Mari finds the ledger — decades of appointments, coded entries, a column for "tread remaining." First crack in her skepticism. **Chapter 2 — "Hermes."** Hermes returns openly. He explains the rules: shoes are belief, wear is decline, the shop is the pantheon's last repair bench. Mari learns the trade has duties — a cobbler doesn't just fix shoes, she witnesses gods, and witnessing is a form of faith. She meets the coded regulars and asks the question that hooks the plot: why now, why is everyone's tread so thin? Hermes deflects. She decides not to sell the shop — yet. **Chapter 3 — "The Hunter."** Artemis arrives in crisis: her soles are nearly transparent, and where she walks, woods have been thinning for years. Mari sees the wear pattern and notices something impossible — a clean, deliberate cut across a lace, not wear at all. Someone is *unmaking* the shoes. Artemis is too proud to ask for help and leaves a thread of her ivy-lace behind. Urgency established: this is not slow decline, it is attack. **Chapter 4 — "The Ledger."** Mari investigates the ledger and discovers her grandfather's last months were consumed with a client marked only as "No Name" — entries that stop mid-word. Ares storms in, shoes scuffed to nothing, demanding armor for his soles; through their argument Mari learns the pantheon blames each other for the fading and no one has noticed the cuts. A visit from one of the Fates (or her representative — an old woman buying a single lace tip) confirms the laces are being severed *after* they're spun. Mari names the antagonist: a forgotten god, starving, eating the others' tread to survive. **Chapter 5 — "Resoling."** Mari attempts the impossible: rebuilding Artemis's soles. She fails with ordinary materials — belief can't be faked with leather. The breakthrough: repair works only when it's *witnessed and believed in*; she has to bring Artemis into the shop, work openly, and let the work itself matter to someone. A first small miracle: a new customer, an ordinary trail runner, unknowingly contributes a scrap of genuine awe. Mari starts to understand what her grandfather knew — divinity is communal, and the shop is a temple with a workbench for an altar. **Chapter 6 — "No Name."** Following the cut-lace trail into the city's margins — abandoned rail lines, flood channels, the spaces no one walks — Mari and Hermes find the forgotten god: a thin, hooded thing in shoes made entirely of stolen scraps, including a heel-piece Mari recognizes from her grandfather's ledger. Confrontation reveals the past: her grandfather tried to re-shoe it years ago and failed, because a god with no name cannot be believed in. The cost of the story lands here — to give it a name is to give it a place, and there is only so much belief to go around. Someone will fade in its place. **Chapter 7 — "The Walk."** Climax. Mari's solution: not a sermon but a walk. On the morning of the city marathon — the one day mortals take to the streets in their thousands — she re-shoes Artemis, Ares, Hermes, and the nameless one, and the gods run the route among the crowd, unhidden, glimmering just enough. Belief flows through shared movement; tread thickens with every mile, every runner who keeps pace, every spectator who *sees*. The nameless god is believed into being again — given a name before the finish line — and pays the debt honestly: the fading is spread thin across all of them, a little less of everyone instead of all of one. It's not a restoration of the old world; it's a smaller, living pantheon on a budget of attention. **Chapter 8 — "Regulars."** Quiet resolution, weeks later. The shop has regulars again. Artemis brings mortal trail runners whose shoes she blesses; Ares volunteers as a high-school track coach; the nameless god — now called something small and good — sweeps the floor of the shop, keeping the last of its stolen scraps in a box, a reminder. Mari writes her own name into the ledger beside her grandfather's. Final beat answers the prompt directly: a young god, new-made, walks in off the street wearing box-fresh sneakers bought at the mall — because gods dress for the company they want to keep, and these days, mortals wear sneakers. Mari smiles, takes the shoes, and gets to work.

# How a Human Might Approach This Piece A human writer given "Gods wore sneakers" would almost certainly *not* build an eight-chapter novelistic arc with a coherent magic system, a five-god ensemble, and a thematic thesis. That's what a writing *program* does. Here's what a human actually does: **Latches onto one thing and obsesses.** A human reads "Gods wore sneakers" and gets stuck on a single detail that won't let go — maybe the image of a god's heel dragging, or the fact that sneakers are what you wear when you *expect to walk among people*, or the absurd specific smell of a Nike box fresh out of the mall, applied to Zeus. They build the story out from that obsession, and the rest of the mythology serves the obsession, not the other way around. The prompt is past tense — "wore" — and a human would sit with that. *Wore*, not *wear*. That tense suggests memory, aftermath, maybe even death. A human might write the whole thing as a eulogy. **Writes from what they know, sloppily.** The cobbler premise in the plan is good, but a human who chose it would either be an actual maker or would go learn one weird true fact that infects the whole story — that cobblers traditionally kept customers' old soles, that shoe repair is one of the last guild trades, that "cobbler" originally meant someone who *botches* (a slander word). The story would be full of stuff that's true and unaccounted for, not details selected *to be* atmospheric. **Doesn't know the ending.** The plan above knows the ending before writing a word, and every chapter is engineered backward from it. A human drafts chapter one, discovers Mari halfway through chapter three, realizes the story is actually about resentment and not wonder, and either follows it or fights it. The final text bears scars. Human stories have seams, detours, and occasionally a chapter that's clearly the writer's favorite and does "too much" — and readers can feel the writer's heat even in the excess. **Commits to a reaction.** "Gods wore sneakers" is either funny or devastating, and a human picks a lane and *stays* in it at the risk of being misread. The plan hedges: "bittersweet with wry warmth, melancholy undercurrent but generous with humor" — that's a committee tone. A human writes it deadpan and lets the sadness leak in sideways, or writes it as grief with the comedy arriving uninvited, in dialogue, because grief in real life is full of stupid jokes. **Under-explains.** Humans trust readers. They never say "belief flows through shared movement." They show Hermes noticing a stranger walking his pace and matching steps for three blocks, and don't comment on it at all. --- # Telltale LLM Approaches (and How They'd Damage This Piece Specifically) **1. The system-builder instinct.** LLMs respond to fantasy prompts by writing rulebooks: shoes = belief, tread = worship quantified, laces spun by the Fates, a ledger with a "tread remaining" column. This turns myth into a spreadsheet. Real mythology is *inconsistent* — no ancient text explains Hermes' sandals, they just work. The magic system in the plan is very tidy, and tidiness kills mystery. Worse, once the rules are legible, the plot becomes rule-arithmetic: protagonist learns rules, applies rules, exploits rules. Chapter 5 ("repair works only when witnessed and believed in") is a rule being *discovered and stated*, which is the least mythic thing a story can do. **2. Everything is load-bearing.** In the plan, the grandfather's ledger connects to the nameless god, the cut lace connects to the antagonist, the marathon connects to the theme, the final sneaker-god connects to the prompt. Nothing is wasted. Human stories waste things — a customer whose shoes are just shoes, an anecdote that goes nowhere, a god Mari never fully understands. Total narrative economy reads as artificial because life isn't economical. Some details should just be *there*. **3. The kindness-maximizing resolution.** This is the biggest problem in the plan. The intention *says* "something must be lost or paid" — but look at what actually gets paid: "the fading is spread thin across all of them, a little less of everyone instead of all of one." That's not a cost. That's a payment plan. Nobody dies, nobody is diminished beyond comfort, the villain is fed and named and *sweeps the shop floor*. Ares becomes a *track coach*. The denouement is a restored community montage: Artemis blesses trail runners, regulars return, Mari writes her name in the ledger. This is the LLM's deep aversion to letting anyone be genuinely lost or genuinely unredeemed. Real endings leave wounds. **4. Theme stated, then restated, then costumed.** "Godods dress for the company they want to keep" is explicitly written in the Intention as the thesis — and then executed in dialogue-worthy clarity in the finale ("gods dress for the company they want to keep, and these days, mortals wear sneakers"). When a story hands the reader its meaning in a polished aphorism, it's the model showing its work. A human would bury that insight so deep that maybe half of readers get it and that's fine. **5. Spectacle escalation.** The marathon climax — thousands of mortals unknowingly worshipping, belief flowing through "shared movement" — is a very LLM (and very Hollywood) move: solve an intimate problem with a crowd scene. The story is about a workbench, an old shop, one woman's hands. Its climax should probably happen at that scale, not across a city. **6. Characters as plot functions.** Hermes "deflects" at exactly the right plot moment. The Fate conveniently appears as an "old woman buying a single lace tip" to deliver exposition. Artemis is "too proud to ask for help" — a trait assigned because the chapter needs friction, not because Artemis is a person. Everyone operates on schedule. **7. The reluctant heir.** Mari inherits the shop "out of obligation," is "quietly planning to sell it," and arc-completes into belonging. This is the most stock protagonist opening in fiction. It's not wrong, but it's prefabricated — nothing about Mari is odd, particular, or uncomfortable yet. **8. Cute symmetry.** Chapter titles ("Walk-Ins," "Resoling," "The Walk"), exactly five gods each with a role, a victim-antagonist-resolution — the structure is so balanced it reads as machine-tooled. --- # Deep Dive: Critique of the Intention & Plan, Chapter by Chapter **Ch. 1:** The bee-coin is a nice image. But "first crack in her skepticism" is an emotional beat *scheduled* rather than earned. Also the ledger with a "tread remaining" column — quantify divinity and you've killed it. A ledger with entries in *words* — "D. much worn; warned him" — is more human and more haunting than a measurement. **Ch. 2:** Hermes explaining "the rules" is the system-builder failure in its purest form. A human version: Hermes explains almost nothing, is cagey in a *personal* way (maybe he owes the grandfather money), and Mari learns by getting things wrong. Also Hermes should be weirder — petty, vain about his shoes, annoyed at being mistaken for a courier guy. Gods who are only dignified are museum mannequins. **Ch. 3:** Artemis's condition mapping literally to woods thinning ("where she walks, woods have been thinning") is mechanical — domain-as-health-bar. The discovery of the *cut lace* is the strongest plot beat in the whole plan (wear vs. sabotage is a real mystery) and should carry more uncertainty. But "too proud to ask for help" is a stock trait. Give her an actual flaw — she's contemptuous of Mari, or of the whole idea of *repair*, which is a form of cheating. **Ch. 4:** "No Name" entries stopping mid-word is a good creepy detail. Ares "storming in demanding armor for his soles" is fine, but the chapter's function — everyone assembling the antagonist's identity via shared exposition — is detective-plot machinery. The Fate-as-old-woman-buying-a-lace-tip is a *conveniently theatrical* device. And "Mari names the antagonist: a forgotten god, starving" — a character *deducing the theme of the story aloud* is the model's habit of narrating comprehension. **Ch. 5:** "Repair works only when it's witnessed and believed in" — a hard rule stated, discovered mid-story, and then used in the climax. This is the mechanical heart of the problem. Also the "first small miracle" (an ordinary trail runner unknowingly contributing awe) is sweet in the way LLM outputs are sweet: warm, safe, agreeable. Nothing here can embarrass anyone. **Ch. 6:** The forgotten god with shoes of stolen scraps, including a heel from grandfather's ledger — good connection, but this is where the story most needs teeth and the plan is already softening it ("Confrontation reveals the past"). The grandfather "tried to re-shoe it and failed because a god with no name cannot be believed in" is a tidy, quotable law. Human version: the grandfather *refused* it. Maybe he turned it away, or charged it and it couldn't pay, and something followed him to his death. Give Mari a reason to be angry at the old man. **Ch. 7:** The marathon. This is the plan's weakest structural choice, and it compounds with the fake cost ("a little less of everyone"). It's the fantasy-urbanoia cliché of mass civic belief (every urban fantasy eventually runs a "the city believes in itself" scene). And "given a name before the finish line" is stagey — the climax literally staged at a finish line. **Ch. 8:** The denouement hits every LLM closer note: community restored, everyone's new wholesome life listed, the named god humbly sweeping, protagonist writes her name in the ledger, and a final image that *explains the prompt*. The box-fresh sneaker god is a thesis statement in costume. **The Intention overall:** The tone paragraph promises "bittersweet with wry warmth... melancholy undercurrent but generous with humor" — a hedge that will average out to pleasant blandness if not enforced with actual risk. The "what to avoid" list is good (no brands, no sprawling ensemble, no bows) but the plan then proceeds to tie a bow anyway. --- # Brainstorming: Ways to Make It More Human **Complicate Mari beyond the template.** She inherited the shop and she's *broke* — not symbolically reluctant, actually in debt. She charges Hermes real money and feels bad and does it anyway. Or she's good at the trade but hates leather work, took it up because she's got her grandfather's hands and no other plan. Give her something non-functional: an ex she keeps almost texting, a petty rivalry with the shoe store next door, a concrete memory of her grandfather that isn't warm. **Give the grandfather a stain.** Instead of a heroic custodian, make his legacy uneasy. Maybe the ledger shows he *overcharged* the gods. Maybe he refused the nameless one and never told anyone. Maybe Mari finds evidence he was scared at the end. A human lets the dead grandfather be a flawed man rather than a plot-backstory. **Let one god stay unpleasant, unrehabilitated.** Ares as track coach is rehabilitative whimsy. What if Ares just *leaves* — takes his scuffed shoes and walks off, and Mari never fixes him, and we don't know if he's fine or not? Or Hermes remains a bit of a mooch and a liar to the last chapter. Not everyone completes an arc. **Cut or shrink the marathon.** Options: kill it entirely and make the climax a single dawn walk — Mari and Artemis walking the thinning woods, one witness, a schoolkid on a bike who stops and stares, and Artemis's tread thickening by *one step's worth*, which has to be enough. Or keep the marathon but have it *fail partially* — the gods run it and the crowd believes in them the way crowds believe in a great runner: briefly, and then everyone goes home and the tread fades again by winter. Miracles with a decay rate are more human than permanent ones. **Make the nameless god truly costly.** The spread-thin payment is a dodge. Alternatives: naming it *requires* a donor — and someone volunteers (Artemis, already half-gone, who'd rather end as a named stranger's seed than as a fading hunter). Or the naming is *botched* — the new name doesn't fit right, the god limps on it forever, and Mari has to live with a repair that isn't quite right, the way cobblers live with every repair that isn't quite right. An imperfect repair as the ending image is *thematically* better than a perfect one: that's what the trade actually is. **Underwrite the magic.** Delete Hermes's system exposition. Never explain why laces are spun by the Fates, or — better — imply the Fates *know* the laces will be cut and spin them anyway, and never account for this. Mari misinfers things; a god corrects her in chapter 6 in passing. Let at least one god be unable to articulate how their own shoes work ("They were a gift. I don't ask"). **Let a chapter be a wrong turn.** Mari fixes the wrong god first and makes something worse — re-soles a god who *shouldn't* have been re-soled (a god whose job was nearly done, who wanted to wear out). A god who *wants* to fade, and is content, and Mari can't accept it — that's a genuinely human discomfort, and it gives the theme a counterweight: maybe not everything worn out is a tragedy to be repaired. That idea alone could make the story worth writing, and it's exactly the kind of ungovernable thought a plannerly outline excludes. **Add dead-end texture.** One mortal regular with nothing to do with the plot — an old man who brings in the same pair of loafers every year and talks. Mari's own shoes, which are falling apart and she never fixes them — noticed, never commented on. A mythological anecdote Hermes tells that has no thematic purpose and is just strange and a little gross. **Local and specific over generic.** "Mid-sized American city" is placeholder. Pick a place with a real texture — rust-belt, a river town, somewhere with an actual marathon or a defunct one (a marathon that was *cancelled* years ago and only its route remains painted on the roads is a far better setting detail than a thriving one). **End on an unfinished beat.** Instead of the box-fresh sneaker god explaining the prompt, end mid-workday: the bell over the door rings, Mari looks up, and we never see who came in — or we do, and it's someone ordinary, and that's fine, and she takes the shoes. Leave the thematic summation unspoken. The reader who's been paying attention has already assembled it. **Preserve the plan's best bones.** The cobbler premise, the wear-vs-sabotage mystery, the cut lace, the ledger, the walking-together theme, Mari's hands — all strong. The critique is not that the plan is wrong but that it's *too complete, too kind, and too legible*. Humanizing means introducing friction the outline can't fully resolve: an unrehabilitated character, a botched repair, a payment that actually hurts, a god who wanted to wear out, and an ending that trusts the reader to finish the thought.

# Intention **Premise.** Mari Vega, twenty-eight, broke, inherited her grandfather's shoe repair shop in a rust-belt river town — and inherited, without knowing it, the old gods as customers. Their divinity lives in their footwear; their tread wears as belief fades. She's not a reluctant heir in the symbolic sense; she's three months behind on rent and actively negotiating with a buyer when the story opens. Gods wear sneakers — and boots, and woven things — because gods dress for the company they want to keep, and this is never said aloud. **Setting.** A specific, concrete place: a river town with a shuttered mill, a deflated main street, and a marathon that was cancelled in the nineties — the route numbers still faded on the asphalt. The setting is itself a worn-out thing, which quietly rhymes with the gods. No brand names; divine footwear is original and purpose-made. **Magic: underwritten, never explained.** No scene where anyone explains the rules. Mari learns by doing things wrong — fixing a god's shoe the mortal way produces something wrong and slightly disturbing, and she isn't told why. The Fates appear only as a rumor Hermes won't elaborate on. If asked how their shoes work, gods shrug: "They were a gift. I don't ask." The reader assembles the system from behavior, never from exposition. **The grandfather: flawed, not heroic.** He kept the gods' bench for decades — and, the ledger reveals, he *refused* the nameless god, turned it away when it was starving, and spent his last months afraid. Mari's arc includes real anger at a dead man, unresolved into anything tidy. **Tone.** Deadpan first; the sadness arrives sideways, in details and dialogue, not in narration. Humor is uninvited — gods are petty, vain, cheap, and funny *because they're treated seriously*. Mari's interiority is dry and practical; she thinks in costs and thread-counts. No "bittersweet-with-wry-warmth" balancing act — the blend is emergent, not declared. **Stakes and costs that actually cost.** The nameless god is named — and the naming is botched; the name doesn't fit right and the god limps on it forever, and Mari lives with that the way cobblers live with every imperfect repair. Ares storms in, doesn't get what he wants, and walks off unresolved — no rehabilitation, no track-coaching epilogue. One god — the mill god — *wants* to wear out, and the story lets him, and Mari has to sit with the discomfort that not everything worn out is a tragedy. The climactic miracle is one step's worth of tread, witnessed by one kid on a bike, and it is *enough for now, not forever*. **Voice & style.** Close third person on Mari. Prose is plainspoken, craft-sensory (leather, wax, the smell of cement), with lyric lifts rationed. Chapters run ~1000 words: one scene, one movement, no scene that exists only for flavor. **To avoid.** Magic-system exposition; a "tread remaining" metric (the ledger is in words — *"D. much worn; warned him"*); mass civic-belief crowd scenes; villains redeemed into sweeping floors; every character completing an arc; anything load-bearing (there will be dead-end texture: an old mortal regular named Aldo and his loafers, a gross pointless anecdote from Hermes, Mari's own broken shoes she never gets around to fixing); the thesis stated anywhere, including the last line; a resolved ending — the doorbell rings and we don't fully see who came in. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — "Walk-Ins."** Three weeks after the funeral. Mari is cataloguing inventory for a buyer, hating herself a little, good with her hands and broke. At closing, a man in impossible, immaculate sneakers — Hermes — comes in asking for her grandfather by name, calls the shoes "tired, not broken," and pays with a coin that is a live bee by morning. Mari finds the ledger: decades of handwritten entries in plain words, names she half-recognizes from a mythology unit she slept through, notes like *"much worn; warned him."* She doesn't cancel the buyer. She just... doesn't call him back either. **Chapter 2 — "Regulars."** Hermes returns openly — petty, vain about the shoes, dodging the fact that he owes her grandfather eleven dollars from 1989. No rules get explained. Mari fixes the shoes of a quiet elderly woman the mortal way, with ordinary cement and thread, and the woman leaves and something is subtly wrong with the rest of her day in a way no one explains. Mari learns the bench is a duty by *getting it wrong*. Enter Aldo, a mortal regular with loafers he brings in yearly, who talks and talks and has no plot function whatsoever. **Chapter 3 — "The Hunter."** Artemis: woven-ivy sneakers worn to transparency, contemptuous of repair as a form of cheating ("You don't patch a hunt, you end it"). Mari, holding the shoes, finds the thing that unhooks the story from slow decline: a clean, deliberate cut across one lace — not wear. Sabotage. Artemis takes her shoes and leaves rather than accept help. Mari, terrified and half-competent, keeps the severed lace. End on the woods outside town going quiet in a way the paper attributes to blight. **Chapter 4 — "No Name."** Mari interrogates the ledger. Entries marked *"No Name — refused"* decades back, then entries in her grandfather's shaky last-year hand: *"No Name again. Foolish. Old now. Afraid."* Ares arrives — high-tops scuffed to nothing, aggressive, demanding soles "armored." Mari refuses; she doesn't know how and won't fake it. He calls the shop a fossil, calls her grandfather a coward, and walks out; she never sees him again. Hermes, cornered, reluctantly confirms the shape of it: something with no name has been eating tread and cutting laces, and her grandfather turned it away hungry. Mari is furious at a dead man. This chapter plants her anger and lets it stay planted. **Chapter 5 — "The Mill God."** A small god comes in — the god of the river crossing, or the mill: cracked work boots, unhurried, kind. He doesn't want repair. He wants Mari to *finish* him — cut the last strand of his lace cleanly, the way it's done, so he can wear out with dignity instead of fraying. She refuses, angry; he shrugs, warm about it, and shuffles out. The chapter ends with Mari unable to sleep, doing something small and human and unwise: starting a practice re-sole on scraps at 2 a.m., and getting it wrong, and not knowing who it was for. **Chapter 6 — "The Flood Channel."** Mari and Hermes follow the trail of severed lace — flood channels, the dead rail line, places no one walks — and find the nameless god: thin, hooded, wearing shoes stitched from stolen scraps, including a heel-piece her grandfather's ledger described. Confrontation without choreography: it is starving, not evil; it wants a name, not shoes; it cut the laces out of spite older than her grandfather. Hermes goes still when Mari asks the obvious next question and doesn't answer it. Mari offers repair. The god tells her what the bench costs and what naming costs, obliquely, and she doesn't fully understand the price until she's already agreed. **Chapter 7 — "The Route."** Dawn, on the faded paint of the cancelled marathon route. Mari names the nameless god — impulsively, imperfectly, with a name that doesn't sit right on it. It takes. The god limps on that name forever and doesn't complain, because a limp is walking too. Artemis arrives — asked, not rescued — for a last walk down the route before she goes wherever worn-out hunters go. Mari walks with her. A kid on a bike stops and stares at Artemis the way kids stare at things that are true. One step's worth of tread comes back. Artemis decides to keep walking for a while — not saved, just *not done*. Mari notices her own shoes are ruined. Doesn't fix them. Doesn't comment. **Chapter 8 — "Regulars."** Months later, winter. The shop has its odd clientele again; Mari is still broke, less so. Ares is simply gone — no postcard, no resolution. The mill god's boots come back to the shop empty, left on the doorstep, worn out at last and finished cleanly; Mari keeps them on a shelf and doesn't call it a tragedy. Hermes still owes her eleven dollars and now also a ladder. The named god comes by on its limping feet to sit in the warm. Aldo brings his loafers. The buyer has stopped calling. Final beat: the bell over the door rings; Mari, mid-repair, looks up — and the story ends before we see who it is, or sees only that it's someone ordinary, which is enough.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Mari Vega **Background & personality.** Twenty-eight. Grew up above the shop until she was eleven, then the divorce shuffle — mother to Phoenix, summers here with Emilio, sanding and waxing and learning the stitch she hated. Went to community college for two semesters of business before money ran out. Worked retail at a shoe store in the mall for six years, which she describes as "close enough to the trade the way a lifeguard is close enough to a fish." She came back when Emilio got sick, not out of duty she'd admit to — because he asked, and he never asked for anything. She's good with her hands, genuinely, and it annoys her. She thinks in unit costs, thread-counts, and days-until-rent. **Flaws & idiosyncrasies.** She's cheap in a way she inherited and would deny — she reuses cement beyond when it's safe, which is why her repairs occasionally smell faintly of vinegar. She keeps a drafts folder with texts to her ex, Devon, that she writes and doesn't send; she has never once fixed her own shoes, which are down to the sock on the left heel. When nervous, she reads labels and receipts out loud. She still charges Hermes for the bench time even when he's clearly doing her a favor, and then lies awake about it. **Physicality.** Sturdy, small, her grandfather's square hands and knuckles. A white burn scar on her right forearm from a cement pot when she was thirteen — she tells people it's from a fryer. Carries herself hunched over the bench without noticing; straightens up when customers walk in like she's been caught at something. **Motive, allegiances, relationships.** Her initial motive is money and the exit; the buyer represents the door out. Her anger at Emilio is specific: he never told her what the bench was, which means he either didn't trust her or wanted to spare her, and both options insult her. By the end her motive is smaller and truer: the bench is the first thing she's been better at than anyone she know. Her allegiance to the gods is reluctant, transactional, and real — the way you're loyal to customers who keep showing up. **Voice — flavor quotes.** *"Okay. I'm going to need you to pay me. In currency. This decade."* (Internal, reading the ledger) *"Warned him. Warned him about what, you cryptic old miser."* And of the trade: *"Nothing's ruined. Ruined is a lazy word. Everything is just at a different stage of being fixed or being finished."* — She'd never say this out loud; it's the kind of thought she has while stitching and pretends is about shoes. --- # Hermes **Background & personality.** The gods' go-between, and the only member of the old crowd whose divinity is *thriving-ish*: people still send things, still travel, still move packages at unreasonable speed, and he knows it, and it's made him insufferable in a low-grade way. He's the shop's front door because he's the one who talks to mortals. Petty, vain about his sneakers ("They don't touch the ground *fully*, it's a feature"), and chronically, unapologetically cheap. He has owed Emilio eleven dollars since 1989, and when Mari brings it up he changes the subject with the smoothness of a man who has had four thousand years of practice. **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** Tells long anecdotes that go nowhere and are usually a little gross — the story about the mule in Thebes, the thing with the innkeeper's soup. They have no thematic function; he just likes telling them. He's cagey in a *personal* way, not a mystical one — when Mari asks what naming costs, he goes still, and it's not because of divine law; it's because he's watched this exact thing go wrong before and doesn't want to be the one who talked someone into it. He always arrives at 4:58, two minutes before close, every time, as if by policy. **Physicality.** Narrow, quick, a man who seems to have already left any room he's in. Immaculate sneakers, laces in a knot no cobbler recognizes. Talks fast but walks slow when he's in the shop — savoring the one place where he sits still. He never sits, actually; he leans, on everything. **Motive, allegiances, relationships.** He genuinely liked Emilio — the eleven dollars is a weird artifact of that, a debt kept unpaid *because* keeping a small debt keeps the relationship open, and Hermes knows this about himself and would deny it. His allegiance is to the pantheon's survival but his policy is non-intervention; messengers deliver, they don't advise. His flaw is that this policy is self-serving and he half knows it. **Voice — flavor quotes.** *"Eleven dollars. I have a system. The debt predates your birth, which makes it historical, and you don't charge interest on history."* *"I don't make the news, I carry it. There's a difference and it's the difference that lets me sleep."* When Mari asks how his sneakers work: *"They were a gift. I don't ask. You want to try the soup story? The soup story's good."* --- # Artemis **Background & personality.** The hunter, the wild, the moon — and she has spent eighty years being the god of woods that got turned into parking lots. Her divinity runs on wild places and on people who look up from their phones at animals, and there's less of both every year. Contemptuous of repair as a category: "You don't patch a hunt, you end it." She thinks the bench is cheating, thinks Emilio was a decent man who enabled vanity, and is only in the shop in chapter 3 because the cut in her lace frightened her — and admitting fear is worse for her than the lace. **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** Pride so dense it functions as armor and blinders both. She refers to mortals by what they were doing when she first noticed them ("the sewer one," "the one who whistles"), and Mari is "the cobbler's girl" until chapter 7, when, unprompted, she calls her Mari once. She won't sit in the shop; she stands by the door like a customer who suspects the store is a scam. She has a soft spot she'd deny: she once spent a decade keeping watch on a family of foxes under a highway overpass and told no one. **Physicality.** Moves like someone who has never once been looked at without her permission. Ivy-woven sneakers worn translucent. Tired in a way that's in her tendons, not her face. When the kid stares at her on the route, she stands perfectly still — prey animal stillness, all her training reversed. **Motive, allegiances, relationships.** Her motive in the story is to settle her own accounts on her own terms — she came for answers about the cut, not salvation. Her arc bends only slightly: the one step of tread on the route doesn't save her, it just makes her *postpone* herself, and she chooses that openly. She has no allegiance to the pantheon — considers them a retirement home — and her only real loyalty is to whatever's left of the actual woods. **Voice — flavor quotes.** *"You don't patch a hunt. You end it. Anything else is taxidermy."* *"Your grandfather glued a moon back on once. Glue. I still came out at night, didn't I. Beads and gum."* And quietly, at the end of the route, not to Mari exactly: *"I'm not done. That's not the same as saved. You can write that down if your ledger needs it."* --- # Ares **Background & personality.** War isn't fading — that's the joke of him; there's plenty of war, it's just that modern war is drone feeds and procurement contracts, and it doesn't march, and Ares is a god of marching. So he's not starving — he's *irrelevant and furious about it*, which is a different disease the shop can't treat. Steel-shanked high-tops scuffed to nothing, because his is a scuffer's divinity: he breaks ground, things wear out, that's the job. **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** He speaks about shoes the way other people speak about soldiers — "good pair, died well." He chews cinnamon toothpicks, a habit picked up from a supply sergeant in 1917 that he refuses to admit is an affectation. He's not stupid — he catches the flaw in Mari's arguments faster than Hermes does — he's just constitutionally unable to retreat from a position, which is a fine quality in a bayonet charge and a terrible one in a conversation. **Physicality.** Fills doorframes. Voice pitched slightly too loud for rooms, correct for parade grounds. His scuffs are the loudest thing about him; you hear the damage in every step. **Motive, allegiances, relationships.** He wants soles "armored" because he wants to *still be used* — armor is a request to be marched on, and the shop refusing him reads to him like the world saying the marching is over. He calls Emilio a coward not because it's true but because Emilio once told him the trade doesn't do armor, it does *care*, and Ares has hated that sentence for thirty years. He walks out in chapter 4 and never returns; the story does not resolve him, and that's the point — some gods you lose, and you don't get to know how it went. **Voice — flavor quotes.** *"Armor them. Whatever's in it, whatever it costs, I can pay. Wars pay, little cobbler. Ask anybody."* *"Your grandfather talked about care. Care. I've seen what care does on a retreat. It's not a load-bearing word."* --- # The Nameless God ("No Name") **Background & personality.** A god that never got its foot in the door — perhaps it was local once, a crossing-spirit or a house-spirit whose people moved away or died in a bad decade, and belief in it lapsed before it was ever written down. No name means no shape for belief to hold onto; it has been starving a long time and has survived by *scavenging*: eating tread, cutting laces, wearing shoes stitched from the scraps of other gods' divinity. It isn't evil. It's feral, spiteful, and very patient — its spite is older than Emilio and older than Mari's whole country. **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** It has no words of its own. A god assembled from scraps speaks in scraps: it talks entirely in things it has overheard — fragments of prayers, overheard arguments, a fishmonger's oath from 1803, a voicemail greeting. This is genuinely unnerving until Mari starts to hear the pattern, and then it's worse, because she recognizes one of the fragments: a phrase of her grandfather's, from the day he turned it away, which it has been carrying and wearing like a stolen heel-piece. Its fatal flaw is that it wants to be *witnessed* more than it wants to be fed, and it will take a botched naming over a good meal. **Physicality.** Thin to the point of translucence at the edges, hooded in gray nothing; you mostly see the shoes, which are the loudest thing about it — a museum of thefts. It moves like it's apologize for occupying space. After the naming, it limps, and never complains about the limp, ever, in any century. **Motive, allegiances, relationships.** Wants a name, not shoes — the shoes were always the means. Its relationship to Emilio is the story's wound: he refused it, was afraid of it, and it both hated him and *kept a piece of him*, and cannot explain which feeling that is. Its relationship to Mari is wary, transactional, and then suddenly, horribly, trusting — the most dangerous thing it does in the story is agree with her. **Voice — flavor quotes.** (All borrowed, always.) *"We're closed on Saturdays."* (a shopkeeper's phrase, some century, wrong context, its way of saying *go away*.) *"Foolish. Old now. Afraid."* — Emilio's own words back, worn smooth from re-use, offered when Mari asks what happened. And when she offers to name it: *"...You'd get it wrong."* (a woman at a bus stop, 1974, about love, but it will do.) --- # The Mill God (Ludo) **Background & personality.** A small god — the crossing, the millrace, the safe passage of grain trucks over the river. The mill shut in the eighties and his congregation became a historical society plaque. Unlike the others he is not desperate, not bitter, not at war with time. He is *tired*, in the way of a man who worked the same shift for a century and liked it. He wants to wear out with dignity: for Mari to cut the last strand of his lace cleanly, the way it's done, instead of letting himself fray to nothing over decades. **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** Carries a tin lunch pail he doesn't need and knows he doesn't need. Remembers every worker's name, all three hundred and some, and can be prompted for them like an organ grinder — Mari gets four names out of him over one visit and cries about the fourth and pretends she didn't. His flaw, such as it is: patience so total it reads as indifference, and he genuinely cannot understand why anyone would refuse him this — which makes him gently, unbearably cruel to Mari without ever meaning to be. **Physicality.** Broad, earthbound, cracked work boots, forearms like a man who unloaded sacks. Unhurried to the point that time seems embarrassed around him. He doesn't radiate anything — no shimmer, no moonlight; he is the least god-looking god in the story, which is the most god-like thing about him. **Motive, allegiances, relationships.** No allegiances; he liked his patch and his people and considers his account balanced. He has no grievance with the nameless god ("everyone's got to eat; it never took from me — I have nothing worth taking"). His kindness to Mari is uncomplicated, which is exactly what makes him the hardest character for her to deal with: he is offering her a death the way other customers offer her a broken heel, trusting her the way you trust a tradesman, and the trust is the unbearable part. **Voice — flavor quotes.** *"Don't look at it like a funeral. Look at it like the end of a good shift. Somebody has to turn the lights off, kid. Might as well be somebody who liked the room."* *"Walter Doane. Fourth name. Fell in the race in '61 and made everybody laugh about it all night at the Legion. There. That one's free."* --- # Emilio Vega (the dead grandfather) **Background & personality.** Present in the story only as ledger, smell (Borkum Riff pipe tobacco, soaked into everything), and argument. A stubborn, stingy, secretive man who kept the gods' bench for over fifty years, overcharged them occasionally because "they'll live, they can pay retail," and refused the nameless god — the ledger says *"refused"* and the later shaky hand says *"afraid,"* and the story never reconciles the two, because Mari can't. He asked Mari to come back when he got sick and never told her why the shop mattered, which is either protection or distrust and she'll never get to ask. **Idiosyncrasies.** Wrote everything in plain words, no mysticism, all lowercase — *"much worn; warned him"* — as if the gods were boiler trouble. Kept customers' old soles in labeled boxes; the shop is full of them. The heel-piece the nameless god stole was from his box, one of the few gaps on the shelf. **Function & relationships.** He is the story's unreliable saint. Mari's anger at him never resolves into either forgiveness or a verdict; the best she gets is chapter 6, learning he was *afraid*, which is worse than either. His relationship to every god is on a sliding scale from warm (Ludo) to adversarial (Ares) to indebted-adjacent (Hermes, the eleven dollars, likely a tab he kept open on purpose). **Voice — flavor quotes (all from the ledger).** *"much worn. warned him. he never listens, the big one, but his boots are honest."* *"No Name again. foolish. old now. afraid. — ref. Marisol, if you're reading this: it isn't your problem. nothing here ever was. that was the whole trick of it. — E.V."* (She finds this note in chapter 4 and it makes everything worse, exactly as he'd have wanted, the old miser.) --- # Aldo Petrosian (mortal regular) **Background & personality.** Seventy-nine, widower seven years, brings in the same pair of brown loafers every year for a resole they don't need. His wife bought them in 1974 for a wedding they drove to in a Corvair that broke down in Barstow; he tells this story every visit, with the Barstow breakdown gaining detail annually. He is the shop's only entirely plotless customer and exists to be exactly what he is: proof of what the trade is for on the mortal side, texture, and the only person who asks Mari how *she's* doing and waits for the answer. **Idiosyncrasies.** Corrects anyone who calls the loafers shoes — "those are loafers, shoes work for a living." Browses the same three old shoe-polish tins on the shelf every visit as if comparison shopping. Has never once been seen to buy the polish. **Physicality.** Loud shirts post-widowhood — a retired-person's rebellion he took up at seventy-two and is committed to. Slightly deaf on the side Mari works, so all bench consultations are conducted at parade volume, which annoys her and which she'd miss if he stopped. **Motive & relationships.** He wants the ritual, not the resole; Mari worked this out in year two and resoles them anyway, lightly, and charges him for real, and he pays happily. His allegiance is to the shop as a place — he has watched the street die and refuses to accelerate the process. He never learns about the gods, or notices them, and if he did he'd probably ask them if they'd gotten anything decent on the radio lately. **Voice — flavor quotes.** *"Loafers. Shoes work for a living, Marisol, these retired in '98 and they've earned the rest."* *"How's the elbow? Don't tell me it's fine, nobody's elbow is fine, that's not what elbows do after forty."*

# Chapter 1 — Walk-Ins The shop smelled like her grandfather, which was to say like pipe tobacco and contact cement, two smells that had soaked into the plaster sometime around 1980 and had no plans to leave. Mari had been cataloguing the inventory for three days and had gotten as far as the workbench, which was the hardest part because everything on it was worth something and her grandfather had labeled none of it. The buyer was coming Thursday. His name was Twardowski and he owned four other shops in three other dying towns, and he'd told her on the phone, kindly, that what he was really buying was the location. "The fixtures, the bones of it. The tools I'll take as a courtesy." She was twenty-eight years old and three months behind on the apartment over the shop, and a courtesy was not going to cover it, but the number he'd floated would, barely, once. She wrote: *Anvils (2), American make, needs cleaning.* Then she stopped, because the bigger anvil — the one her grandfather called the good one — had a shoe on it, half-lasted, pinned and laced and waiting, and she'd been staring at it for three days trying to decide whose it was. It was a small shoe. A child's sandal, maybe, tan leather, hand-stitched with a seam she didn't know. It looked brand new. It looked like it had been waiting there since before she was born, and she hadn't been able to bring herself to unpin it. That was the thing about the shop. Every drawer had a story and all of them were her grandfather's, and he was three weeks dead, and she had a spreadsheet open. The bell over the door rang at 4:58. They never came at 4:58, whoever they were; whoever needed the shop came at lunch or on Saturdays, and they needed it less every year. Mari looked up from the anvil and saw a narrow man in a gray jacket leaning on the display case with his whole side, the way people lean when they've decided they're going to be a while. He was somewhere between thirty and fifty. He had the kind of face that made you think you'd sold him something once. "Emilio," the man said. "I need the bench tonight if he can — " "He died." The man stopped leaning. It was interesting to watch. He'd been poured onto the case like the case was furniture in his own house, and the two words picked him right up off it. "When," he said. "Three weeks ago. Friday." She heard herself add, for no reason, "In his sleep." The man looked at the floor for a second. Not at her — at the floor, at the green linoleum tiles her grandfather had laid crooked in 1988, like the floor was the one who'd told him. "That's a lie, probably," he said, not unkindly. "He never slept. But thank you for saying it." He was holding shoes. She hadn't noticed him holding them, the way you don't notice a bird is holding a worm. Sneakers. White, low, simple, absolutely immaculate — no scuffs, no creases, no wear at the toe, nothing, a shoe that had come out of a box a minute ago except that she could see the whole shape of a foot in them. The midsoles had a sag to them, a settled, tired sag, like a good horse at the end of a long day. It was the strangest contradiction she'd ever seen on a counter. New shoes that were worn out. "Tired," the man said. "Not broken. There's a difference and Emilio always — " He stopped again. He set the shoes down on the glass, gently, the way you'd put down a thing with a pulse. "I'm his granddaughter," Mari said. "Mari. I'm running the shop until Thursday." "Until Thursday," the man repeated. "I'm selling it. Thursday." He looked at her then, fully, for the first time, and she had the uncomfortable sense of being measured for something that wasn't clothes. "Do you have the hands?" he said. "I'm sorry?" "Emilio had the hands. Do you." She held one up without deciding to — square palm, stubby fingers, the knuckles that had never once been mistaken for a woman's hands by anybody who saw them do their work. It was a stupid thing to do, like being carded, and the man studied it and nodded once, like she'd passed a test she hadn't agreed to take. "The bench stays with the shop," he said. "Whatever he told you about the shop, the bench is the shop. I'll come back for these Friday. If they're still here." "And if they're not here Friday?" "Then I'll come back anyway," he said. "That's how it works." He paid in advance. She hadn't asked him to; she'd barely agreed to the work; but he set a coin on the glass, heavy and yellow, not a quarter, not anything, stamped with a wing and worn smooth on one side like it had spent a few centuries in a pocket. When she looked up to tell him they took cards, the bell was still swinging and he was gone. She should have chased him. She knew the price of the repair he'd ordered — she didn't even know what the repair *was*, tired-not-broken was not a service she offered — but the coin weighed four times what a quarter did, and she was three months behind on rent, and she put it in the register tray under the tens and closed the drawer and stood there with her hand on it for a while. That night she went looking for the receipt book, the carbon one, because Emilio had kept receipts for everything, for the dentist and the plumber and the mill's historical plaque donation in 1994, and if the narrow man was in the book she'd have a name. She wasn't in the book. None of them were. What she found instead, wedged behind the drawer like it had been put there by a man who assumed nobody would ever be dumb enough to clean behind it, was a ledger, canvas-bound, soft with age, and she sat down on the stool with it and did not open it for a full minute because she already understood, in the animal way you understand weather, that everything on Thursday's spreadsheet was priced wrong. *hermes — clean, light work. re-stitched the seam he ignores. no charge, he pays in something else and i hate it.* *the big one — much worn. warned him. he never listens, the big one, but his boots are honest.* She read until two in the morning, in the shop, under the one good lamp, in the smell of her grandfather. Names she half-knew from a mythology unit she'd slept through in tenth grade, all written lowercase, all treated like boiler trouble. The coin was a bee by morning. It was on the windowsill, working at nothing, warming itself in the square of sun over the sink, and the drawer was shut tight the way she'd left it. There was none. A child's sandal had more presence than this. They were woven — actually woven, vine over vine, ivy leaves gone translucent at the toe like frost on glass, still faintly green back by the heel as if the green had been leaving for years and was almost done. The laces were a milk-white that wasn't a color thread came in. They smelled like October. Mari's hands knew leather and rubber and eleven kinds of cement, and her hands reported: *nothing here we recognize, and hold it gently.* "Cobbler's girl," the woman said. "The lace. The left one. Tell me what you see, and don't be polite about it. Politeness is for churches." Mari took the shoe to the lamp. She worked laces; she had a whole drawer of tips and a wheel of thread stock, and she knew what laces did when they died. Wear was honest. It happened at the aglet, at the eyelet, wherever the lace worked — fuzzy, gradual, in the places the shoe did its living. She ran the left lace through her fingers, and halfway down, at the throat of the shoe where nothing rubbed, her thumbnail stopped. The light was bad and then it wasn't. She got the good lamp. The lace had been cut. Mid-span, in a spot where no friction had ever touched it, one clean face to the break — a blade, a single pass, someone who'd done it before. Mari stood there a while with the shoe in her hands, in her grandfather's smell, feeling the specific cold of a person who has found the one thing in the house that proves the noise outside is real. "This wasn't wear," she said. "Wear is honest. It happens where the shoe works. Nothing works at this spot — no eyelet, no rub, no heat. Somebody cut this and then frayed the ends after so it would look like a lace dying of old age." She looked up. "They did it well. In this light, in a normal shop, I'd have sold you a new lace and felt good about it." The woman was looking at the shoe the way Mari's grandfather had looked at the river in flood years: not afraid of the water, familiar with the water, but aware that it had changed. "I thought so," she said. "It's been taking the tread for years. That I understood. Everything wears. This is different. This is — " she took the shoe back and turned the cut lace end to the light with two fingers, " — field-dressing. Taking me apart in pieces while I'm still standing, and it's patient, and I can't find it." "Who? Who would — " "Things get hungry," the woman said, and her voice was quieter and worse. "And some things would rather eat than be eaten, and some things would rather eat *specifically.*" Mari was already reaching for the thread wheel. "I can stitch a locking seam over the cut. Anything else is taxidermy." She said it the way you'd say a thing you'd said many times, alone, to no one, in the dark. "Emilio understood that. He'd glue things and give them back and I'd walk out on them anyway, and we were both right. He glued a moon back on once. Glue. I still came out at night, didn't I. Beads and gum." She took the shoes back. Her hand, taking them, was not entirely steady, and she saw Mari see it, and the steadiness came back like a shade drawn down. "Can I keep this piece?" # Chapter 4 — No Name She read the ledger like a woman auditing a man who couldn't defend himself, which was the only kind of auditing she could afford. Three nights she sat under the good lamp with it, and on the fourth she found the pattern she'd been sleeping around. Between the regulars — *hermes, clean, light work; the big one, much worn, warned him; the lady with the moths, do not hurry her* — there was a customer who never got a service line. Just a notation, over and over, across fifty years: *no name. asked at the door. refused. — '76* *no name again. refused. hungry this time. — '81* *no name. emilio says no. i am getting tired of saying no. — '89* She read the last one twice. She'd never once heard her grandfather refer to himself in the third person, but there it was in the handwriting, and the handwriting had changed by then. By the last year it had gone shaky, and the entries had gone short: *No Name again. foolish. old now. afraid.* That was the whole file. Something had come to the door of this shop, hungry, for fifty years, and the man who fed gods their tread had said no, and eventually started being afraid, and then died, and left the shop to her with the ledger hidden behind a drawer like a note in a bottle. She was still holding the book open when the door made a sound it didn't usually make. The man filled the frame. That was the first fact about him, that the doorway had been waiting all these years to be the right size for somebody. The second fact was the noise he made walking — she heard every step across her floor, a dry gritty rasp, the sound of soles worn past leather into the steel of the shank. He smelled like cinnamon, which was so wrong in the shop that she noticed it before she noticed his face. He put two fingers in his mouth, took out the toothpick, and pointed it at the bench. "Emilio's girl." "Granddaughter. Mari." "Emilio's girl," he said again, at a volume calibrated for parade grounds, and put his foot up on the bench stool, presenting the high-top like a wound. She took it. The toe was gone to the canvas. The sole was worn through at the ball, through to the steel shank, which itself was scored like it had been doing the walking. These were not scuffs. Scuffs are incidents. This shoe had served. "What do you do in these?" she said, before she could stop herself. "Everything," he said. "Where they'll let me." She turned it over under the lamp the way she'd turned the ivy shoe. Honest wear, her hands said. Nothing but honest wear, front to back, wear like a biography. "I can resole them," she said. "Standard build. It'll be good work." "I don't want a resole. I want them armored. Steel through the whole outsole, whatever's in it, whatever it costs. Wars pay, little cobbler. Ask anybody." "The trade doesn't do armor," she said. "Armor's not a thing leather does. It does repair. It does care." He looked at her for a long moment, and she watched thirty years of something cross his face. "Say that again," he said quietly, which was worse than the parade volume. "The trade does care, and — " "His sentence. Thirty years I've hated that sentence." He took the shoe back gently, which she had not expected, and turned it in his own hands. "I've seen what care does on a retreat. It's not a load-bearing word." "I don't know how to armor them," Mari said. "I'm telling you flat. I don't know how, and I won't fake it and take your money." He nodded slowly, and the nod was almost — she hated this — respectful. "First honest sentence said on this bench in years, and it's *no.*" He put the shoe back on. She heard the steel touch her floor. "There's no shortage of war, girl. You think I'm starving. I'm not starving. There's a shortage of *marching.* My whole design, and it's done from chairs now, by men in slippers. I wanted soles that could take a road. This bench — " he looked around the shop, the labeled boxes, the moths' window, the crooked linoleum, " — fossil shop in a fossil town. He kept it for the walking days, your grandfather, and he was kind to what he liked and locked the door on what he didn't, and that's not courage, that's a shop." The bell rang him out. She stood at the window and watched him go up the street toward the water tower, unhurried, every step of him audible from inside the glass, until the sound of him was the sound of the street, and then gone. He left the toothpick on her counter, snapped in two, smelling of cinnamon. She threw it away and then took it back out of the trash, and she never knew why, and it's possible she still has it. Friday at 4:58, Hermes came in and didn't get to lean. She put the box on the counter and opened it. The cut lace lay there on the manila tag, *cut — not wear*. "Tell me about No Name," she said. "The mule story — " "Tell me about No Name." He didn't go still the way people go still. He went still the way rooms do. When he spoke again the voice was the same voice pitched down a floor. Concrete walls, a trickle of rust-colored water, the banks growing nothing in a strip that ran along the channel like a path. Mari noticed it before she let herself notice it: the strip was too neat. Nothing grew where something walked, and something walked here often, and things that leave a dead strip behind them are either sick or deliberate, and she couldn't see any difference from up here. It was under the mill bridge. She saw the shoes first, because everyone did. They were a museum. Scraps of sole leather stitched over scraps of sole leather, decades deep, no two pieces alike — a grey kid-leather heel she'd have sworn was from a pair of moths-embroidered slippers; a strip of woven ivy, dead-thread white, that she had last seen snapping under her own fingers; a scored steel shank from a boot like Ares's, worn past walking and walking anyway. And on the left shoe, at the heel, a piece of harness-colored outsole, and she knew it. She knew it the way you know a shelf's gap. Three boxes of a dead god's old tread, swept clean by a frightened man, and here it was, worn at the heel of a thing her grandfather had said no to for fifty years. The shop was walking around down here. She put her hand against the concrete wall. It was thin to the point of translucence at the edges, hooded in gray nothing. It moved like it was sorry for occupying the space. "We're closed on Saturdays," it said. Mari stood still on the bank. The voice wasn't a voice. It was a shopkeeper's voice, some century, some counter, the words worn smooth from re-use, and it took her a second to understand that the sentence was aimed at her like a broom. "I'm not here to buy," she said. "I'm here about a lace. You cut one. Artemis. The hunter. Left shoe, clean pass, dressed after to look like wear." "Everything must go," the thing said. She looked at Hermes and Hermes was looking at the channel floor, still as a room. "You stood at my grandfather's door," she said. "Fifty years." "Asked at the door," the thing said. "Refused." It had heard him say it, over and over, to the shop, to the ledger, to himself, and it had carried the words off like heel-pieces. "Foolish," it said, in a voice that was nearly Emilio's. "Old now. Afraid." "That's not yours," Mari said, and her voice came out lower than she meant. "Those aren't yours to wear." "No," the thing agreed, which stopped her. "None of it. You'd like this — the mule — " It stopped. Recycled. Started again in a fishmonger's bark, an oath from some other country: "Fresh this morning! As God is my witness." It looked down at its shoes, the whole museum of them. "Nothing on me is mine. You've reached the Vegas. Leave a word." Her grandfather's voicemail. It had his voicemail. She had sat in this shop last Tuesday and it had sat somewhere and *kept him*, and she could not tell, looking at it, whether the keeping was hate or the closest it had ever come to being fed by anybody. "You want a name," she said. "Not the shoes. The shoes are groceries. You want a name." The hood came up. She couldn't see a face in it and stopped trying. "You'd get it wrong," it said. A woman's voice, tired, kind, a bus stop somewhere, 1974, about love. "What does it cost?" Mari asked Hermes. "Naming something. What does it cost?" Hermes went still, the way he'd gone still over the ledger, and he didn't answer, and the not-answering had a history in it. She thought: he's watched this. He's watched somebody try this. "All sales final," the thing offered, gently. "Non-refundable." "That's not an answer either." "It comes out of you," it said, in somebody's voice, and she never found whose. "Doesn't come back.
