The hunter stood at the edge of the road in her translucent shoes, looking at the route like it was a clearing she was deciding about. "That's it? You asked, so I came." She looked down the empty street. "You have no idea how long it's been since somebody did that. Asking. It's a lost art. Everybody transacts now." "I didn't transact anything." "No," Artemis said. "You didn't. That's why I'm standing here." The god watched them both. Of the three of them it was the only one who had any business being nervous, and it was. "First come, first served," it offered. Mari took out the receipt book. Her hands, at least, knew what to do with one. She clicked the pen her grandfather had never had to click because his pens had worked, and she stood there over the carbon with the dawn coming up gray behind the mill. She had meant to find the right name. She knew, by then, that she was going to say the first true thing that came, because that was the whole trade — you worked with the foot in front of you, not the foot in the catalog. What came, when it came, surprised her anyway. "Saturday," she said. The god went very still. She wrote it on the ticket, all caps, the way shop tickets went: *SATURDAY — ONE (1) NAMING — PAID.* She tore out the original and held it out, and the god took it in two fingers like a heel-piece, like water, and read it for a long time. "Saturday," it said. First own word. Nobody's voice, nobody's century. Its own. The naming took the way cement grabs: one second it hadn't, and then it had, and there was no moment in between you could point to. The god's edges stopped being translucent — not solid, nothing showy, just *weighing what it weighed now*, a thing you'd bump into in the dark. The scraps on its shoes stopped looking like a museum and started looking like shoes. It took a step to try it. The left shoe — Emilio's heel-piece, the harness-colored one — turned a quarter inch off-square, and the step hitched. It walked a few steps up the dead route, hitching on the left every time, and turned around. "Close enough for government work," it said, in somebody's borrowed American, and that was all the complaint it ever filed, on that name, in any weather after. "Are you walking it or watching it?" Artemis asked. "Walking," Mari said. "I'll wait at the end," Hermes said, from the marker. "Somebody should be at the end." So the three of them walked the old route north out of town, past the bank and the closed mercantile, past the water tower, the god limping its quarter-inch limp, Mari keeping pace, Artemis unhurried with her eyes on the edges of everything. Nobody talked. It was four miles of orange suggestion and nobody talked, and it was the least strange strange morning of Mari's life. The kid came off the river road on a bike, fishing rod across the handlebars, early for the trout. He was maybe eleven. He saw them from thirty yards and braked so hard the bike fish-tailed. He stared at Artemis. She stood perfectly still while he did it — that reversed stillness, all her training turned inside out, the hunter holding still for the watcher. She had not been looked at like this, flat and absolute, the way kids stare at things that are true, in a very long time. "Cool shoes," the kid said. Then he rode off toward the river, standing on the pedals, and the fishing rod bobbed, and the morning closed up behind him like water. Mari looked down. At the toe of the left shoe, one woven leaf of the ivy had gone green again. Faintly. One step's worth, and no more. "Huh," said Artemis. They walked on. At the finish line, where the orange paint said what finished meant in this town, Hermes peeled a dollar off his roll and put it in Mari's jacket pocket without a word about it. "Two off the eleven," he said. "Namings are serious business. Nine to go." "I'm not done," Artemis said, at the line, not to anyone in particular. "That's not the same as saved. You can write that down if the ledger needs it." And then, unprompted, in passing, without weight, so casually that Mari almost lost it: "Thanks for the walk, Mari." She went north up the route as it left town, unhurried, watching the edges of things, and Mari did not watch her out of sight, because that would have made it a goodbye. Hermes went wherever Hermes goes. Mari and the god walked back along the route in the risen light, and the god said "Long time no see" to the water tower, and "Thank you for your business" to a gas station, and limped the whole way, and never once mentioned it. Her left sock had gone through at the heel somewhere around mile three; she could feel the road through it, direct, at the price roads charge. She'd fix her own shoes tomorrow. She was going to fix them tomorrow for the rest of her life, probably. Halfway home, cold, she rubbed the white scar on her forearm against her jacket and reached for the memory of the cement pot — the shop, the winter she was thirteen, the smell — and got the fryer first. The fryer came fast and easy, grease and the diner and the lie, and then the pot came slow, and secondhand, and somebody else's, like an entry read out of a ledger in a hand she knew. She stopped on the shoulder of Route 9 and stood there a minute, working at it. It had come out of her, and it hadn't come back. That was the price. She couldn't even say for certain what she'd lost — only that the space where it used to sit was the exact shape of the thing she'd given away, and that the god walking ahead of her, limping on a quarter-inch of her grandfather's heel, had needed it more. "Nice day for it," the god called back to her, in a stranger's voice, kindly. "Sure," said Mari, and walked on, on her ruined shoe, into town.

# Chapter 8 — Regulars Winter came in off the river and settled, and the shop kept its hours. She kept them too, opening at nine whether the door was likely to ring or not, because that was the trade and the trade was open. Her entries were in the ledger now, her hand, lowercase, plain, because that was the house style. Twardowski gave up in October. His last message said the market had softened. Hers said nothing back, and she stood holding the phone afterward in the smell of the shop, and then went back to the bench, and that was the whole of the negotiation. The landlord was down to one month behind, which felt like wealth. She'd asked Hermes in November about the big one — just asked, no message, whether he was all right, wherever he was. "I deliver," Hermes said. "I don't chase." Which wasn't an answer, and she let it not be one, the way the shop had let things not be answers for fifty years. The broken toothpick was still in the drawer. She never knew why, and it's possible she still has it. Off Route 9, the birds came back. The extension office revised the blight prognosis — cool spring, recovery in a few seasons — and the hunters quoted in the paper just said the owls were loud again since fall, no reason anyone could name, which the paper didn't print. Mari read it at the bench and put a line in the ledger under the hunter's name: *still walking.* No entry about whether she'd been there when the owl came back. There hadn't been one. You can't write down what doesn't happen to you. Saturday came on the cold days. It let itself be called that now, out loud, by name, and answered to it, and it came up from the flood channel in its museum shoes and sat by the pot-bellied stove in the back and didn't ask for anything, and the sitting was the whole visit. In January it said "warm" — nobody's voice, its own, first own word since the route — and looked startled to have done it, and Mari said "Yes," like she was confirming a repair, and wrote *saturday — sits. no charge* in the ledger, and that was the transaction. Once she offered to true up the left heel-piece, the quarter inch, Emilio's leather, her crooked inheritance on his foot. Saturday considered the offer longer than it had considered the name. "Close enough for government work," it said. The account with Hermes stood at nine dollars and one ladder. The ladder was from September, when he'd borrowed the shop's to fix the gutter above the door and called it a draw against his 1989 balance, and when she objected he'd said the debt was historical and so was the ladder, and anyway it had come back — eventually — with a rung missing, which he called patina. The lady with the moths came in October for the right strap. Mari didn't reach for the cement. She stitched while the lady watched, ankles crossed, and the lady said nothing the whole time, and this time the nothing was warm the whole way through. The window filled up that week — grey ones on the inside of the glass, in the cold, holding still like a display — and Mari got used to counting them the way you count the register. The mill god came back in May, as promised, lunch pail and all, and asked again. This time she said yes. She asked for number forty-one first. Roy Tibbets, the crank housing, the walk home, Dr. Ellis under protest; he told it slow, all the way to the waiting room, and she made the one clean pass at the mark on the last word, and the last strand let go like a thread coming through leather, easy, done, and the old man in the flannel shirt let out a breath he'd been holding, as near as she could tell, since the mill shut. "Walter Doane," he said, at the door. "Number two hundred eleven. He'd have laughed at this. That's the highest thing I can say about a morning." *l. — clean pass, may. paid in advance, years of it. — M.V.* The boots came back in November, in the first snow. Empty, on the step, laces cut clean at the mark, worn out at last and worn out right, the pail beside them, washed, empty. She stood over them a long minute in the cold with her hands in her pockets. Then she carried them in and put them on the high shelf, and she did not call it a tragedy, and that was the truth and not a comfort, and she was a little surprised at which one it was. In the fall she'd finished the sandal. Three evenings, the two-thread staggered seam, locked at every third pass, and it came out right — right the way her grandfather had meant, she thought, though he'd never said what for. [Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of mythological fiction that operates with considerable sophistication. Let me work through its strengths and weaknesses systematically. STRENGTHS: The prose voice is the story's greatest achievement. It maintains a consistent, dry, working-class register that never breaks — the shop smell, the ledger entries, the carbon receipt book — and uses this mundane texture to make the mythological intrusions genuinely uncanny rather than merely decorative. The line "She hadn't noticed him holding them, the way you don't notice a bird is holding a worm" is the kind of metaphor that earns its place: it's strange, it's precise, it tells us something about perception and predation simultaneously. Hermes's running tab, Artemis's tendons wearing out while her face keeps, the mill god's roster of three hundred and eleven names — these are characterizations that feel genuinely mythologically resonant while being entirely original. The decision to make the unnamed thing's hunger about names rather than worship is clever and thematically coherent. The ledger as structural device is excellent. Emilio's voice comes through the entries without ever appearing directly, and the shift from his handwriting to Mari's at the end is earned. The lowercase house style is a lovely touch. The dialogue is consistently strong. Hermes's mule-story deflections, Ares's parade-ground volume, the mill god's patient arithmetic — each voice is distinct and serves characterization. "Elbows are where the arms keep their regrets" is the kind of line that sounds like it could be a proverb and isn't, which is exactly right for Aldo. The naming of the unnamed god as "Saturday" is genuinely inspired — it's a day-name, it's the day shops close, it's the day between work and rest, it carries the weight of something that exists in the gaps. The receipt-book formality of the naming ceremony is perfect. WEAKNESSES: The piece occasionally tips into self-conscious cleverness. "She was twenty-eight years old and three months behind on the apartment over the shop, and a courtesy was not going to cover it, but the number he'd floated would, barely, once" — the "barely, once" construction is the kind of stylistic tic that appears several times and starts to feel like a mannerism rather than a choice. Similarly, "the anger was still there in the morning, sitting on the bench where she'd have to work around it" is a nice image but the story does this kind of personification-of-abstract-states frequently enough that it loses some force. The piece ends mid-sentence, which is either a deliberate formal choice (the sandal unfinished, the story unfinished, the work ongoing) or a generation cutoff. If deliberate, it's too cute; if accidental, it's a real flaw. Given the context, it reads as a cutoff, which is a significant structural problem for the final chapter. The Ares chapter is the weakest. His characterization — the war god wanting armor, being told the trade does care — is the most on-the-nose mythological translation in the piece. The other gods are more oblique; Ares is almost allegorical in a way that feels less earned. The price Mari pays for the naming — losing a memory of the cement pot, gaining the fryer memory instead — is the most opaque moment in the piece. The idea is interesting (naming costs something personal, something formative) but the specific mechanics are unclear enough that the emotional weight doesn't fully land. We don't know what she lost precisely, and the story acknowledges this ("she couldn't even say for certain what she'd lost") in a way that feels like it's covering for the vagueness rather than making it a feature. The mill god chapter asks Mari to cut the last strand of a god's existence, she refuses twice, then agrees in the next chapter with relatively little shown transition. The ledger entry "paid in advance, years of it" is doing a lot of work to justify this, but the transformation from refusal to assent needed more on the page. The piece is occasionally too pleased with its own rhythms. "She went upstairs angry at him and the anger was there in the morning, sitting in the shop when she came down, patient, like a customer" — this is good, but the story has several moments where it pauses to admire its own sentence construction in a way that slightly interrupts momentum. OVERALL: This is genuinely impressive work — original, consistent in voice, mythologically inventive, emotionally grounded. Its flaws are mostly those of a writer who is very good and occasionally knows it too well. The incomplete ending is a real problem. The Ares chapter is the weakest link. But the naming of Saturday, the ledger as structural spine, and the consistent shoe-as-metaphor-for-divine-wear are all genuinely excellent. # Brainstorming ## Interpreting the prompt's core mystery The prompt gives two facts I need to mechanize: **the fish died first**, and **then they spoke**. The causal link between those two facts is the spine of the whole story. Options: 1. **Their speech IS the thing that kills.** The megastructures communicate in pressure waves/infrasound scaled to their own biology — creatures maybe miles long, for whom shouting is a normal register. Every sentence ruptures swim bladders for a hundred miles. The die-offs are punctuation. First contact is metered in tons of dead sea life. 2. **The dead fish are the mouthpieces.** The aliens are chemical/organic communicators; they assemble speech through decaying biomass. Creepy, Lovecraftian, possibly too gross for the tone I'm imagining. 3. **The die-off was them tasting the ocean.** Sampling mission before speaking. Functional but less poetic. 4. **The die-offs are patterns — the deaths themselves are the message.** The waves of fish dying pulse in prime numbers, in rhythmic sequences. The kill IS the transmission. 5. **The fish deaths are an accident of arrival.** Displacement, heat, chemistry. Their speech is separate. Clean but boring — the coincidence is what makes the prompt eerie, so I want 1 and 4 braided together: their language kills, and the kill is legible. ## Where the "they spoke" twist could go (wide net) - **The whales were invited.** The structures came because of the Voyager Golden Record — the 1970s humpback whale song hurtling through interstellar space for fifty years. They came to meet the Singers. Humans were never the intended recipients. The aliens consider *cetaceans* the civilization of Earth, and humans the silent irrelevance on the shore. - **They're refugees.** The megastructures are arks fleeing something worse. Fish die-offs are them refueling. The real contact is an asylum request. Good political resonance, but dilutes the ocean-acoustic poetry. - **They're the shepherds.** The structures are whale sanctuaries from elsewhere; whales were seeded here; they came to check on a garden. Neat but too tidy. - **Human-made future echo.** The structures are ours, from downstream. Twist-y, cheap, cut. - **They came to mourn.** They heard whale song, traveled to meet the singers, and found the ocean half-empty — the singers nearly exterminated by the very species now pointing missiles at them. First contact as a murder confession. - **They address only the whales.** All human attempts at contact (radio, mathematics, nukes) are ignored; they only respond to song. This forces a unique and poignant plot: humanity must learn to speak by *borrowing another species' voice.* The Voyager hook and the grief/mourning twist can be combined: they came for the singers of the record, and their opening hail — the whale song played back, amplified beyond lethality — is what emptied the coastal waters. **Their hello killed the fish.** ## POV / character options - **Dr. Maya Reyes (or similar), marine bioacoustician.** Wrote a fringe-dismissed paper on structural grammar in humpback song. Perfect lens: she literally studies how the ocean speaks. Strong candidate. - **A fisherman/widow of the arrival.** Maximum grief resonance, but can't plausibly drive the decoding plot. - **A Deaf linguist who thinks in vibration.** Lovely resonance with a pressure-language, but risks gimmickry. - **Military sonar operator.** Thriller-shaped, limited emotional ceiling. - **A whale POV interlude.** Bold. Maybe one short passage late in the story, italicized, as a risky flourish — or better, keep it strictly human and let the whales be heard, never inhabited. - **Personal stakes for Maya:** her father, a commercial fisherman, went down with his boat the day the structures surfaced — the displacement wave. She is the one human who must translate the speech that killed her father and her town's way of life. Grief and duty in one body. ## Supporting cast (keep to 3–4 named) - **Dr. Aiko Tan / "the mentor"** — Maya's former advisor, disgraced for claiming whale song is language, now elderly and half-dismissed by the field. Vindication arc, possible dementia for pathos. - **Commander Voss, Navy liaison** — antagonist-adjacent; the countdown clock; wants to strike before understanding. Not a cartoon — he's protecting a scared species. - **Ellis, a sound engineer / archive keeper** — practical hands, light warmth, the one who digs up the Golden Record master tapes from the archive. - **A specific whale** — "Old Cricket," last carrier of a song lineage. An offscreen character with more weight than some humans. ## Tone options - **Wonder-forward (Close Encounters):** awe, light, transcendence. - **Dread-forward (Roadside Picnic):** indifference of the cosmic, humans as ants. - **Grief-forward literary (Station Eleven):** melancholy, elegiac, guilt and grace. The fish die-offs demand this register — the story is *about* an extinction, possibly several. - Best fit: grief-forward literary with wonder bleeding in at the end. This is an elegy that earns a sunrise. ## Structure / pacing for 8 chapters (~1000 words each) Rough sketch of one possible shape: 1. Arrival + die-off + Maya's summons (personal grief established). 2. Maya spots the pattern — the die-off waves are sequenced. The deaths are a signal. 3. Decoding: it's *whale song*, played back, wrong. Realization: they're not talking to us. 4. Global response — missiles move, Maya's theory ignored, then vindicated. The message partially translated: "WHY ARE THE SINGERS SO FEW?" 5. The plan: answer in song. Reconstruct the 1970s Golden Record humpback song — a song no living whale still sings. Deadline pressure. 6. The broadcast. Silence. The fish stop dying. Then the answer, and it's worse: they ask who silenced the singers. 7. The confession. Maya plays the archive — 60,000 recordings, including the sounds of harpoons and factory ships, flensing decks, the industrial audio of whaling. The structures grieve; the largest die-off yet — or the first gentle word. Their offer: "WE WILL CARRY THE SINGERS TO A SEA THAT KEEPS THEM." They offer to take the whales away. 8. Resolution: refuse or release. Bittersweet close. ## Motifs to seed through all 8 chapters - Lateral lines / hearing through the whole body. - "Loud" as a moral question — a language where every word has a cost. - The dead song no whale remembers; the archive as graveyard and seed bank. - Whale song as the only human artifact that ever actually left the neighborhood. # Reflection Let me pressure-test what's in the net. The **necro-mouthpiece fish** idea (brainstorm 2) is striking but tips the story into body horror, which fights the elegiac tone. Out. The **refugee plot** is compelling but it's a different story — political rather than acoustic — and it would crowd out the whale revelation, which is my strongest card. Out as main plot, though the structures can retain a slight ambiguity about why they travel. The **Voyager Golden Record twist** is the emotional engine. It reframes the entire premise retroactively: the megastructures didn't come for us, and everything human in the story — the navies, the committees, the panic — is misdirected noise on the aliens' side too. Symmetry: both species are shouting past each other at the beings they actually came to meet. The whale-song hail being lethal to fish solves the prompt mechanically and thematically at once: *their hello killed the fish.* Every word costs a mass die-off. That gives me a clean explanation for "first the fish started dying, then they spoke" — the dying *was* the speaking, and I can land that reveal at the end of Chapter 2, which is the right place for the prompt's second sentence to detonate. The one risk with the Voyager hook: sentimentality, and the soft-SF handwave of FTL travel chasing a 50-year-old signal. I think it's survivable — the record is a real, documented object with real whale song on it, and the emotional truth of "we sent an invitation in someone else's voice" outweighs orbital mechanics. I'll keep the aliens' biology vague and scale-focused: vast, slow, aquatic, speaking in pressure. What matters is that they are *polite monsters* — they never intended harm; they simply speak at their own scale, and learning to whisper is their character arc. The **confession chapter** (7) is where this rises or falls. Playing the whaling archive — the actual sounds of the hunt — as humanity's answer to "who silenced the singers" is devastating if I keep it restrained. No speechifying. Maya answers with tape. The risk is melodrama; the fix is understatement: report the alien response in sonar-technique language, not poetry. The subsequent die-off — but *arranged*, gentle, an elegy in their own medium — is the payoff for the "the deaths are legible" mechanic planted in Chapter 2. The **final dilemma** (they offer to take the whales to a safe ocean) is the best hard choice I've found. It inverts first-contact conventions: the aliens' generosity is a wound. Losing the whales forever to save them — or refusing and keeping them in a wounded sea we made. For an 8,000-word story, I lean toward humanity *refusing* — owning the restoration as an obligation rather than outsourcing it — and the structures responding by learning to whisper. The final image: their last message kills nothing. One sentence, softly spoken, and the fish live through it. That's the tonal destination the whole arc aims at: a conversation that began in mass death ends without costing a single life. Then they leave a listening buoy and depart, promising to return when the ocean is loud again. Epilogue beat: years later, Maya on a boat, humpbacks returning, and under the waterline, faint, an answering hum. On POV: single, tight third person on Maya. Eight chapters at 1,000 words cannot afford head-hopping. Her personal grief (father lost in the arrival wave) makes her the right translator with the right wound — she has every reason to hate the voice she must learn. But I should be careful: father-dead-on-day-one is efficient but borders on convenient. I'll complicate it slightly — his boat was found, he wasn't; ambiguous loss, unresolved. Her arc: from wanting the structures silenced to being the one who teaches them to whisper. Mentor character (the disgraced whale-song professor) earns the vindication beat in Chapter 4–5, but I'll trim the military subplot to a single pressure point (a strike deadline in the middle chapters) so it serves as clock, not plot. Structure check against the 8 × 1,000 budget: Chapters 1–2 setup and pattern-discovery; 3–4 reveal and vindication; 5–6 answer and silence; 7 confession and the offer; 8 choice and whisper. That's a clean escalation with a hook ending each chapter, one main reveal per chapter, and room for the quiet scenes the tone requires. The whale POV interlude — I'll resist it. The whales' mystery is the story's gravity; stepping inside them would deflate it. Working title to plan against: **"The Loud Ones"** or **"Whisper"** — the second is the destination. Next step: chapter-by-chapter outline with beats, reveals, and image anchors.

# Intention **Plot shape — the committed choices.** The story's spine: the megastructures came because of the Voyager Golden Record — the humpback whale song humans hurled into space in 1977 without permission. The aliens came to meet the Singers; humanity is not the addressee. Their speech is pressure at their scale, so every sentence they speak kills fish for a hundred miles — the die-offs of the prompt's first sentence are the medium of its second. The dying was the speaking. The arc: Maya discovers the pattern, identifies the source recording, watches humanity's hails go ignored, decodes the question (*why are the singers so few?*), helps answer in song, and then must answer the question beneath that one — who silenced them — with the only honest artifact we possess: the whaling archive. Hydrophone tape of harpoon cannons and dying whales, played into the deep. The structures grieve in their own medium, offer to carry the whales to a safe ocean, and humanity refuses — the restoration of the sea is an obligation we keep, not one we outsource. The ending: they learn to whisper. Their last sentence kills nothing. They leave a listening buoy and promise to return when the ocean is loud again. **Cut from the net:** the necro-mouthpiece fish (body horror fights the elegy), the refugee subplot (political pressure crowds the acoustic poetry), the human-future-echo twist (cheap), any whale POV passage (the whales' mystery is the story's gravity; inhabiting them deflates it). **Voice and character.** Tight single third-person POV on Dr. Maya Reyes, a marine bioacoustician who wrote a fringe-dismissed paper on structural grammar in whale song. Her father's fishing boat went down in the arrival wave — his boat was found, he wasn't; ambiguous loss, unresolved. She is the right translator with the right wound: she has every reason to hate the voice she must learn, and her arc runs from wanting the structures silenced to teaching them to whisper. Supporting cast kept lean: Professor Halloran, her disgraced mentor, vindicated too late to fully enjoy it; Commander Voss, the strike clock, written as a frightened protector rather than a cartoon; Ellis, the archive engineer with dry warmth. "Old Cricket," a last carrier of a dead song lineage, does more work offscreen than most humans do on it. **Tone and style.** Grief-forward literary with wonder bleeding in at the end — an elegy that earns a sunrise. Hard-SF texture through bioacoustic specificity (spectrograms, lateral lines, infrasound, playback-speed transforms) rather than technobabble: the science is how the emotion stays disciplined. Restraint as policy — the confession chapter reports the alien response in sonar-technique language, never poetry, and trusts the reader to break. Chapter breaks engineered: one reveal per chapter, each ending on a hook. **Things to avoid:** sentimentality that costs nothing; military escalation as plot fuel (Voss is a clock, not an antagonist); explaining the aliens' biology or motives beyond scale and grief; head-hopping; neat forgiveness — the structures' grace is a wound too. --- # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — The Tall Water.** One month after arrival. The structures: nine columns breaching the Pacific from the abyss, twenty miles apart, unmoving. The coastal death toll of fish — and of people, quietly, in the displacement wave. Maya at her station, doing grief by doing work: her father's boat was found weeks ago; he wasn't. Navy summons. Establish her dismissed paper, her estrangement from Halloran, the texture of a town that hates the sea now. End hook: the sonar tech plays her the water around the structures — the pressure readings aren't noise. "They're modulating." **Chapter 2 — The Pattern.** Maya works the die-off data like an animal migration — and finds sequence. The fish kills arrive in waves that pulse in patterned intervals; the geometry of the dead matches the geometry of the sound. Reveal that detonates the prompt's second sentence: the dying *is* the speaking. Their voice is pressure at their scale; every sentence costs a hundred miles of swim bladders. Then the chapter-end turn: when Maya slows the recording four hundredfold, it stops being signal and becomes — song. **Chapter 3 — The Old Song.** Identification. The song is humpback — but not any living song. Spectral match against archive recordings: the 1970 Roger Payne recording, the master that went on the Voyager Golden Record. They came for the singers. Every human hail — radio, mathematics, nukes flexed in their view — goes unanswered because we are not the addressee. Reintroduce Halloran (in from the cold, sharp, old, maybe beginning to fray) whose career said exactly this. End hook: Maya's partial decode resolves the repeated figure into a question: *where are the singers?* **Chapter 4 — Why Are the Singers So Few.** Voss and the committees; a strike posture with a date on it. Maya's decode buys her a seat and a deadline: the message isn't one question, it's an escalating worry — they've measured the ocean and heard how empty it is. Vindication beat for Halloran, played small. The committee's plan: answer in song. The problem that ends the chapter: the aliens repeat the *dead* song, the 1970 recording — but whale song culture evolves, and no living whale has sung it in decades. We can't find the addressee they're calling. We may be the only species on Earth that remembers it. **Chapter 5 — The Archive.** Ellis surfaces the Golden Record masters from a basement archive. Two candidate answers: broadcast the original tape back (perfect, and a lie — a recording of the dead) or answer with a living voice. Maya argues a changed voice is a living voice. They find Old Cricket, last carrier of a lineage adjacent to the dead song; Maya's team splices a bridge — old recording seeded into live whale song, Cricket learning fragments from the playback. The broadcast goes out. End hook: the structures go silent, and for three days nothing dies. The team can't tell if they've been heard or if the ocean is holding its breath. **Chapter 6 — The Answer.** The response — and it's worse than silence. They have understood. They speak slower now, carefully, and the new decode lands: *who silenced the singers?* They've been reading the ocean's history — the silence of centuries, the empty frequencies. Navy posture hardens; Voss's clock runs. Humanity has an answer and it cannot be spoken in mathematics. Maya, listening to the structures' grief-tones, realizes the only honest reply we possess is tape. End hook: she formally requests the whaling archive. **Chapter 7 — The Confession.** The archive: hydrophone recordings from 1950–1975 — harpoon cannons, factory ships, flensing decks, the last calls of taken whales, then near-silence. Maya plays it into the deep, the whole thing, no narration, no plea. The structures respond with the largest die-off yet — but arranged: laid out in slow, deliberate sequence, an elegy in their own medium. Then, decelerated, gentler than anything they've managed: *we will carry the singers to a sea that keeps them.* They offer to take the whales. End hook: the choice, and Maya — the one human with the most right to hate them — is asked to help answer. **Chapter 8 — Whisper.** The refusal — argued by Maya and Halloran: the whales are not ours to give or to send away; a sea can only be made whole by the species that emptied it, or the guilt just changes address. Humanity answers in Cricket's voice and its own: *they stay. We stay. We will make it loud.* The structures accept. Their final act: they compress their voice to ocean-safe scale — they learn to whisper — and their last sentence kills nothing. They leave a listening buoy in the abyss and depart, promising to return when the ocean is loud again. Epilogue beat, years on: Maya on her father's rebuilt boat, humpbacks singing their changed song, and under the waterline, faint, from very far away, a hum answering back.

Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. # How a Human Might Approach This Piece A human writer handed this prompt would likely start from an itch, not an outline. The thing that makes the prompt unsettling isn't the megastructures — it's the causal coupling: *their speaking is our dying*. A language where every word has a body count. A human would fixate on that and write the whole story from inside the discomfort of it, possibly without ever resolving the discomfort, because humans don't write to resolve; they write to look at something longer than is comfortable. Other human instincts that would shape this particular piece: - **Starting with a person, not a premise.** A human who has lost someone will write Maya's grief as uneven and inconvenient — intrusive memories at the wrong moments, numbness at the "right" ones. Grief in human writing is not an arc; it's weather. - **Under-writing the big scene.** A professional would know the confession broadcast (Chapter 7) is the trap, and would handle it sideways: cut away before the payoff, report the aliens' response in flat technical language, refuse to tell the reader what to feel. - **Leaving things unconnected.** Humans are wasteful in ways that feel real. The father's death doesn't have to rhyme with the whale die-off. Some character detail exists because the writer's uncle did that. Not everything is load-bearing. - **Doubting the premise mid-draft.** A human might realize at Chapter 4 that the strike deadline is boring, and let a torpedo actually get fired. They'd allow the story to be messier than planned, because the plan is a map, not a cage. - **Moral discomfort without a verdict.** A human would suspect their own story of preachiness (the whaling guilt) and would deliberately install an ugly counter-voice to sabotage it — someone who resents that the world mourns whales more than drowned fishermen. The plan we built is, honestly, a very good *architecture*. But it is architecture — and the risk now is executing it like an architect rather than a squatter. # Telltale LLM Approaches, and What They'd Cost Here **1. The perfect machine.** LLM fiction is suspiciously well-made: every gun fires, every setup pays off, one reveal per chapter, hooks at every ending, the epilogue mirrors the opening. This reads as craft but feels like furniture. Human stories have load-bearing accidents — scenes that shouldn't work but do, threads that dangle. Our plan specifies "one reveal per chapter, each ending on a hook," which is a Netflix adaptation outline. Chapters of equal weight with equal escalation is precisely inhuman; a human's Chapter 5 might be the quietest thing in the book. **2. Summary instead of scene.** LLMs narrate weeks in a paragraph and give every important moment two sentences. This story has eight scenes that need full embodiment — Maya's first listen to the slowed song, the confession tape playing — and an LLM will be tempted to *report* them ("For three days, the team waited") instead of rendering them. The 8×1000 budget makes this worse: the plan is dense, and compression-by-summary is the LLM's default coping mechanism. **3. Prose that performs.** "The ocean was a graveyard." "They spoke in a language older than words." "For the first time in months, Maya felt..." Chest-tightening, breath she didn't know she was holding, em-dash aphorisms delivered as profundity. LLMs also write *rhythmically samey* — every paragraph the same shape, every sentence gesturing toward the luminous. The great human stylists alternate the luminous with the flat and reportorial. Our stated intention ("restraint as policy") is correct but must survive contact with execution. **4. Safety and moral tidiness.** LLMs resolve ambiguity, soften antagonists, deliver catharsis on schedule, and make sure every character is forgivable. Note how our plan has *already* pre-softened Voss ("frightened protector, not a cartoon") and guaranteed the strike never fires. That's the safety instinct applied at the planning stage. Humans let conflict cost something. **5. Competence porn.** The protagonist is right, everyone excellent, the plan works. Maya decodes, Maya vindicates, Maya's broadcast lands. Humans let their heroines be wrong first, embarrassingly, and let the rightness arrive sideways or at personal expense. **6. Theme announcement.** We named our motifs — "loud as a moral question," whisper, the archive-as-graveyard — and named the title *Whisper*, which telegraphs the destination. LLMs salt the dish they already named. The motifs need to be enacted once, obliquely, and then trusted. # Deep-Dive Critique of the Intention & Plan **The ending is the biggest LLM fingerprint in the plan.** The Chapter 8 epilogue — "humpbacks singing their changed song, and under the waterline, faint, a hum answering back" — is the AI-poem ending: reassurance delivered as image. It converts the refusal's bittersweetness into comfort and closes every loop (structures gone, buoy listening, whales returning, hum answering). A human would either cut it, make it one flat line, or make it *uncomfortable*: the hum is ambiguous — buoy or being? Maya can't tell and the story doesn't say. Even better: the final whisper is addressed to Cricket, not to Maya, and she translates a message that was never for us. That's colder and more honest. The structures learning to whisper *for the whales' sake*, not ours, keeps their radical indifference — they still don't consider humanity the addressee, right to the end. **Chapter 8 is also over-stuffed.** Refusal speech, whisper, departure, buoy, epilogue — five closures in 1,000 words. That's an LLM compression scenario: each beat gets its tidy paragraph. A human would pick one or two and let the rest happen offstage (a news report overheard; Maya not in the room). The refusal itself risks being a beautiful speech ("the guilt just changes address" — that's an aphorism, and aphorisms are the LLM's drug). A human refusal would be *mixed and unflattering*: partly scientific self-interest, partly nationalism, partly Maya's own private selfishness, partly a shouting match or a hung vote. The noble speech and the ugly motives can coexist; only the speech is fake. **Voss has been pre-defanged.** "Clock, not antagonist" was my own smoothing move. Frictionless clocks tick but never ring. Consider: the strike *happens*, once, small — a single torpedo, one structure, and nothing occurs. No explosion, no retaliation, the structures don't even appear to notice. Scale-indifference is scarier than conflict, it gives Voss a real failure instead of a redeemed near-miss, and — here's the human move — the firing ends up *on the confession tape*. The aliens receive our violence and our apology in the same transmission, because the archive acquisition was messy and nobody sanitized it. That's the kind of accident a human writer has the nerve to keep. **Maya's competence arc is frictionless.** Her paper is dismissed → she's summoned → she decodes → she's vindicated → her plan works. Every professional beats in sequence. A human version: she announces an early decode that turns out to be wrong — publicly, embarrassingly, costing the committee's trust right when she needs it for the confession request. Her slowdown discovery shouldn't be a genius montage either; make it accidental and slightly stupid (Ellis leaning on equipment, a grad student's mistake, Maya noticing it while doing something unrelated). When asked *why* four hundredfold, she says "because they're big," and that's the whole justification. Human discovery is disproportionate to its dignity. **The father is braid-machinery as written.** Boat found, he wasn't → grief → arc of forgiveness. Setup-payoff, IKEA-grade. And the LLM failure mode for this subplot is *thematic tidiness*: her grief rhyming with the whales' grief, her reconciliation arriving with the structures' whisper. Fixes: (a) make their last contact a fight — about her dismissed paper, about her wasting her life on "fish songs" while his industry dies — so the aliens' arrival vindicates her and kills him in the same gesture, contaminating her grief with guilt and a horror of her own vindication; (b) let her be unambiguously petty at least once — a scene where she drafts a false translation, something that would make the structures leave, and doesn't send it, and no one ever knows; (c) refuse resolution. He's never found. She never gets to make peace. The LLM instinct is to close this wound; the human one is to let it scar. **Missing: the un-mourned.** The plan mourns fish and whales and Maya's father. It never notices that a whole town's people died in the arrival wave and the world's grief went to the *ocean* — which is both the prompt's strangeness and a real human resentment. A deckhand who survived her father's boat, who blames her (she was called to the station; maybe her father went out *toward* the wave looking for news of her), who spits at the committees mourning "a bunch of fish" while his crewmates got a paragraph on page six. This character is the story's ballast against its own piety. Without him, the whaling-guilt material curdles into a lecture — exactly the moral-safety failure. **Halloran is a function, not a person.** "Vindicated too late to fully enjoy it" is a summary of a character. Human options: his dismissal was partly deserved (a fudged dataset in the 90s), so vindication is contaminated; he's dying and the aliens' answer may not come in his lifetime, giving "answer soon" a small, personal clock the LLM plan never has; he's cruel to the committee that mocked him and not entirely wrong to be. **The whales have no agency in the plan.** They're objects — the addressee, the gift, the symbol. Cricket is equipment ("learning fragments from the playback"). A human would let Cricket refuse — swim away for a week, ignore the bridge-song, make the humans confront that their rescue plan is one more instrumentalization. The whales' non-cooperation would be the story's quiet joke and its honest question. **The confession scene is pre-written as a solemn montage.** "No narration, no plea" is the right instinct, but the LLM execution will be a stately procession of harpoon sounds and stunned faces. Human texture for the archive: it's banal in places — someone coughs, a sailor laughs during a kill, radio chatter about lunch, a man singing. The playback machine breaks and they broadcast a partially corrupted tape. The aliens' response should be *interpretively contested*: Maya calls the great die-off an elegy; a colleague calls it disgust or rage; the story never adjudicates. The LLM will adjudicate. **Alien benevolence arrives too completely.** They come, they ask, they grieve, they offer, they accept, they whisper, they leave a gift. That's a therapeutic arc — every emotional need met. The darkest ambiguity worth preserving: *do they forgive us?* The plan implies yes. A human would leave it unanswered, or answered only for the whales. **Prose-level anticipations to ban preemptively:** "the ocean had never been so quiet"; "a language older than words"; "for the first time, she understood"; anything-tightening-in-her-chest; the breath she didn't know she was holding; symmetric sentence triads; a metaphor in every paragraph. This plan, executed on autopilot, produces all of them. # Brainstorming: Making It More Human - **The survivor.** Add her father's deckhand — alive, angry, inconvenient. He resents whale-mourning and scientist-vindication both. He never gets a redemption beat. He's wrong about some things and right about others and the story leaves him unresolved. - **The fight as last contact.** Maya's final conversation with her father was an argument about her career. Voicemail she can't delete. Her grief arrives with guilt and a shameful flicker of vindication. - **The secret draft.** One scene where she writes a false translation designed to make them leave, and deletes it, and no one ever knows. Interiority that is not noble. - **The accidental discovery.** The four-hundredfold slowdown found by equipment misuse or lunch on the console. Justification: "because they're big." - **The public error.** An early decode that's wrong, humiliating her before the committee, so her later authority is paid for, not granted. - **The torpedo that lands in the apology.** Voss fires once; nothing happens; the firing is inadvertently on the confession tape; the aliens hear our violence and our confession as one document. Keep the mess. - **Cricket's refusal.** The whales don't cooperate. The rescue plan is briefly stalled by the whales' own indifference to being rescued. - **Contaminated vindication.** Halloran's old fudged dataset; his cruelty to former colleagues; or his dying on a clock that the aliens don't know or care about. - **Banal archive texture.** The whaling tapes include coughs, laughter, singing, lunch chatter. The machine breaks. The broadcast is corrupted and they send it anyway. - **Unadjudicated response.** Elegy or disgust — Maya and a colleague disagree, the story doesn't referee. - **The cold ending.** Final whisper addressed to Cricket, not humanity. Maya translates a message not meant for her. Or: the epilogue hum is ambiguous forever. Cut "the ocean is loud again" reassurance. - **The un-mourned town.** Church signs, a fish market selling nothing, kids swimming off a pier over dead water, laminated government notices. The neighborhood, not the world. - **Chapter-shape variance.** One chapter mostly data-logs and transcripts; one mostly dialogue; one a single quiet scene (Maya on the found boat, doing nothing); only some chapters end on hooks. Deliberately uneven weights. - **Flat-sentence quota.** For every luminous paragraph, two reportorial ones. Let spectrograms be spectrograms. Trust the reader with numbers. - **One thread left unresolved on purpose.** Pick one: why nine structures; whether they took anything when they left; whether the fish sampling was accidental. Never explain it. The plan's architecture is sound and none of these require demolishing it — they require letting people be unlovely, letting mess stand, and refusing to hand the reader their feelings back, ironed.

# Intention **The committed story.** Nine megastructures rose from the abyss a month ago because of the Voyager Golden Record — because in 1977 humans hurled humpback whale song into interstellar space without asking the singers. The structures came for the whales; humanity is not the addressee and never becomes one, not even at the end. Their speech is pressure at their scale, so their hello emptied the coastal waters: **the fish died because the aliens were talking.** The dying was the speaking. Maya Reyes, a marine bioacoustician whose whale-song-grammar paper got her quietly exiled from her field, decodes this, watches humanity's hails go ignored, answers in song, and then faces the question beneath the question — *who silenced the singers?* — which can only be answered with tape: the hydrophone archive of the industrial hunt, harpoon cannons and all. The structures grieve in their own medium (a great, deliberate die-off whose meaning Maya and a colleague will contest and the story will never referee), offer to carry the whales to a safe ocean, and are refused — by a hung committee and a woman with mixed, unlovely motives, not a noble speech. They accept. They learn to whisper. Their last sentence kills nothing, and it is addressed to a whale, not to us. They leave a listening buoy in the deep and depart. Whether they forgive humanity is never answered. **What is cut.** Necro-mouthpiece fish; refugee politics; human-future-echo twists; whale POV passages; a redeemed Voss; any resolution of Maya's father's death; any ending where the structures' grace and humanity's grief are exchanged and both closed. **Humanity commitments, itemized.** (1) Maya's last contact with her father was a fight — his voicemail still on her phone, undeletable; her grief is contaminated by a shameful flicker of vindication, because their arrival killed him and proved her right in the same gesture. He is never found. (2) Her discovery is accidental — the four-hundredfold slowdown happens because of equipment misuse, and her justification, when challenged, is "because they're big." (3) She is publicly wrong first: a confident early decode collapses in front of the committee, so her later authority is paid for, not granted. (4) In one scene she drafts a false translation designed to make the structures leave, deletes it, and no one ever knows. (5) Voss fires once — a single torpedo, no effect, the structures don't appear to notice — and the firing ends up, unsanitized, on the confession tape, so the aliens receive our violence and our apology as one document. Keep the mess. (6) Denny, her father's surviving deckhand, blames her (her father went out toward the wave looking for news of her), resents a world that mourns fish and whales more loudly than drowned fishermen, and never gets a redemption beat. He is wrong about some things and right about others and stays unresolved. (7) Halloran's vindication is sour — there was a fudged dataset in the nineties, his enemies weren't wrong about everything, and he is dying on a personal clock the aliens neither know nor care about. (8) Cricket, the last carrier of the old song lineage, refuses to cooperate for a week and has to be waited for; the whales are the only party in the story with clean agency. (9) The archive is banal in places — coughs, laughter, lunch chatter on the kill ships — and the playback tape is partially corrupted and gets broadcast anyway. (10) Why nine structures is never explained. **Voice, tone, style.** Tight single third-person on Maya throughout. Grief-forward literary with wonder arriving late and understated. Hard texture through real bioacoustics — spectrograms, lateral lines, playback-speed transforms, actual numbers — trusting the reader with data instead of stroking them with lyricism. **Prose rules:** for every luminous paragraph, two reportorial ones; the big scenes (the confession broadcast, the whisper) are handled sideways or in flat technical register — no stately montages, no stunned faces, no aphorism climaxes, nothing tightening in anyone's chest. Chapter shapes deliberately uneven: one chapter runs on logs and transcripts, one is a single quiet scene, only some chapters end on hooks. No thematic announcements — "loud" as a moral question is enacted once, obliquely, and then trusted. The title is **The Loud Ones** (the aliens' own eventual designation for us is a possible late beat); *Whisper* telegraphs the destination and is rejected. **To avoid at all costs:** summary in place of scene; equal chapter weights; every gun firing on schedule; catharsis delivered to the reader pre-ironed; aliens whose benevolence arrives complete and therapeutic; the ocean described as a graveyard; "a language older than words." --- # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — The Tall Water.** Texture chapter, no reveals. One month after arrival: the nine columns, the dead water, the town gone wrong — laminated notices, a fish market selling nothing, church signs. Maya doing grief as paperwork; her father's boat found, he wasn't; the fight voicemail established without explaining its content yet. Navy summons, delivered by a corporal who won't meet her eye. Denny outside the station — first cold exchange, blame planted without being underlined. End: a sonar tech shows her the pressure readings around the structures. "They're modulating." **Chapter 2 — The Pattern.** Maya works the die-off data like migration math and finds sequence — the fish kills pulse in patterned intervals; the geometry of the dead matches the geometry of the sound. The reveal that detonates the prompt: the dying *is* the speaking; every sentence costs a hundred miles of swim bladders. The slowdown happens by accident — Ellis's coffee, a leaned-on console — and Maya's justification for the four-hundredfold factor is "because they're big." At chapter's end the slowed recording stops being signal and becomes song. No cliffhanger dressing; end on her sitting alone with the headphones, listening. **Chapter 3 — The Old Song.** Identification. Humpback — but no living song. Spectral match to the 1970 Payne master, the recording that rode Voyager. They came for the singers; we were never the addressee; every human hail has been shouting past them. Halloran arrives from the cold — brilliant, cruel about old enemies, dying, and carrying the fudged-dataset history that keeps his vindication from being clean. Quiet scene weight; this chapter is mostly two people and a spectrogram. End: the repeated figure in the signal might resolve to a question. **Chapter 4 — Why Are the Singers So Few.** Committee chapter, transcript-heavy. Maya presents a confident decode ("they're counting our ships") that collapses under Halloran's audit — public, humiliating. Then the corrected decode lands: *why are the singers so few?* They've measured the ocean and heard how empty it is. Voss gets his clock: a strike posture with a date. The plan: answer in song. The problem that ends the chapter — the structures repeat the *dead* song, and no living whale has sung it in decades. We may be the only species on Earth that still remembers it. **Chapter 5 — The Archive.** Ellis digs the Golden Record masters out of a basement; the banality of the archive boxes against what's on them. They find Cricket — last carrier of an adjacent lineage — and Cricket refuses: swims off, ignores the playback rig for a week, forces the humans to confront that their rescue plan is one more instrumentalization. They wait. The bridge-song gets built: old recording seeded into live voice, Cricket learning it on Cricket's own schedule. Maya's secret scene: the false translation drafted and deleted, unwitnessed. Broadcast goes out. End flat: the structures go silent, nothing dies for three days, and no one can tell if that's being heard or being ignored. **Chapter 6 — The Answer.** The response, spoken slower, carefully: *who silenced the singers?* They've read the ocean's history in its silences. Somewhere in this chapter the torpedo fires — once, ordered in the panic after the question lands, no effect, the structures don't seem to notice, and it is buried in the record. The committee fragments; Denny gets his scene here or in 5 — his resentment given full voice, unrefereed. Maya, listening to the structures' grief-tones, requests the whaling archive. End on the requisition form, not a speech. **Chapter 7 — The Confession.** The archive is mundane and human — radio chatter about lunch, a man singing, a cough — and horrifying, and the tape is partially corrupted and they send it anyway, and nobody sanitizes the torpedo sounds out of it, possibly nobody notices. Maya plays it into the deep: the whole thing, no narration, no plea. Rendered sideways — technical register, what the hydrophones did, not what anyone's face did. The structures answer with the largest die-off yet, but arranged, slow, deliberate: Maya calls it an elegy; a colleague calls it disgust; the story doesn't referee. Then, decelerated, gentler than anything they've managed: *we will carry the singers to a sea that keeps them.* **Chapter 8 — The Loud Ones.** The refusal — hung vote, ugly argument, mixed motives: nationalism, scientific self-interest, Maya's own private selfishness, Halloran's one clean statement. No noble speech; the noble line is said badly by the wrong person and lands anyway. The answer goes out in Cricket's voice: *they stay. We stay.* The structures accept. Their final act: a voice compressed to ocean-safe scale, one sentence, and this time nothing dies — and the sentence is addressed to Cricket. Maya translates a message that was never meant for her, and does not fully give it to us. They leave the buoy and go. Epilogue, kept flat and short: a season later, Maya on her father's rebuilt boat, the water loud again in the ordinary way — and no confirming hum from the deep. Whether they forgive us, whether they're even still listening, whether her father is anywhere: unresolved, on purpose.

# Dr. Maya Reyes **Background.** Forty-one. Grew up in Puerto Montt-tier nowhere — let's say a Pacific Northwest harbor town, Bellhaven (fictional), where her father Emilio Reyes ran a sixty-foot trawler, the *Perla*, crewed by family and neighbors for three generations. Her mother left when Maya was nine ("went to Reno" was the family euphemism; Maya has never said the word *divorce* out loud). She paid for her PhD by counting fish for the same canneries her father sold to, which they used to joke about — the joke stopped being funny the year her dissertation data contributed to a catch-quota ruling that cost the fleet money. The fight about "fish songs": at her father's retirement dinner in 2019, after the whales were already mostly gone from the grounds he fished, she told him his industry had helped empty the water he was mourning. He called her a tourist with a microphone. Her paper — "Recursive Structural Patterns in North Pacific Humpback Vocalization Across Song Cycles" — was rejected by three journals with the word *anthropomorphism* in at least one reviewer comment, and then published in a minor journal and cited four times, twice by herself. She's spent the last six years doing coral-bleaching acoustics for a federal lab, which she privately calls "listening to a hospital." **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Processes grief through logistics — when her father went missing she alphabetized the Coast Guard incident forms. Listens to recordings at dinner, has opinions about spectrogram color scales (jet is for children; grayscale is honest). Will not delete the voicemail from her father's last night — two minutes of him starting and stopping sentences — and also cannot listen to it; she knows the number of seconds (1:47) the way other people know a scar's shape. Flawed in the ways the story needs: capable of petty score-keeping against colleagues; prone to forming contempt quickly and revising it slowly; secretive about her work until it's bulletproof, then oversells it (the Chapter 4 collapse). The false translation in Chapter 5 comes easily to her, and that ease frightens her more than the act does. She gives money to a whale stranding network and once, drunk, told a colleague that if the structures left and took the whales she'd consider it a fair trade — the colleague never spoke to her the same way again. **Physicality.** Compact, sea-fit in the specific way of someone who spent childhood hauling nets, not gym-built. A habit of standing with her weight on her heels, hands in pockets, chin down — she looks like she's waiting for bad news and has learned to receive it standing. Chews pen caps to ruin. When she's listening — really listening — her eyes go unfocused and her breathing audibly slows; Ellis calls it "going underwater." **Motives, allegiances, relationships.** Her core want, underneath everything: to have been *right* in a way her father would have had to acknowledge — and the horror of getting exactly that, delivered by the thing that killed him. Allegiance-wise she's loyal to data over people, which costs her; the only two people she reliably protects are Halloran (out of debt) and, strangely, Denny (out of guilt). She resents the committees, resents the Navy's money, resents Halloran a little for being right first. Her relationship to the structures is the story's real arc: she starts wanting them gone and ends as the only human who can translate them — and keeps translating, privately, after the committees stop asking, out of something she won't name. **Voice.** > *Internal, on the modulating pressure readings:* "That's not a machine. Machines don't hesitate." > *To the committee, when challenged on the four-hundredfold transform:* "Because they're big. That's it. That's the whole argument. You want a better one, fund a better one." --- # Professor Edmund Halloran **Background.** Seventy-eight. Career made in the seventies doing the foundational work on humpback song exchange that the whole field built on — and then spent it: in 1994, a paper of his claimed a grammar-count in humpback song that no one could replicate, and it emerged two of the recording sessions were partially fabricated, stitched from two different populations to fill a gap where a hydrophone failed. He never denied it cleanly; his defense — "the data was true, the tape was damaged" — became a cautionary punchline. Institutional death followed: Grant money gone by 1997, emeritus status by 2002, the "Whales Don't Talk" panel at the 2003 conference where a moderator introduced his work with air quotes. He kept publishing in a journal he edited from a mail drop. Diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis in the year the story opens — three years median survival; he does not tell Maya until Chapter 4. Taught Maya her first field methods course in 2004; wrote the one peer review (unsigned, but she knows) that praised her rejected paper for "asking the only question worth asking." **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Vindictive memory — he can name, with dates, every colleague who was polite at his funeral-of-a-career, and is not gracious about it now that he's right. Carries a Sony analog recorder everywhere because "digital forgives you; analog doesn't." Smokes, badly hiding it from his own doctors, and is genuinely rude to people who remind him of the diagnosis. Idiosyncrasy: he refuses to say "whale song" anymore — says "whale speech" — which is a small, stubborn act of vindication that embarrasses Maya. A cruel flaw the story keeps: he sabotaged a rival's tenure case in 1989, before his own fall, purely from envy; he has never regretted it. His kindness is real but narrow — he's gentle with Maya, gentle with students, merciless to peers. **Physicality.** Big frame collapsed inward; sits like a coat on a chair. Voice is the thing — a ruined baritone, gasping on long sentences and finishing them anyway, with precise diction on the words that matter. His hands are still young, elegant around a pen, and he conducts when listening to tape. **Motives, allegiances, relationships.** His motive is *time*: he wants the answer to arrive before he does. This gives Chapter 7 a private clock no one at the committee knows about — he sits through the confession broadcast knowing the structures may never speak again before he stops being able to hear anything. Allegiance: to Maya, who he regards as the field's apology to him. To the whales, in the unembarrassed way of a man who spent fifty years listening. His relationship to his own disgrace is complicated — he'll admit the 1994 tape was fudged if Maya presses, but only at 2 a.m., only once. **Voice.** > *At the committee, to a former colleague:* "You air-quoted me in 2003, Gerald. I have the program. Write it down — the old man was right." > *Internal, on the structures' question:* "Fifty years I asked them in my own tongue. Somebody finally asked in theirs." --- # Commander Dan Voss **Background.** Forty-eight, Navy career officer, ASW — anti-submarine warfare — background, which means his entire professional life was built on the premise that *noises in the ocean are threats until proven otherwise.* The son of a Vietnamese-refugee mother and a shipyard electrician; Annapolis via a hardship nomination; spent a decade tracking diesel boats in the Pacific. A family detail that shapes him: his mother crossed the Pacific in a boat when she was eight, and he grew up on the story of lights on the horizon — from below, every large vessel is either refuge or catastrophe, and you don't know which until it's too late. Widower — wife died of cancer three years ago, teenaged daughter lives with his sister. He volunteered for the megastructure task force because he was already hollowed out and the mission didn't scare him the way it scared everyone else. **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Courtly, precise, old-fashioned formal with civilians (calls Maya "Doctor" every time, which she notices, because almost no one does). Keeps a paper logbook against regulations because he doesn't trust the servers with something this big. Flaw: he *needs* the structures to be a threat, because a threat is a thing his thirty years of training can address, and grief and confusion are not. He orders the torpedo strike in Chapter 6 not as a monster but as a man who watched the structures' question unravel every committee and thought: we should at least know if it can be hurt. Afterward, when nothing happens — no counterstrike, no acknowledgment, no change in modulation whatsoever — he is the one who says, quietly, into the room: "They didn't even flinch." And it's worse for him than a retaliation would have been. He owns the failure; he asks, in Chapter 8, for it to be on the record. That's the character: a man whose decency arrives late and through failure. **Physicality.** Taller than his voice suggests; a stillness that reads as calm until you realize he's coiled. Small habit: he takes off his wedding ring and turns it when making decisions. Sits with his back to walls, scans rooms, once thanked Maya for holding a door "for the watch." **Motives, allegiances, relationships.** Motive: protect the one thing he has left to protect — a coastline of people — when every institution he trusts is guessing. Allegiance to the Navy is genuine but cracking; his real act of loyalty in the story is to the *record*: he refuses to let the torpedo be buried and doesn't understand, at first, that his honesty is what accidentally delivers the violence into the confession tape. Relationship to Maya: mutual grudging professional respect; she distrusts his certainty, he distrusts her certainty, and both are right. **Voice.** > *Justifying the strike posture:* "Doctor, I've spent thirty years being laughed at for assuming the worst. I've never once been promoted for assuming the best." > *After the torpedo, to Maya, low, off the record:* "My whole career was listening for things under the water that wanted to hurt us. Turns out the first thing that actually came — didn't even know we fired." --- # Ellis Okafor **Background.** Thirty-four, sound engineer/archivist — the one who can make anything work. Grew up in Lagos and Croydon, learned audio doing grime production in a bedroom studio with a cracked copy of a DAW, then got a physics degree nobody expected, then an archive job nobody understood, then a cleared federal contract nobody could staff because it required someone who could *both* rebuild 1970s tape decks *and* write machine code for modern analysis tools. He is, functionally, irreplaceable, and knows it, and covers it with jokes. The coffee-on-the-console incident in Chapter 2 — his — is the accident that finds the four-hundredfold transform, and he spends the rest of the story half-ashamed, half-inflated about it. ("I discovered first contact." "You spilled a latte, Ellis.") **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Sings under his breath while calibrating — the same three songs, badly, so everyone in the lab can tell what he's working on by the tune. Names the equipment (the analysis rig is "Brenda"). Sends his mother in Lagos voice notes of whale recordings with commentary like a sports announcer. Flaws: procrastinates on documentation, hoards the good cables, and has a showman's weakness — in Chapter 7 he's the one who wants to *fix* the corrupted confession tape before broadcasting, and Maya has to argue him out of scrubbing it clean; his instinct to perfect everything nearly launders the evidence. Earbuds in one ear only — "I keep one for the room." Talks with his hands when explaining signal processing, physically drawing the waveforms in the air, which makes civilians think he's dancing. **Motives, allegiances, relationships.** Motive: he is the only character whose motive is pure craft — he wants to *hear them properly* before anyone blows anything up, and he treats the structures' signal with the reverence of an engineer meeting a superior engineer. Allegiance to Maya, earned early when she defended his accident against the committee's anger. He's the story's warmth and its comic relief, but the plan keeps him from being comic relief *about* the material — his jokes are about cables, budgets, and Brenda, never about the dead water. **Voice.** > *On the corrupted tape, Chapter 7:* "Forty seconds is gone, Doc. I can interpolate it, it'll sound whole. It'll sound better than it is." > *To Maya, quietly, mid-story:* "You talk about Cricket like she's a person who owes us an answer. She doesn't owe us the time of day. We're the ones who've been recording her relatives since 1970 without asking." --- # Denny Kowalcik **Background.** Fifty-five. Deckhand on the *Perla* for twenty-two years — but that undersells it; he was the *Perla*'s other half, the man Emilio yelled at most and trusted completely. Second-generation Polish-American fisherman, Bellhaven born, has never been farther inland than a wedding in Spokane. Survived the arrival wave because he was on the dock arguing with a fuel supplier when it hit; his crewmates — three of them, men he'd known for decades — went out with Emilio toward the wave. He was the one who told Maya that her father had gone out *looking for her* — the station was on the water side, and when the displacement came, Emilio had turned the *Perla* toward where her lab was. He tells her anyway, because he's constitutionally incapable of a kind lie, and resents her for making him the messenger. **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Fixes things — the story's rule is that Denny is always holding a tool or a part when he speaks. Maintains the *Perla*'s recovered hull in the boatyard out of pure stubbornness, repainting a boat that will never fish again. The story lets both stand. **Physicality.** Big forearms, bad knee, moves like a man on a deck in any room, braced against an invisible swell. Fisherman's squint even indoors. He cannot cry in front of people — instead his voice goes flat and formal, which is worse. **Motives, allegiances, relationships.** Motive: somebody has to be held responsible, and he'll take an alien over a coincidence, because a coincidence means his friends died for nothing. Voice: she has none in dialogue, and that's the point — but the bridge-song itself, when she finally takes it up, is described in technical register, and the last line of the story's broadcast archive is the notation: *HP-NP-114, song acquisition, 04:12, complete transmission received.*
