# Chapter 1 — The Tall Water The boat came back on a Tuesday. Her father did not. Maya had the thought in that order, and corrected it, and then stopped correcting it, because the fact was the Coast Guard had found the *Perla* forty miles out, hull intact, running lights on, and had not found Emilio Reyes or the three men who were on it with him. That was five weeks ago. The boat sat now in Kessler's yard on jack stands, tarped to the gunwales, and Maya drove past it twice a week on her way to the station because the road went that way and she had stopped taking the long way around. The long way around felt like mercy, and she didn't trust it. One month since the structures came up. Nine of them, in a line across the abyssal plain west of the coast, twenty miles apart each, and the Navy's numbers on them had leaked to the internet within nine days: two hundred meters wide at the top, tapering, going down past the six-kilometer mark where the sonar stopped pretending. They did not move. They did not light up. They had no visible seams. The water around them was warm by four degrees and dead in a way the word *dead* was not really built for. Because first the fish had started dying. That was in all the reports. She had helped write some of them. The die-off came in waves — a hundred miles of sardines floating belly-up one week, then the bottom feeders, then things nobody ate, things with scientific names and no common ones. Bellhaven's fish market had been open every day since, selling nothing. There was a laminated notice on the door, from the county health office, about water contact, and beneath it someone had taped a hand-lettered sign: CLOSED UNTIL THE OCEAN FIXES ITSELF. Below that, smaller: WE ARE OPEN. It was not clear which sign was newer. Maya's days had a shape to them now, and the shape was paperwork. She was the federal lab's acoustics lead, which since the arrival meant: sample the water, log the water, write up the water, attend the calls about the water. She alphabetized things. In the first week, when the Coast Guard forms had come in — *incident, incident, incident, no next of kin action required, next of kin action required* — she had alphabetized those too, and had noticed herself doing it, and had kept doing it. Her phone held a voicemail from her father, dated the night before the structures surfaced. 1:47 long. She had not played it in five weeks. She knew its length the way she knew the layout of her own kitchen, without ever having to go in there. That morning there was a Navy corporal waiting at the station door when she came in. Young, rain-dark on one shoulder, holding a folder against his chest like a hymnal. "Dr. Reyes?" He said it twice. "Dr. Reyes." "I'm Reyes." He held out the folder without extending it fully, so she had to step to him. "You're requested at Whidbey. Day after tomorrow. It's — there's a liaison number inside." "Requested by who?" "Ma'am, it's all in the folder." He looked at her collar, her chin, the door frame. Anywhere but her eyes. He'd been told who she was, she figured, and what had happened to her family, and somebody had decided that not looking at her was the respectful way to carry it. She signed his clipboard to let him go. Inside, the folder was mostly boilerplate: a tasking order, a command letterhead she didn't recognize, a memo listing her clearance status and, stapled behind everything else, a printout of her 2019 paper — the one nobody had cited. Somebody had highlighted two paragraphs. She read them standing up, her wet coat still on, and felt nothing she could name, and drove home early for no reason she wrote down. Denny was in the yard when she pulled in. He was always in the yard now. He'd taken over the maintenance of his sister's pickup, the fence, anything with parts. Today he had the weed trimmer apart on a tarp, its guts laid out in rows, and he was kneeling among them with a socket wrench he didn't appear to need. Fifty-five years old, bad knee, forearms like dock line. He'd taught her to splice when she was eight. He had not looked directly at her since the funeral-that-wasn't, because there had been no body and no funeral, just a lunch at the Polish hall with too much food and nobody able to say *memorial* out loud. "Denny." "Maya." Flat. Formal. His voice went like that now — stripped down, the whole Bellhaven polish gone out of it. He turned a bolt a quarter turn it didn't need. "They finally want you. I saw the car." "Day after tomorrow." "Good," he said, and it didn't sound like good, it sounded like a word occupying the space where a sentence should go. He was the one who'd told her about the fuel and the minutes — that her father had turned the *Perla* out of the harbor and *toward* the wave, toward the water side, toward where the station was, where she was. Denny had been on the dock. He'd said it once and never again, and they'd both been careful since then, walking around that fact like a hatch in the floor. "My mom's rosary's in the church box," he said to the tarp. "If you want it for the trip." She didn't know what the rosary had to do with anything. She said thank you. He nodded at his parts and she went inside. At Whidbey, two days later, they put her in a room with bad coffee and a sonar technician named Okafor who had been briefed on her paper and wanted to skip the briefing. He was young, half-sitting on a rolling chair, one earbud in. "Doctor. Okay. So. Everybody wants to know what they are. What they're made of, where they're from. I'm not the guy for that. I'm the guy for the sound." He pulled up a screen. "Everybody also says they're silent. They're not silent. The whole government has decided they're silent because they're not talking to us, on our frequencies, in our formats. But I've had hydrophones on column four for twenty-three days, and I want to show you what the water's doing." The screen filled with pressure readings. Blue water, and through it, low and repeating, a long slow argument of lines. Maya put down the coffee. She leaned in and heard herself breathe the way she breathed when a recording started to matter — Ellis would have said she was going underwater. "That's not noise," she said. "No," Ellis agreed. "That's not noise. They're modulating."
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] Chapter 1 of "The Loud Water" (or "The Tall Water" as titled here) is a remarkably controlled piece of opening fiction. Let me assess it across the relevant dimensions. **Craft and Prose Quality** The prose is disciplined in exactly the way the plan demands: reportorial paragraphs dominate, with lyrical moments arriving sparingly and earning their place. The opening — "The boat came back on a Tuesday. Her father did not." — is a clean, devastating inversion that avoids sentimentality while landing hard. The self-correction that follows ("Maya had the thought in that order, and corrected it, and then stopped correcting it") is psychologically precise and characterizes Maya immediately without telling us she's a scientist who processes grief through logic. The description of the fish market with its layered signs is excellent texture work — specific, observed, slightly absurd in the way real grief-adjacent bureaucracy is. "CLOSED UNTIL THE OCEAN FIXES ITSELF" followed by "WE ARE OPEN" is the kind of detail that earns its place without announcing itself. The voicemail detail — "1:47 long. She had not played it in five weeks. She knew its length the way she knew the layout of her own kitchen, without ever having to go in there" — is the chapter's best metaphor. It's precise, domestic, and avoids the trap of making grief luminous. The kitchen comparison is slightly imperfect (you don't usually know your kitchen's layout without going in there; you know it *because* you go in there), but the emotional logic holds and the slight wrongness actually serves the dissociation. **Character Work** Maya is established with economy and accuracy to her profile. The alphabetizing of Coast Guard forms, the wet coat she doesn't remove, the "felt nothing she could name" — these are behavioral rather than declarative. The plan called for her grief to be contaminated by vindication, and while that's not yet explicit (appropriately for Chapter 1), the highlighted paragraphs of her paper create the right seed. Denny is handled with particular skill. The "flat and formal" voice, the unnecessary quarter-turn of the bolt, the rosary non-sequitur — these are all behaviorally specific. The hatch-in-the-floor metaphor for the fact of Emilio turning toward Maya is earned and not overworked. The plan's note that Denny is "always holding a tool or a part when he speaks" is faithfully executed. Ellis is introduced efficiently — the half-sitting posture, one earbud in, wanting to skip the briefing — and his voice is distinct from Maya's without being caricatured. **Following the Plan** The chapter hits its marks: the structures established, the dead water, the town's wrongness (laminated notices, fish market), Maya's grief as paperwork, the voicemail established without content, the Navy summons, Denny's cold exchange with blame planted, and the chapter ending on "They're modulating." # Chapter 2 — The Pattern The Navy wanted answers about the structures. Maya found herself unable to care about the structures. What she had, on the drive back from Whidbey, was a screen full of pressure lines and a fifteen-year-old habit, and the habit won. Before the arrival she had spent her whole career treating animal movement like data, because that's what it was. Migration was math. Die-offs were math too — you plotted extent against tide and temperature and you got a smear, noise, the world being messy the way the world is. So on the third night, unable to sleep, she pulled the fish kill records — state surveys, stranding network logs, the canneries' own complaint filings, which nobody had thought to include and which were the best dataset of the four — and plotted them the way she'd once plotted gray whale strandings, and waited for the smear. She did not get a smear. The kills were rings. She saw it by 2 a.m., cleaned up by 4: each die-off event, when you mapped extent against time, arrived as an expanding ring centered on one of the nine columns, opening outward over four to nine hours, at a speed that made no sense for current or toxin or temperature — and perfect sense, if you wrote the number down, for pressure. Sound in the deep moves at about 1.5 kilometers a second. The rings moved slower, because they were being written by dying fish, not by water. But every ring had a birth, and every birth coincided with an utterance from a column. Modulation, then death, then the ring. She pulled the necropsy summaries next. Barotrauma. Swim bladders ruptured, hemorrhage, gas emboli in the tissue of things that had no business having gas in the tissue. The veterinary pathologist who'd signed the reports had used the phrase *consistent with acute pressure event* and then, in a footnote, apparently unwilling to leave it alone: *unprecedented in scale.* The utterance logs went back twenty-three days. Ellis had been keeping them without being asked, because he was the kind of man who kept logs nobody asked for. Every vocalization had a duration and an amplitude. Every ring had an area. She plotted one against the other, all 200-plus events, and the points fell along a line so clean she sat back from the screen and looked at the wall for a while. Loudness predicted death the way dose predicted symptoms. A short utterance: a ring a few kilometers wide. A long one, the kind Ellis had flagged at 0300 on day nine, a hundred miles of dead water reaching the coast of Vancouver Island. They were not killing the fish and then speaking. They were speaking, and the fish were dying, and these were the same event. She thought about it in the flattest terms she could find, because the flat terms were the only ones that held still. Their voice is pressure. At their scale — and whatever they were, they were not small — a conversational sentence was a detonation. The first thing they'd said, the day they arrived, had emptied a sea's worth of water for a hundred miles in every direction. The hello had been the wave that took the *Perla* out. She sat with that fact for a moment, in the empty lab, holding it the way you hold a hot pan, by the handle only, and then she put it down and kept working, because the other thing she'd learned in fifteen years of grief-shaped science was that the data does not care what it costs you to look at it. At 6:40 a.m. she called Whidbey. Ellis answered on the first ring; he had clearly not been home either. "I need your full logs. The raw files, not the summaries." "Sure. Also, hi, did you sleep? Because I—" "Ellis. The fish kills. They're not damage from the arrival. They're ongoing. Every time they talk, everything with a swim bladder within range dies. The amplitude of an utterance predicts the radius of the kill, R-squared point nine four. Two hundred and eleven events. It's phase-locked." There was a silence on the line with some shuffling in it. "Okay," he said. "Okay. So the whole time we've been saying they're silent, they've been — talking. And every sentence—" He stopped. She heard him set something down. "Bring the plots. Bring everything. There's a briefing at ten, and I'm going to need more coffee than this building has." The coffee turned out to matter. She had been at Whidbey three days when it happened. The briefing had gone the way briefings go: the officers took the phase-lock finding and argued about what it meant for the strike posture, and Maya, being the only person in the room who had plotted the data herself, spent the afternoon in Ellis's lab, re-verifying, while Ellis rehearsed his own segment and drank. His lab was a converted sonar shack with analysis rigs he'd built himself from salvage and prayers, and he had a long-running habit of balancing his cup on the console shelf while he talked. The shelf held the transport rate controls. She was watching the spectrogram render, half listening to him run his patter, when he set the cup down, leaned back in his chair, caught the cup with his elbow, said a word he'd learned in Croydon, and lunged. The cup went over. Nothing got wet — the cup was empty, a fact he maintained loudly for the rest of the day — but his hand slammed the transport panel, and the playback, which had been running at analysis speed, dropped to a crawl, and the room filled with a sound that had not been a sound before. She heard it before she understood it. Something in the low pressure lines had unfolded. The modulation that had run for weeks as texture, as line noise, as the thing everyone had learned to filter past — slowed by the factor displayed on the cracked readout, 400:1 — had opened up into a shape. It had structure. Not signal structure — she'd seen that already, that's what had brought her here. This was different. This had phrasing. Repetitions that came back changed. A figure that arrived, and waited, and arrived again with something added, and somewhere in her, in the part of her that had spent fifteen years listening to things that were not supposed to be saying anything, a light went on. "Ellis." Her voice came out slow. "Leave it." "What — it's running wrong, the rate's—" "Leave it exactly like that." She picked up the headphones, took them to the window, and sat down on the floor, which was the only place the cord reached. The rate control had jammed at 400:1, and Ellis asked her, later, more than once, why four hundred — why that number, out of all numbers, the one a dropped cup had found — and she'd told him what she'd told the committee when they asked the same thing with worse manners. Because they were big. That was all. That was the whole argument. The lines moved through the headphones, stretched into their true length, and the room went away, and Whidbey went away. She sat on the floor until well past midnight with the cord pulled taut, listening, and did not once, the whole night, write anything down.

# Chapter 3 — The Old Song It took her two days to say the word out loud. She listened the first night on headphones in Ellis's shack, then took copies back to Bellhaven and listened there, doors shut, on the kitchen speakers, volume low. She did not call anyone. The thing that had unfolded at 400:1 had units grouped into figures, figures into themes, themes that returned with additions — and she had spent the ten years before her exile learning to read exactly that structure. The reading was effortless. That was the problem. She did not trust anything effortless anymore, because the last time she'd trusted it, her field had taken her funding and then, by a slower process, her name. On the third morning she said it to the empty kitchen. "Humpback." Then she went to work, because a hunch was nothing and she knew it. The grammar was humpback — the way the units were built, the rising sweeps, the way a phrase repeated exactly three times before the singer moved on. She knew the signature the way she knew the layout of her own kitchen. But the content matched nothing alive. She ran the slowed song against every catalog she could reach in a week: the current North Pacific song, the eastern Australian population, the breeding-ground archives from Hawaii to Mexico, her own field recordings — including the fifty-one hours she had of an old female she logged as HP-NP-114, whose lineage was the oldest thing in her files. Every living singer sang something newer. Whale song is culture; it drifts; it turns over in years the way human songs turn over in weeks. This vocabulary was not in the ocean anymore. The grammar was alive and every word in it was dead. She called Ellis from her kitchen at 1 a.m. "How old are the oldest song recordings?" she asked. "SOSUS goes back to the fifties, some of it declassified, most of it unlistened to. And then there's Bermuda. Sixty-nine, seventy." "Get me Bermuda." The Payne and McVay recordings. Every person in her field was born knowing them — the 1970 record that had sold a hundred thousand copies, that had been pressed into a plastic disc and mailed inside a magazine, that had done more for the anti-whaling campaign than a decade of papers, including hers. She had heard the opening theme maybe ten thousand times. She had never once needed to match it against anything, because everyone alive already knew what it was. She ran the match at 4:40 in the morning. The slowed song from column four was the Bermuda recording. Not descended from it — it. The same themes, the same units in the same order, carried at a scale that ruptured swim bladders a hundred miles out. With differences. There were embellishments the original never had, figures that bent lower and held longer, things added in the empty spaces, the way a man who has learned a language from a single tape will speak that language in his own rhythm, wearing his own accent. The skeleton was 1970. The voice around it was two hundred meters wide. She sat there and made herself finish the thought, because the thought had a conclusion and she was not permitted to skip steps. That song did not exist in the ocean. It existed in archives. And one archive of it had left the planet — a gold-plated copper disc, launched in 1977, carrying greetings in fifty-five human languages, the sound of a train and a kiss and rain, ninety minutes of music, and between the Bach and the Chuck Berry, eleven minutes of humpback whales. "We sent an invitation in someone else's voice," she said, and then felt embarrassed, alone in the kitchen, at how the sentence sounded, and wrote the plain version in her notes: *content source identified. Voyager golden record, 1977. Match to Bermuda 1970 master, structural identity, presentational variance (large).* The hail logs were already in hand by then. Ellis had kept them, because he kept everything. Eleven modalities: radio on every band, laser, math pulses, the protocols from every contact novel ever written, a nuclear test deliberately scheduled inside their sightline. The reply rate to all of it was zero. The reply rate to the record's content was continuous, daily, in utterances that cost a hundred miles of water each. They hadn't come for us. They hadn't ignored us, either — that would have required noticing us. We were a coast the message was not addressed to. Halloran arrived nine days later, at the Whidbey gate, with no clearance, no appointment, and a Sony analog recorder in a case that had been repaired with aircraft tape. The guards called her down to vouch him through. He stood at the gate the way a coat hangs on a chair — all that frame collapsed inward over itself, leaning on a single point of refusal. He had heard, of course. Requisitions leave trails, and the field was small; a request for the Bermuda masters meant either her or him, and everyone who mattered knew what each of them had been saying for twenty years. "Doctor Reyes," he said. His baritone had ruin in it now; long sentences came out in installments, and he paid the installments rather than shorten the sentence. "You've found speech. Don't tell me I've come all this way for a modulation." "I found a recording, Professor. Being played back." "By whom?" "That's the briefing." "Then brief me," he said, "while I still have the wind to argue with." She briefed him in Ellis's shack. He took the good chair, which nobody had known was the good chair until he sat in it. Twice he stopped her to make her repeat a number. Once he took off his glasses and held them against his chest and looked at the spectrogram for a while without saying anything, and his hands — his hands were still young, she noticed, elegant around the pen — moved slightly in the air, following the phrase the way some men conduct. At some point she said, "Your review of my paper. 2019. It was unsigned. It was you, wasn't it." "Anonymous review," he said, "is anonymous, Doctor." And put the glasses back on, which was a yes. They worked until nearly 2 a.m., the two of them and the one screen, arguing about whether the embellishments were ornament or grammar. It was Halloran who found it. The same figure, returning — every fourteenth theme-cycle, always in the same slot, the same rising tripartite shape, and each time it returned it was longer, slower, spaced out like a man repeating himself to the hard of hearing. "It opens," Halloran said. "Every other figure closes. This one doesn't." He tapped the screen with the pen, gently. "It's a question, Maya. Whatever else they've said — that figure is a question." He asked her to play it once more, and conducted to it, a little, and did not explain the look on his face, and she didn't ask.

# Chapter 4 — Why Are the Singers So Few The joint committee met in a hangar at Whidbey that had been converted in a week, badly. Maya counted forty-one chairs, three flags, and one man named Commander Dan Voss who sat with his back to the wall and called her Doctor every time, which she noticed, because almost no one did. He kept a paper logbook against regulations and turned his wedding ring when he spoke, and when the chairwoman introduced the morning's agenda he wrote something down before anyone said anything worth writing. Maya had thirty minutes. She'd been up four nights with the decode, and she was sure of it, and being sure was the last thing she trusted about it. The transcript would read: > REYES: The recurring figure — we're calling it Figure Fourteen — is not addressed to the ocean. It's structured. Tripartite, rising, with a terminal emphasis that tracks our shipping noise. I'm confident it's a census. They're counting our ships. They think the ships are the singers, and the question they keep asking is — where are the rest of you. She gave it eleven more minutes than that, with slides. HALLORAN: Doctor. The terminal emphasis. Is it corrected for the northbound lane traffic, or the ambient? REYES: Ambient. Across all stations. HALLORAN: Then why does the emphasis track the tide at station four and not at station nine? Play us both. They played both. It tracked the tide at station nine and not at station four, and she sat there in front of forty people and watched her census dissolve, because the emphasis was following the tide, which was following the fish, which had nothing to do with ships, and Figure Fourteen was about the ocean, not about us. As usual. > HALLORAN: It's not a census, Doctor Reyes. I'm sorry to do this in this format. > REYES: Yes. I see it. It's not a census. The chairwoman called a recess and the room got loud and nobody got loud at her, exactly, which was worse. Ellis brought her coffee and said, "You know what you found in one of the two branches of a conditional, though. Most people find nothing in either." She didn't answer. She'd oversold it. She'd done it before — in her last year of funding, with her last paper, and she knew the smell. Halloran came over and stood beside her, not facing her. "I had it coming once, in 1994," he said, to the coffee. "You didn't. That's the difference. Yours will cost you a week. Mine cost me twenty years." She knew about 1994. Everyone knew about 1994. She'd heard the story as a warning since graduate school, and she had never once heard him claim it out loud, and she didn't know what to do with it now, so she said nothing, and he didn't stay for her to manage it. The corrected decode came from the fish, in the end. She went back to the die-off rings and found what she'd been too hasty to see: the mortality radius wasn't uniform per utterance. Figure Fourteen killed wider. Every time it came around — every fourteenth theme-cycle — the ring opened larger than the surrounding speech, as if the figure was *meant* farther than the rest. The question was being shouted. It was being repeated to the hard of hearing across the whole basin, and the hard of hearing was the ocean floor, and they had been asking it since arrival, every day, at a cost of dead water each time. She rebuilt it in nine hours. Halloran audited it, at her request, publicly, and it held. > REYES: It's not a census and it's not a location request. We know that because of the follow-on. Every Fourteen, they run a survey sweep — full-band listening, the columns go quiet for six hours, they sample the entire soundscape, whales, weather, us, everything. Then they play back what they heard, minus the noise floor. The playback is a count, sirs. They're counting singers. And the question that ends every count is a comparison. The Figure Fourteen utterance is: the singers are so few. Why are the singers so few. She made them sit with the translation while it rendered on the wall, in her plain typed words, because she had learned in eleven humiliating minutes what a confident performance was worth. She did not perform it. She read it flat and let the room go quiet on its own. Voss turned his ring and then stopped turning it. "Doctor. Are they accusing?" "They don't know us well enough to accuse. They're asking." "Same question, though," Denny would have said, and she was glad Denny wasn't in the room. The committee did what committees do. Arguments about whether the translation could be trusted, which was fair, and about what it meant that they'd been answering the Voyager disc on a loop for a month to a species that had never picked up the phone. Arguments about the strikes posture, which was not fair to call an argument — Voss gave it the numbers and the numbers came with a date, sixteen days out, and the date went into the minutes and stayed there. An action date. A clock, in a hangar, with three flags. Then a NOAA delegate, a marine-mammal person Maya had cited once and never met, said the obvious thing last, which was the only way obvious things got said in that room. "Whatever we decide to tell them — we can't say it. They don't take radio. They take song." So the plan, by end of day, was the only plan: answer in song. Compose a reply, put it in the water, hope the grammar they'd already learned was enough. There was one problem, and Maya brought it to the evening session herself, because after the morning she was not going to be the one who didn't bring it. The structures were playing the Bermuda master — the dead song, the 1970 recording. If the reply was going to be an answer, it had to answer in the same language, which meant the same song. But humpback song was living culture; it had turned over maybe ten times since 1970. No living singer had that vocabulary anymore. She'd checked every archive in the Pacific basin. The last recordings of it in the wild were from decades before anyone present was born. "So we play the recording back," the NOAA delegate said. "We have it." Their first full sentence in the new register cost eleven fish, and Maya sat there doing the terrible arithmetic nobody asked her for — the exchange rate, the tuition, the oldest lesson on earth rendered in a pressure signature — and then went back to work. The decode took two days. It was Halloran who saw the bearing first. The utterance wasn't omnidirectional. The propagation focus ran down a single axis, west by northwest, away from the coast, away from the shipping lanes, away from everything with an engine. "Doctor," he said. "They're not asking us. Look where it's pointed." It was pointed at the Kodiak grounds. They were asking Cricket. *Who silenced the singers.* The figure resolved on the second night, and it was not a new figure — it was Figure Fourteen, the tripartite rising shape, the same question they had asked since arrival, except that the third element had changed. Not *why are so few.* The new termination was an agent-marker. The question presumed a somebody. And it was being put, carefully, quietly, at the cost of eleven fish, to the last carrier of a lineage that had a shape with holes in it. "The 'who' means they've ruled out natural," Maya said at the briefing. "We don't know how. My best read is they can hear the gaps in the song culture — lineages that stop mid-phrase, no young voice picking them up. A generation gap is audible if you're listening at their resolution. They've heard a massacre in the archive of the water." "Or," the chairwoman said, "they're hunting." The room went the way rooms go. If they were looking for whoever did it, and they concluded it was us — the coast, the noise, the species that wouldn't stop hailing them in radio — then the question was what a retaliation looked like at an amplitude that had once opened a hundred-mile ring. The 72-hour deferral was expiring. Voss's strike package came off the table not as an option but as the only instrument in the building with a date on it, and someone asked whether the question constituted a threat, and Maya said the truth, which was that she didn't know, and the truth helped nothing. Voss asked for one weapon. His reasoning entered the record the way he entered everything, in his paper logbook, in complete sentences: *If the answer comes back adverse, we will need to know whether they can be hurt before we need to know anything else.* A capability test. One torpedo, one column, surface-supported, minimum exposure. The authorization took six hours to assemble and was granted at a level Maya never saw. She watched it on the feed from the shack, with Ellis and Halloran and nobody speaking. The torpedo ran its run, forty-one minutes into an utterance, and struck the column's flank at the waterline, and the screens did nothing. No change in modulation. No counter-anything. The utterance continued through the impact without a seam — no flinch, no pause, no acknowledgment that the strike had occurred inside the sentence. The column went on speaking its careful question at the Kodiak grounds while a mark burned itself into the record, and the ocean absorbed the detonation's signature into the general noise floor, and the hydrophones logged it like weather. Voss came to the shack afterward, alone, still with his back to the wall. He turned his ring. "Thirty years I listened for things under the water that wanted to hurt us," he said. "Turns out the first thing that actually came didn't even know we fired." He looked at the flat screens for a while. "Put it in your set, Doctor. Whatever you send them next. I want it on the tape." Nobody had the nerve to tell him they might already be past that. She drove home that night, because there was a meeting at the Polish hall about the fleet — compensation claims, grounds closures — and because she was the only person in the state who could no longer tell whether she was avoiding her own town or documenting it. The answer is everything we have on the question, in order.* Ellis had digitized forty reels before he started coming to find her between reels instead of after them. He was quiet in a way nobody had seen on him. The tape was not what he'd expected, he said. He'd expected horror and found paperwork. Radio chatter about lunch. A man coughing through a six-hour flensing operation in 1953. Two sailors arguing about a football match, sixty kilometers off Kamchatka, while the winches ran. Somebody singing — badly, happily — on a deck with a catch alongside. On one reel from 1961, captured from the water side, a whale's last runs and then, clear as a neighbor, a crewman laughing at something someone said, and the laughter and the death on the same channel at the same level, no distinction at all in the tape between them. "They're just at work," Ellis said. "That's the part I can't — they're just at work." Reel 212 had water damage. Forty seconds, gone — somewhere in 1967, mid-decade, mid-slaughter, a gap with nothing in it. Ellis brought it to her with the interpolation already half-built: he could model the missing seconds from the surrounding signal, he said, splice the room tone, and it would sound whole. It would sound better than it was. "Leave it broken," Maya said. "It'll sound better—" "I know. Leave it broken." He looked at her for a moment and then nodded slowly and did not fix it, and she saw what that cost him, because Ellis fixed things; it was the whole shape of his soul; and he put the forty seconds of nothing into the set like a man swallowing a stone. The strike went in at the end. Voss's request, from the shack, was in her notebook verbatim. She didn't take it to the committee. She logged the torpedo audio — the Navy's own range hydrophones had the whole run, forty-one minutes of it, detonation and all — as the final entry, after reel 300, after twenty-five years of tape ended in the ordinary silence of 1975. The document they were about to transmit was therefore this, in order: what we did for twenty-five years, and then what we did three weeks ago when you asked us who did it. The chairwoman would have removed it, Maya was fairly sure. Nobody asked the chairwoman. Voss, when he heard it was in, wrote one line in his paper logbook, initialed it, and closed the book. The broadcast ran eleven days. That was the length of it. Four hundred and ten hours, transmitted from the array at ocean-safe amplitude, in order, twenty-four hours a day, the archive played at true speed because anything else would have been an argument. Ellis ran the deck in shifts. The mission log recorded amplitude, bearing, reel numbers. It recorded that during the eleven days the columns produced no modulation at all. Halloran slept in the lab most nights. On day nine she found him in the chair with his headphones on and his eyes open, conducting, very slightly, to a Japanese coastal recording from 1958, and she did not interrupt, because he had told her about the lungs by then — told her badly, as a footnote to an argument about whether the embellishments were ornament — and there was a private clock in the room that none of the timelines in the hangar knew about. On the twelfth day, the columns answered. The response came at full amplitude — the largest utterance on record, higher than the arrival hail — and the ring it opened was the widest of the whole affair. And it was a catastrophe; there were hundreds of tons of dead water in it; Maya did the arithmetic as it happened and could not stop doing the arithmetic. But the ring was not one ring. It was nine, sequenced down the line of the columns, one every forty minutes, opening in order, east to west, and the spacing was the spacing of the archive — she verified it twice — the intervals matched the transmission log of the eleven days, compressed. A rhythm laid out in dead fish across four hundred miles, matching the rhythm of the tape. The same document, played back, in their own medium. "Elegy," Maya said, at the debrief, and put the overlay on the wall. "Disgust," the NOAA delegate said, and put his overlay up next to hers, and his numbers were as good as hers — the amplitude was maximum, the amplitude was rage if you read it that way, and the sequencing was also a flinging-down, an accusation laid out along the coast like evidence in a courtroom, itemized. They looked at the two readings together for a while. The minutes recorded that the interpretation was *contested*. It was still contested when the second utterance came, and there was no arguing about the second one, because the second one was quiet. It came four hours after the last ring closed, at the new careful register, slower than anything they had managed, each unit given room to land. It ran fifty-two minutes. It cost the sea almost nothing. And it was not addressed out to sea, not pointed at the Kodiak grounds, not for Cricket. It was omnidirectional. For once, aimed at everything that could hear. The decode resolved by evening. Halloran did the final pass himself, in the chair, and then made Maya read it off the screen while he watched her face instead of the text, which she understood and forgave and did not mention. The translation, in her plain typed words, went up on the hangar wall at 21:40: *We heard who. We will carry the singers to a sea that keeps them.* The room did what rooms do, which was noise. Maya stood at the back of it, doing the only arithmetic that was left to her: *carry* was a verb with a destination in it, and the singers were not ours to give or to send, and the offer was generous, and the offer was a wound, and both of those were true, and no one in the room was going to be able to say which one was the offer.

# Chapter 8 — The Loud Ones The committee argued the offer for two days, and the argument was not about the whales. It was about us, which nobody said out loud until the second afternoon. The acceptance case was made best by a delegate whose name Maya never learned to spell: better an ocean somewhere with singers in it than a museum here without them. Give them the forty. We had our fifty years. The refusal was uglier, and came in pieces. The Navy would not transfer anything out of national waters, in that language. A fisheries-industry delegate — a man who had fought every closure since the nineties, and had been fighting Maya's quota papers since before she had a doctorate — got up red-faced, mispronounced *cetacean* twice, and said: "We already shipped their families out once. In cans. Now we're going to finish the job politely?" He said it badly. The room stopped arguing anyway, because it landed. Halloran spoke last, in installments, paying for each. "If the singers go," he said, "then no one — ever again — has to make this water whole. The offer is very kind. That is all the offer is." Maya stood to second the refusal, principle, restoration, obligation, and heard her father in her own mouth, *tourist with a microphone*, and understood the basement under her principle, which was that she could not bear an ocean gone permanently quiet — could not bear the listening life ending with her own instruments — and sat down having said none of that, and voted with the mixed and the selfish and the right, all at once, in one raised hand. The vote hung, nineteen and nineteen with abstentions, and the minutes recorded no majority, and it was the youngest delegate in the room, a political officer nobody had heard from yet, who read the bearing logs and said the only clean sentence of the two days: "The offer isn't ours to accept. Check who it was about. We can't refuse on their behalf either. We can relay it." They relayed it for nine days, the carry-figure rendered in the bridge grammar at safe amplitude, played to the Kodiak grounds from the research vessel, while Cricket did what Cricket did. She fed. She moved, if anything, further onto the grounds. On the ninth day she sang the bridge-song through three cycles with company — another whale, shadowing at half a kilometer, the first logged association for HP-NP-114 since 2011 — and the mission log recorded, in Maya's flat typed words: *No acceptance. No refusal. Continued presence.* The human addendum went out on day ten. Maya composed the terminal figure herself — *they stay; we stay* — in the old grammar, and her hands were not steady, because she had written exactly one thing before in that language and deleted it, and no one needed to know why the second thing took four checks. The answer came four days later, at 02:11. Three minutes and forty seconds, at the new careful register, amplitude beneath every threshold on record. The stranding networks logged no mortality attributable. It was the first utterance of the entire affair that killed nothing, and it was not omnidirectional. It was pointed at the Kodiak grounds, at a whale with a notch in her fluke, and it was not for us. Maya decoded it alone. The log recorded the decode as complete. The committee received a summary — *acceptance; departure; no further contact requested* — and no one pressed her, and the file exists, and this is all that will be said here. One word from it she did share. Their speech had carried a marker since arrival — a long unit, low, recurring whenever the shipping noise crossed their bands — and Maya had always logged it as neutral, a designation, the way you'd log a buoy. In the final sentence the unit carried the small-amplitude emphasis. The care-marker. The gentle register, applied to us. Their word for us was long. In her plain typed translation, closest to: *the loud ones.* They said it quietly. She dubbed the sentence onto analog tape for Halloran, because analog doesn't forgive you, and he listened to it twice in the chair with his eyes open, conducting, a little, and did not explain his face, and she did not ask. The departure took nine days. The columns went down one at a time, west to east, and the tide gauges — she checked, everyone checked — recorded no anomaly. No displacement wave. The thing that had emptied a coast on arrival left without moving a mooring line. Whatever else they were, they had learned our scale, and the first fully polite thing they did, they did leaving. > VOSS, paper log, final entry on the matter: *Departure complete. No anomaly. Recommend the record reflect that we fired first.* He retired that winter. His book is in an archive now too. They left one object behind, at column four's position: small, inert, sampling. The hydrophones caught it listening, never transmitting. Ellis was asked what he'd named it, because Ellis named everything, and he said, "Not this one. It's not ours." In the spring Maya asked Denny about the *Perla*. She'd been into Kessler's yard twice over the winter and said nothing about the boat and neither had he. Then she asked, and he said nothing for a week, and then he spent a weekend on the bilge without discussing it with anyone, and on Sunday handed her the keys and a socket wrench she'd need and wouldn't have, and said, "Salt the fuel lines if you lay her up again." That was the entire transaction. It was the only peace on offer, and neither of them dressed it up. She took her father's boat out over the grounds in April, alone. The water was loud the ordinary way. Herring, thick on the hydrophone like weather. Sea lions at the haulout, arguing. A young humpback working a song two lanes over — and she recognized the joins, rough ones, wrong ones, but the units were the old ones, the 1970 units, wearing new accents, a dead language being spoken by something that had learned it from a whale who had learned it from a rig the humans built. The lineage was carrying. She logged it and the log didn't care that her eyes had gone unfocused and her breathing had slowed. Cricket surfaced at 400 meters with her companion. Six blows, then the arch, then the dive. Maya wrote it down. She took out her phone, then, on the console, in the wind. 1:47. She held it a long time, the way you hold a hot pan, by the handle only. She played the first five seconds — *Maya, it's your old man* — and stopped it, and put it in her coat, and did not write down that either. Then she dropped the hydrophone over deep water and listened past the herring, past the boat noise, past everything, down to where it goes silent and keeps going. She stayed out past dark. There was no hum. There was nothing to confirm, and she had stopped expecting it, and she listened anyway, out of something she declined to name, and it got dark, and the water went on being loud. She logged the day before she headed in. Under remarks she wrote one word, the way her father used to write it on the catch sheets, meaning good water, meaning full: *loud*

# Brainstorming ## The Prompt Itself "The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸" — the genius of this is the ambiguity. Blood drop emojis sent at midnight could mean anything from a medical emergency to a period-related SOS to a goth being dramatic to an actual dead body. In British teen WhatsApp culture, three of anything is a distress signal — "🚨🚨🚨" means come now, don't ask questions. So 🩸🩸🩸 reads as: *come now, don't ask questions, and it involves blood.* Or does it? The unreliable decoding of the message could be the entire engine of the story. Possible meanings to explore: 1. **The literal reading**: someone is bleeding. Injury, accident, nosebleed at the worst possible moment. 2. **The period code**: established between friends as "code red — bring supplies and chocolate, extraction urgent." Classic female friendship shorthand. 3. **The dead/alive animal**: someone has killed something with a car, or the neighbour's pet has met an accident, and a midnight burial is required. 4. **The dead body**: a genuine Heathers/Bodies Bodies Bodies escalation. Something terrible has happened at a house party. 5. **The joke that curdles**: it's meant to be funny/dramatic, but the protagonist takes it seriously and the journey reveals it's either far worse or far sillier than assumed. 6. **The wrong sender**: the code arrives from a number it shouldn't come from — an estranged friend, a dead friend's phone, a parent who's somehow got hold of it. 7. **The absurd**: 40 litres of pig's blood from dad's abattoir van, needed for the school production of *Carrie: The Musical*. 8. **The grim reality**: a friend cleaning up after an incident at home — a mum's boyfriend, a sibling, self-harm — blood on a kitchen floor at 1am, jokes as coping. ## Character Ideas (wide net) - **The narrator (16–17)**: dry, sardonic, deadpan. Reads as the sensible one but is secretly flattered to be needed. British YA needs a voice-first narrator — think Georgia Nicolson's diaries meets *The End of the F***ing World*. Name options: Nell, Iris, Bea, Sadie, Juno, Florence. - **The sender of the text**: chaotic best friend. Either genuinely in crisis, in absurd crisis, or being a drama queen — the mystery of which drives the plot. Could be: Priya, Amber, Darcy, Zara, Ness. - **The estranged/dead friend**: if the text comes from someone impossible, the story becomes about grief or reconciliation. Very rich emotional territory for dark comedy. - **A boy complicating things**: the sender's older brother, a boy at the party, a boy who's also been summoned. Love interest, liability, or both. - **The parents**: absent, useless, or grimly helpful ("Mum's on nights, there's fish fingers in the freezer"). - **Peripheral Brits for comic cameos**: a nosy neighbour in a dressing gown, a night-bus driver, an A&E receptionist, a Community Support Officer who wants to go home. ## Tone & Texture Options - **Pure farce**: escalating misunderstandings, one terrible decision compounding another, everything at 2x speed. *Fawlty Towers* with teenagers. - **Dark comedy with an emotional undertow**: jokes on the surface, grief or love underneath. This is where British YA lives best — funny *and* true. - **Cringe comedy**: embarrassment as the primary weapon — white jeans, school trips, parents who insist on helping. - **Mock-gothic**: Yorkshire moors, a coffin-shaped coffin of a mystery, vampire obsession played straight-laced. - **One-night structure**: the whole story is a single night. Midnight to dawn. Every chapter an hour. Very contained, very filmic, forces escalation. ## Plot Pitches (wide net) **Pitch 1 — The Burial:** Best friend has run over the neighbour's beloved dog (or hit a deer, or the school's pet pig has died on her watch). 🩸🩸🩸 summons narrator to help dispose of the evidence. Eight chapters of bungled burial, near-misses with walkers/police/the dog's grieving owner, a twist (the dog isn't dead? the "dog" is actually something else entirely?), and a landing about why we bury things. **Pitch 2 — The Journey:** Narrator receives the text, embarks on an epic midnight journey across town to help — last bus missed, the walk through the bad part of town, a fox, a crying man, a police stop. Arrives to find the emergency is small (a nosebleed on the wedding dress she was supposed to wear tomorrow). But the journey has revealed the actual emergency was about something else — loneliness, a friendship dying. **Pitch 3 — The Code:** 🩸🩸🩸 is the narrator and best friend's secret period-emergency code. But the text comes from the friend who ghosted her six months ago — or from a boy in their class who somehow knows the code. Forces a reunion/sneak-mission, and a story about why friendships fracture and whether they can be mended. **Pitch 4 — The Dead Friend's Phone:** The text arrives from the best friend who died six months ago. Narrator goes to the phone's owner (the dead girl's mum? the charity shop where her phone ended up?) and instead finds the ghost — or the person the dead girl trusted most. Grief comedy, dark but warm. The code's meaning — something they laughed about when they invented it — becomes the emotional payload. **Pitch 5 — Pig's Blood for Carrie:** The drama department's production of *Carrie* needs blood. Someone's dad works at an abattoir. Someone's "borrowed" 20 litres of real blood, and it has to be returned before Monday. Biohazard cooler, midnight, two teens, escalating terrible ideas. **Pitch 6 — The Real One:** Friend texts because there's blood on her kitchen floor and her little brother is asleep upstairs. Mum's boyfriend. Dark, honest, darkly funny in the "mopping blood while eating crumpets" register — jokes as survival. Harder to keep comic without it curdling, but potentially the most truthful. **Pitch 7 — The House Party:** The text comes from inside a party narrator wasn't invited to. She sneaks in to help and finds chaos of an unspecified nature. Social satire of British teen parties (someone's dad's record collection, someone's crying in the bath). ## Structural / Pacing Ideas for 8 × 1000 words - **Single-night structure**: Ch 1 the text; Ch 2 decoding/response; Ch 3 arriving at the crisis; Ch 4–5 the escalation (worst night of it); Ch 6 the disaster/near-discovery; Ch 7 the quiet hour — the real conversation underneath the jokes; Ch 8 dawn, resolution, callback to the emoji. - **Slow-reveal structure**: don't tell the reader what 🩸🩸🩸 means for two chapters; let them assume the worst alongside the narrator. - **Voice-forward**: each chapter ends on a beat that recontextualises the last one. - **Comic rhythm**: aim for a big set-piece every other chapter; small observational jokes in between. # Reflection Right — what actually works for *darkly comic British YA* specifically, at 8 × 1000 words, opening on that text? The tone is the first filter. The prompt promises something that's funny *and* dark, and British YA does this best when the comedy is a coping mechanism over something real, not just farce for farce's sake. So the purely farcical pitches (5, the pig's blood) are fun but risk being clever without being about anything. The heaviest pitches (6, the domestic violence one) are honest but the comedy might curdle — jokes about mopping up after an abattoir-sized mess are fine; jokes about an abusive boyfriend require a steadiness of hand that's harder to sustain across 8 chapters while remaining "darkly comic" rather than just grim. It could work, but it's the riskiest register to hold. The pitches with the strongest natural architecture for eight chapters are the ones with a **journey or a night**: a contained timeframe forces escalation, which is exactly what an 8-chapter short story needs. Pitch 2 (the journey to a crisis that turns out to be small, revealing a bigger truth) has a lovely shaggy-dog Britishness, and the "one-night structure" maps beautifully onto eight chapters. Its weakness: if the destination is anticlimactic, the ending needs real emotional ballast to avoid feeling like a shrug. Pitch 4 (the dead friend's phone) is the one that most purely embodies "darkly comic" — grief *is* the dark, the ghost/code conceit *is* the comic, and the emoji prompt becomes devastating rather than just intriguing. The risk is mawkishness, but a deadpan British voice guards against that. Pitch 3 (the code from an estranged friend) is a softer version of the same emotional engine — friendship rupture instead of death — and might actually be more sustainable at YA register, with a sneak-mission plot providing comedy while the estrangement provides the heart. Pitch 1 (the burial farce) is the strongest *plot engine*: it generates chapter after chapter of incident naturally (dig, get interrupted, relocate, get caught, twist). It's comedy-forward with an emotional landing available (why we bury things, what we owe each other). Its weakness is a slight thinness of theme unless I deliberately build one in. The most promising direction feels like a **hybrid of pitches 1/2/3/4**: use the single-night, summoned-at-midnight structure (from 2); make the crisis something concrete and escalating but absurd rather than tragic (from 1); and give the relationship between sender and receiver a fracture or a grief underneath it (from 3/4), so the midnight callout is also a reconciliation. That gives me comedy on the surface, heart underneath, a natural eight-chapter escalation, and a reason the text arrived *just after midnight* — because that's when the sender finally broke down and messaged the one person she'd sworn not to speak to. Things to solve if I go that way: - **The crisis needs specificity and escalation potential** — a body (animal or otherwise) to deal with works better than a conversational crisis for generating eight chapters of incident. - **The voice must carry the reader between set-pieces** — so the narrator needs a defined comic register (deadpan, list-making, hyper-specific observation) from paragraph one. - **Chapter 7 needs to be reserved for the quiet truth** — the joke-free or joke-thin chapter where the real thing is said. That's a British YA non-negotiable. - **The emoji needs a payoff**: 🩸🩸🩸 should mean something by the end that recontextualises the opening — ideally something that makes the reader laugh and ache at the same time. On pacing: 1000 words per chapter is tight — about 3–4 scenes max, probably 2–3. Every chapter needs to open with momentum (the night is moving, nobody has time for preamble) and close on a hook or a beat. The single-night container enforces this discipline naturally, which is another point in its favour. The setting should be small and specific — a town where everything is closed by 9pm, so a midnight mission means walking, and walking means talking. That's the whole book, really: two teenagers, a long dark walk, something bloody in a wheelbarrow, and all the things they haven't said to each other in six months.
