"Sir, the review flag is showing Meridian and the escrow's frozen pending—" She'd sold six bottles of the cellar to a Candlewharf broker for coin before the freeze finished printing, because coin was the one thing a review couldn't touch, and she was standing on the fuel deck doing arithmetic about the rest of the cellar when the courier's ramp came down. Mr. Pell was gray, neat, and looked like a mid-level man at any company in the galaxy. He crossed the ring without hurry, thanked the airlock when it cycled for him, and stood at the bottom of the *Copperhead*'s ramp with a paper notebook in one soft hand. "Captain. I'd have come to Harrow. You saved me the trip." Not a question about why she hadn't gone. She stood aside, because boarders' courtesy was older than her pride, and he came up into the galley and sat where the light was good and didn't fidget once. Tam was at the console, cores still jacked in. Doc was at the table with his sleeve down and his coffee in the beaker. "You claimed the *Manifest* at 0400, ship time. Fourteen crates. One custody item, genus Bellidae, live." Pell turned the notebook to a fresh page and didn't write in it. "There's a feeding schedule, Captain. Nineteen hundred, and again at 2200. It's being watered like livestock, which I take as a sign of good faith." "You've read my logs." "Your claim. The logs are yours." He said it accurately, like everything. "Here's my problem. The item's biological, it's out of custody, and it opened your doctor's arm wrist to elbow on a salvaged vessel. Under Meridian admiralty that's not a retrieval, that's a manifest defect, and manifest defects get inquiries. I'm offering you the kind version of the next part." "Which is." "Decontamination and closure. The debt clears — forty-one thousand two hundred, plus accrued dock fees, plus a salvage premium above market. Your account comes back from review by end of day." He paused with the pause of a man laying a card he'd been holding the whole time. "And the indenture paper held against your hull comes out of Grimsby's collateral column. The Hollis girl's contract, transferred clean. Three years, bought out, at no cost to her." Tam had gone still at the console with her hand off the reader, the way she'd moved her thumb off the crew manifest, and Voss watched her not look at anyone. "And the animal," Voss said. "Quarantine. Study." He wrote one line in the notebook in ink. "The animal isn't the liability, Captain. The animal is the evidence." disposition. custody. line items. Wind out of the west, somewhere, and dust going the color of tin — she'd have called it rain coming, that day, if anybody had asked her. Nobody had asked her. "The answer's no." "Captain—" "You heard the number and the number's real. The answer's no." He sat with it. He didn't argue the figure up or soften terms; he closed the notebook, and his face did something small and tired that she understood was displeasure, the way a ledger shows a negative. "I'll tell you what I told my section, so it's said in front of witnesses: nobody's threatened here. But things that stay open generate review, and review goes to other departments, and other departments aren't precise like me." He stood, and thanked the airlock again on the way out, and Voss watched him cross the ring without hurry and did not feel better for having won anything. The escrow seizure hit at noon — the whole account, impounded at Grimsby's office by Meridian review authority, and then Grimsby himself on the comm, aggrieved, sweating through the audio: "Rhea, they came into my office. My office. I can't hold your paper, they made it so I can't even—" and she cut him off mid-word, which she was aware was rude, and burned out of Candlewharf on cash fuel with the stern half of the cellar still aboard and unsold. Doc had left the galley partway through Pell's offer, saying something about his rounds that fooled nobody. Tam hadn't left. She'd stood at the console through the seizure, through the burn, through the first hour of the dark. "You could've asked me," she said, finally, not turning around. "It's my paper. # Five — The Long Dark Four days out of Candlewharf, running dark, and Voss had learned to sleep in the afternoons, because the afternoons were when the *Copperhead* was quietest and because quiet was the only sleep she trusted anymore. Transponder off, beacons off, the coin-fuel burn laid in long and shallow. Tam had moved into the engine room around day two — officially because Grandpa was coughing and somebody ought to sleep near him — and Voss let it stand, because the girl was sleeping at all, and because of what everybody knew and nobody said: Sunday had come down out of the spine around day two as well. It had taken the top of the coolant housing, folded wrong-jointed under the conduits, and stayed. It sang there. Nights, it sang the drive. That was the thing Voss hadn't expected about it. It didn't sing its dead world's chorus, not anymore, not since the galley. It sang the ship. The feed pump's tick. Grandpa's cough, placed dead center of the song like a drum. The drive's hum underneath it all, and its own voice dropped in and out of the layers the way the Perdido recording had moved, like it had never once sung alone and was not going to start now. Voss sat in the corridor outside the engine room past midnight more than once, boots off so as not to be heard, listening to a creature compose her ship. The third night dark, the song lost a beat. Tam was up the ladder and in the corridor before Voss was, wearing one boot, and it took her a while to say what she'd heard because it wasn't the engine. "It's Sunday. He dropped the drive out of the song. He put the other thing in." The other thing. Then Tam did it, flat, mimicking the mimic — the crack. The round sparking off chain housing. Sunday had kept the sound of being shot at and slotted it into the music where the drive belonged, and hearing it again, Voss's hands remembered the grip. "He only does it when a sound goes wrong," Tam said. "He did it when Grandpa's filter clogged, before the gauge moved. Now he's doing it at the drive." The gauges read clean for another four hours. Then, at the edge of the tolerance, the thrust governor's feed valve showed a half-beat lag that no gauge at Candlewharf had flagged, because there was no gauge for the sound of a valve about to die. Tam found it by ear, her head against the housing, one hand flat on the pipe like a stethoscope, singing the beat to herself under her breath. Hairline wear. It would hold for a skim. It would not hold for a run. "We fuel or we drift," Tam said. "I know what it means," Voss said, and went up to lay in the course, and turned the transponder on at the boundary of the Pinos skimming field, because unmanned posts didn't answer ships that didn't exist. She found Doc at 0500 in the med bay with the locker open, doing inventory one-handed on a clipboard. The other sleeve was down, and the cardigan under it buttoned to the throat, dressed for a climate he wasn't in. He had the back of his right hand pressed to his own forehead, that old clinic habit turned on himself, and he took it away unhurried when he saw her. "Auditing," he said. "Half the stock's gone crystallized anyhow." "You want Tam to look at it." "She looks at it every time I sit down. I'm thinking of eating standing up." "Doc." "It's knitting." He wrote a line on the clipboard. "Go fix your valve." The tight beam came in at 0900, as the skimmer field's pylons came up out of the gas giant's amber. One voice, flat, procedural, and Voss took it on the bridge alone because she'd have taken it alone in a crowd. "Vessel *Copperhead*, this is Kite, carrying Meridian admiralty warrant 9-4-1, custody retrieval, one item. Party holding the item is invited to comply and no parties are named. You want it read?" "No." "Rhea." A pause that had eleven years in it. "You still—" "No." The beam held a while, open, nobody spending it. Then he said, "The paper names one item. One. That's all it is, an instrument. I'd rather you knew its shape before it's in my hand." "Since when do you read that close?" "Since always." He cut the beam himself. Voss sat with her hand on the board and did not file the exchange, because there was no file it fit. His ship was already at the post. It had been there a while — riding dark, which was her trick, and she took a long look at that. The *Copperhead* came in on a failing valve with nowhere else to go, and she docked it, because drifting was the other option, and she was still tallying which of the two was the lie when she stepped down the ramp into the ring's one corridor, and he was there. Plain-faced, big-boned, clothes worn and maintained and never clean, a face you'd lose in a dock crowd, which had always been equipment. She checked the corridor's exits without turning her head, and watched him do the same thing to the same exits at the same time, and neither of them said anything about doing it. He had the warrant in his hand. Actual paper. He held it out with his other hand flat and empty beside it, both hands where she could see them, always, that went back further than the badge. "Ansel." "Ma'am." He nodded at the paper. "Ink. Your word against mine doesn't stand up anymore, so it's in ink." She took it. The paper said what he'd said it said: custody item, one. No parties. Kite came forward with a hand truck, efficient, not hurried, neither gentle nor otherwise. He got the crate loaded and strapped, and then he stood next to it a beat too long. Voss saw it. Tam didn't watch. Tam was already gone up the ladder. Voss found her later, or found the absence of her, in the engine room, on the deck where the coolant housing was still warm. The girl had her boots off, which she never did, and Voss stood in the hatch and didn't go in. "You could've told him no," Tam said, at the deck. Not turning. # Seven — Sunrise Terms Three days out from the skimming post, Doc's fever came up with the evenings. He was dressing for it, the way he dressed for everything — cardigan buttoned to the throat, sleeve down, the back of his right hand going to his own forehead at intervals like a man keeping an appointment. Voss came into the med bay and didn't ask how he was, because he'd have answered the way he always answered, and instead held out her hand. "Your cipher." He didn't ask what for. He recited it from the bunk without opening his eyes — personnel code, thirty years old, spoken like something he'd never once needed to look up — and then, eyes still shut, said the rest. "They never purged the juniors. Cheaper to archive a man than delete one. Everything Meridian ever did is still written down somewhere, Captain. That's the whole of them. It's the only whole of them there is." Tam jacked in at the galley console and worked the custody system like she'd been born in it. Voss stood over her and watched the files come up cream and neat, ink and ink and ink. "Bellidae consignment, *Manifest*. Six items." Tam's voice stayed flat, reading. "Five non-viable at intake. One viable, active feed." A pause while the screen caught up with thirty years. "Transfer standing: to vault ship *Providence*. Custody run, waypoint filing, protocol dated—" she squinted "—it's old, Captain. It's really old." Behind them, from the bunk, Doc was talking. Not to them. The fever had him counting. "Day forty. Dusk. Put the gain up, it's still going." His voice was easy, clinic-level, describing a recording to a man named Ravel who had been dead three decades. "No evidence of complex vocal—" and there he stopped himself, mid-word, and was quiet a while, and then, "I counted them. That was my job on the survey, I counted—" "You read the list," he said then, to the room. To Tam. "Mm." Tam kept typing. "You didn't ask." "No." "There's no version where I come out of it," Doc said, quiet, to the ceiling. "I know," Tam said, and kept typing. Voss stood there and held the silence for both of them, because it was hers to hold, and then went up to the bridge. "Tam's going to look at that arm," she said from the hatch, on her way out. "Tonight." "After," Doc said. She didn't ask after what. Kite's ship was on the ring at Kerr Ring, ahead of them, riding a fuel queue like any working vessel. She hailed him tight-beam and got two words back — *the canteen* — and found him at the counter in the corner with his back to the wall, checking the door out of habit, thirty years after it had stopped being his job. "You eaten?" she said. They ate. The canteen's good meal was protein and real bread and cost what a governor valve cost. She bought it and put it in front of him and he ate it standing up, quick, at the counter, like the sitting had never taken. She let him. Pell would have eaten it slow in front of people who couldn't; Kite couldn't help the other thing; it was the same training wearing different men, and she didn't say so. "I'm taking it back," she said. He finished chewing. He looked at his hands, then wiped them, then looked at the counter, the whole process taking the length of a man deciding nothing at all. "My paper's closed," he said. "I don't carry another one." "I know the shape of it." "Mm." He turned his cup a quarter-turn on the counter. "Your thirty-year-old filing says the transfer makes at Deacon's Drop. It doesn't. Protocol moved nine years back. They make the exchange at the *Providence* waystation now — waypoint's in the open fleet register if you read the freight schedules, and you always read close." "I read close. You want to tell me why you do." He didn't answer that. He looked at the door instead, at the queue of hands outside waiting on the co-op board to post the shift list, and what he said was: "Reconciliation man rides out for the ink. He'll want the signature witnessed, that's why he's coming, he doesn't delegate ink. Pair of security on the courier and the *Providence* carries crew." A quarter-turn of the cup back the other way. "You'll be done before anybody's hungry." "Ansel." "You never could abide a rotten order," he said, to the counter, to the cup. "I always figured that's what Greenfall was, at the root of it." The rain-smell of dust going the color of tin moved through her and was gone. She drank instead of answering, and he took it as the answer it was, and stood there a while with his back to the wall and his hands flat and empty beside the cup, both of them where she could see them, one last time before it all came down to what it came down to. "Second bay sells governor valves," he said. "Kerr Ring's got decent machine work, for a co-op." He put his cup down. "Ma'am." He went out into the shift-list crowd and was gone in it, a plain face losing itself in a dock crowd, and she paid for both meals with the last of the coin and did not watch him go. The rest of the cellar went for the valve. The broker at Kerr Ring gave her coin for it and called the vintages peasant-ship luck, and she let him have that too, and the coin went straight across the ring to the machine shop, and by evening Tam had the housing open and the new governor seated, working with her head against the pipe and one hand flat, the way she'd found the fault. At full burn the drive came up clean. No lag, no half-beat. Tam stood in the engine room and listened to it for a long time, and Voss stood in the hatchway and listened to her listening. It sounded like an engine. Nothing else.

# Eight — Dry Thunder The transfer was set for noon, station local, and Pell was there first. The *Providence* waystation kept an empty dock at noon — hands at their shift, shifts at their meals — and Pell would have said he liked punctuality and not have known the difference. Kite's ship stood at one end of the bay with the cream crate already down on its hand truck, readout amber, steady, a full new battery under it. Pell stood at the dock's center with his notebook and his ink and two company men in Meridian gray, and the *Copperhead*'s ramp came down at noon exactly, and everyone walked to the middle of the bay in the flat light like people who had all done this before, which only one of them had. Doc came down the ramp on his own legs. Pell's protocol wanted a condition report from the last attending physician, certified at transfer, so Doc was ink-legal on that dock, sleeve down, fevers or no, and Voss hadn't argued with him about it on the way down, which they both understood to have been the argument. "Viable," Doc said, reading off his own clipboard. "Thin. Sound in limb. Fed daily." "Mm," Pell said, and wrote it in ink. "You're the last holding party, Captain." He turned the notebook to the clean page and laid the pen across it. "It signs here, witnessed, and the file closes, and you've noticed by now I don't say that word idly." Voss signed. She signed her full name, Rhea A. Voss, the way the ink wanted, and handed the pen back with her left hand, and while Pell was blotting the page Tam took the handles of the hand truck. Nobody had proposed any of it. That was how she knew it was hers to do. Tam didn't hurry. She turned the truck in a wide, careful wheel, the way you moved anything with a living readout, and started for the ramp. Doc fell in at the far side of the crate with his good hand on the rail, certifying it all the way. Voss walked backward behind them both, unhurried, and her sidearm was out and low, and her other hand was flat and empty and visible, which had been training once and was now just grammar. Pell closed the notebook. "Recover the item," he said. His voice didn't rise. "It's a recovery, not a shooting. Recover the item." The two in gray looked at the dock. There was a girl of seventeen on one hand truck, an old man with one arm, a woman they'd been told was a salvor, and a file that had been, thirty seconds prior, closed. One of them stepped forward into the space between the truck and the ramp, close, too close, and the crate's wheel caught on the ramp lip and jolted, and from inside the crate came the struck bell. Once. The first sound any of them had ever heard it make. The guard flinched and fired. She had the whole four seconds like something viewed through a spinning fan. Tam hauling. The crate tipping and Doc reaching for it — reaching to steady a box, or to steady the girl, or already moving to put himself somewhere, and afterward Voss could not say which, and there was no version she could check, and she stopped checking. The round took Doc high in the chest. Voss fired twice and could not afterward say at what. Her second round sparked off the bay floor a meter from anybody. The other guard never fired at all. He stood looking at Pell, waiting on an order that was worded for an ink world and didn't cover any of this one. Kite had stepped aside. One step, unhurried, out of the line between the gray men and the truck, before any of it started, and he stood there with his hands flat and empty and his warrant closed and his face like a man reading something badly written, and he did nothing at all, and the nothing held. "Kite—" Pell said. Kite didn't look at him. They got Doc up the ramp between them. He was talking on the deck, clinic-level, easy, somewhere else. "Day forty. Gain up. It's still going." He was counting. "Forty-one, forty-two—" He stopped between one number and the next, and the ramp came up, and the burn was rough and shallow and nobody cared, and nobody agreed afterward on the order of any of it. They buried him on the first green world past the Line, in the morning, quickly. Nobody said anything that would have satisfied an audit. It got done. The rest happened somewhere else. In the evenings now the galley was lit, and the water dish was back on the hold deck at 1900, and Tam had taught Sunday a card game. It held its cards wrong-jointed and careful, the way it held everything, and showed them to the whole galaxy every time it had anything, and lost, every hand, and dealt its winnings back across the table to be beaten again. Voss drank her coffee out of the beaker. Nobody had proposed that either. Past midnight, when the ship was quiet the way the ship was quiet now, Sunday sang Perdido at the viewport. The four-minute chorus, thin, every note a half-tone bent off true — learned off a dying battery and a cracked log thirty years gone, and it sang the errors the way the recording had fed them to it, and it would carry them now for the whole of its life. Nobody aboard had ever heard the true version. Nobody corrected it.

Initial Writing Prompt:
Possession Horror Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: I caught her staring at me again. She thought I'd been sleeping.
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Possession Horror Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: I caught her staring at me again. She thought I&#x27;d been sleeping. -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. The purpose of this reflection is to narrow in on what you think will work best to make a piece that is a. compelling, and b. fits the prompt requirements. Model Output:
# Brainstorming **The opening line gives me a lot to work with.** "I caught her staring at me again. She thought I'd been sleeping." Three things jump out: (1) *again* — this is a pattern, dread with history behind it; (2) the narrator was *pretending* to sleep — so he's already afraid of her, already hiding from her; (3) the staring happens at night, in the most intimate, vulnerable domestic space. The relationship is almost certainly marital or familial. The prompt implies the narrator already suspects something is wrong but hasn't named it yet. **The central question: who is possessed?** This is where the story can go in very different directions. **Option A — The starer is possessed (the expected read).** Mark's wife, Ellie, nearly drowned in the lake behind their house six months ago. She was revived after four minutes. Since then she doesn't quite sleep, doesn't quite blink at the right times, watches him at night. He assumes the staring is the first sign of whatever is wrong with her. Classic escalation: investigation, discovery, failed intervention, tragedy. Straightforward, deeply archetypal, but risks being the possession story everyone has read. **Option B — The narrator is the possessed one (the misdirection).** Ellie stares because she can *see* something attached to Mark — something that settles onto him when he sleeps, something she's been guarding him against or studying. He misreads her vigilance as threat. The horror of misinterpretation: the person watching over you becomes the person you push away, and removing her removes the protection. The prompt itself is a misreading, which is elegant. **Option C — The narrator is the demon (full reversal).** First-person voice of the entity that took a woman's body years ago. "Her" is the original owner — a soul not fully evicted, still pressed up against the inside of her own eyes, staring at the intruder who wears her life. The reader slowly realizes the narrator isn't human. Structurally risky but conceptually striking: possession horror from inside the possessor, unreliable by nature. **Option D — Two souls in one body.** The narrator and "her" share his body. She surfaces when he sleeps. He wakes with mud on his shoes, unfamiliar bruises, a smell of lake water. The staring happens in mirrors, or in the hypnagogic border state between waking and sleep, where he can see her watching from behind his own reflection. Body-horror-adjacent, very intimate, harder to plot outward. **Option E — Parent/child variant.** Teenage daughter stares at the father after a séance or ritual. Mother knows more than she's saying. Family fracture as horror engine. Solid but the marital version is tighter for 8,000 words. **Option F — The possession as parasitic love.** The thing in Ellie doesn't want her life. It wants *him*. The staring isn't predatory menace; it's courtship, study, rehearsal. It's learning how to be loved by him, how to be Ellie convincingly, or how to be a better version of Ellie — and its endgame is Mark himself. **Tone and register options:** slow-burn domestic gothic (Rosemary's Baby, Jackson's "The Daemon Lover"); folk horror with the lake as a thin place; ambiguous psychological horror where madness is never ruled out; body horror with wet, wrong physical detail. The lake gives me folk-horror texture: drowned things, cold water, the way a lake keeps what it takes. **Structural devices:** each chapter anchored to a night (a countdown rhythm); found documents (Ellie's journal, a doctor's notes, a recording); alternating before/after the drowning; Ellie's voice breaking through in fragments; the opening line recurring verbatim at the end, transformed by context. **Ending possibilities:** - The entity transfers to Mark; final chapter is told from inside the entity wearing him. - Cycle inversion: last line mirrors the first — Mark now stares at someone sleeping, possessed himself, and the story loops. - Ellie expels the thing at the cost of herself; bittersweet, quiet devastation. - Ambiguity preserved: was it ever real, or grief and insomnia? - Mark realizes the thing in Ellie has been *protecting* him from the thing that has always been on him. **Pacing beat sheet across 8 chapters (~1000 words each, so roughly 2–3 scenes per chapter):** (1) the staring incident, normalcy cracking, backstory hinted; (2) accumulation of wrongness, investigation, denial; (3) first undeniable proof — a recording, a witnessed event; (4) seeking help, isolation, other people fail him; (5) revelation of the true history/backstory; (6) false victory or catastrophic intervention; (7) climax; (8) aftermath, twist or cycle. # Reflection **On Option A alone:** It's the most legible version of the prompt, but it's also the version readers predict by the end of chapter two. If I go this route, the story only earns its length through the *specifics* — the texture of the drowning, the entity's particular hunger, the wife's fight to remain visible inside her own body. A generic demon will not sustain eight chapters. The possession needs a *want*, and Option F supplies one: the entity isn't haunting Mark, it's courting him. That reframes every earlier scene retroactively — the staring was never menace, it was study. That retroactive recontextualization is what makes possession stories land. **On Option C:** The reversed POV is the most formally interesting, but sustaining an inhuman first-person voice for 8,000 words is a high-wire act, and the twist would need to surface around chapter four or five rather than at the end, or the story becomes a guessing game rather than a horror. It also strains the prompt slightly — the intimacy of "she thought I'd been sleeping" reads human, and the strongest horror here is domestic. I'd rather keep the reader in the marriage. **On Option B:** The misdirection version is genuinely good, and it honors the prompt's built-in misreading. But it tends toward a lonely, abstract antagonist — "a thing attached to Mark" that never gets a body or a face until late, which weakens the middle chapters. A hybrid of A/B/F feels stronger: Ellie *is* possessed — that's real, not misread — but the possession's target isn't her. She's the vessel, the practice run, the reconnaissance. The staring at Mark across the pillow is the entity looking at its *next* body. This gives me both the legible domestic escalation of A and a genuine gut-punch turn. **On the ending:** The cycle inversion is the strongest choice available. The story opens with "I caught her staring at me again" and closes with the same line reversed — the possession has passed, and Mark (or the thing in Mark) watches someone else pretend to sleep. It's economical, chilling, and makes the whole story a single revolution of a wheel that was already turning before chapter one. It also justifies the 8-chapter length: the reader needs enough time inside Mark's fear that the reversal of his position lands as horror, not as gimmick. **On pacing risks:** The danger zone is chapters 4–5, where possession stories typically sag — the "finding a priest / researching the entity" chapters. I can counter this by making chapter 4 about a failed *human* intervention (a doctor, a family member) that isolates Mark further and lets Ellie surface briefly to warn him, and by making chapter 5 a genuine revelation chapter — the truth about the drowning (she was dead longer than anyone admitted; something spoke to her under the water, or she agreed to bring something back). The lake should be the story's spine: cold water as the membrane between things. **On word budget:** 1,000 words per chapter means every chapter needs a single job and one strong scene image — the recording, the mud on the sheets, the moment she blinks wrong, the entity's first words in Mark's voice. No subplots, minimal secondary cast: Mark, Ellie, one skeptic (a sister or a doctor), and the lake. **What I'm converging toward (not yet locked):** a domestic slow-burn — Mark and Ellie, a near-drowning six months ago, escalating wrongness rooted in the staring, a mid-story reframe that the entity wants *him*, and a final-chapter inversion of the opening line. The reflection suggests Option A's structure carrying Option F's heart, with the cycle ending. The remaining open questions for drafting: how explicitly the entity's rules are explained (I lean toward minimal — folk horror over exorcism procedural), and whether Ellie gets a final moment of true self before the end (I lean toward yes, one devastating scene — the drowned woman saying goodbye inside her own body).

Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Core premise:** A domestic possession horror. Mark's wife Ellie nearly drowned in the lake behind their house six months ago. She was revived, but something came back with her. The story is told from Mark's first-person perspective as he slowly realizes the woman in his bed is not entirely his wife — and, more devastatingly, that whatever is inside her is not interested in keeping her. **The engine of the horror:** The staring. The opening line ("I caught her staring at me again. She thought I'd been sleeping") is a misreading that the entire story corrects. Mark assumes the staring is threat. It is actually *study*. The entity is using Ellie as a vessel and a vantage point, learning how to be loved by Mark, rehearsing intimacy, preparing to take him instead. The reader should feel this recontextualization retroactively — every previous scene of staring should curdle in memory once the truth surfaces. **The twist:** The entity's target is not Ellie but Mark. She is the practice run. The reconnaissance. The staring across the pillow was never menace — it was courtship. **The ending:** Cycle inversion. The story opens with Mark pretending to sleep while Ellie stares. The story closes with Ellie (freed, or hollowed, or grieving) pretending to sleep while the thing wearing Mark stares. The final line will mirror the opening line, transformed by everything between. **Voice and style:** - First person, close, present-tense-leaning — claustrophobic interiority - Literary horror register: restrained, precise, imagistic. Quiet dread over spectacle. Shirley Jackson's domestic wrongness, Paul Tremblay's ambiguity, A24's *The Blackcoat's Daughter* stillness - The lake is the story's spine: cold water as the membrane between living and nonliving. Wet imagery throughout — mud, condensation, the smell of lakewater in dry rooms - Minimal cast: Mark, Ellie, one skeptic (her sister Dee), one witness to the drowning (a retired paramedic). No priests, no exorcists, no internet research montages **Things to avoid:** - Exorcism procedural structure (no holy water, no Latin, no rules-of-the-demon exposition) - Over-explanation of the entity. Folk horror implies; it doesn't diagram - Gore or jump scares. The horror is proximity — the wrongness of someone you love being *slightly off* - Secondary subplots. Every scene must advance the staring or the drowning - Elliptical ambiguity that frustrates. The possession is *real*. The reader should be certain by chapter four **Things to aim for:** - Retroactive dread: earlier scenes recontextualized by later revelations - One devastating scene where the real Ellie surfaces — the drowned woman saying goodbye inside her own body - Sensory specificity over abstraction: the entity's wrongness expressed through small physical tells (blink timing, breath rhythm, the temperature of her skin) - The 1000-word-per-chapter constraint honored by giving each chapter one job and one indelible image --- # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — "The Watching" (~1000 words)** Mark pretends to sleep and catches Ellie staring at him across the pillow in the dark. Her eyes don't adjust to the light the way they should. He holds very still. She eventually closes her eyes, but not before he notices she hasn't blinked in over a minute. Morning: Ellie is warm, normal, making coffee, and Mark almost convinces himself it was a dream. Establish their marriage — tender, tired, six months past the accident at the lake. She was underwater for four minutes. That's what he was told. End on a small wrong note: he finds dried mud on her nightstand, though she hasn't been outside in days. **Chapter 2 — "Small Wrongs" (~1000 words)** Accumulation. Ellie hums a melody Mark doesn't recognize — later he'll realize it's the sound of water moving. She stands at the window facing the lake at 3 a.m., perfectly still, breathing in a rhythm that matches the wave pattern. When Mark touches her shoulder she turns and smiles before her eyes find him — like the smile was already there, waiting. He tries to talk about the accident. She deflects with a tenderness that feels borrowed. A lunch with her sister Dee: Dee notices something too, but can't name it, and Mark doesn't push. He starts pretending to sleep every night. She stares every night. **Chapter 3 — "The Recording" (~1000 words)** Desperate for proof — or disproof — Mark sets his phone to record the bedroom overnight. What he hears isn't the staring (staring is silent). It's *after* the staring: a low, rhythmic sound like water moving against a hull, then Ellie's voice, but wrong — flat, rehearsed, saying his name over and over with the cadence of someone practicing a greeting. Then, near dawn, a single sentence in a voice that isn't quite hers: "He's almost ready." Mark deletes the recording. Then sits in the car and wishes he hadn't. **Chapter 4 — "The Surface" (~1000 words)** Mark reaches out. He calls Dee, hints at his fears; she thinks he's cracking under grief and sleep deprivation. He contacts Dr. Voss, a retired paramedic who worked the drowning. Voss is hesitant, evasive, then hangs up mid-call. That night — the pivotal scene — Ellie comes to bed and something in her shifts. For three minutes, the real Ellie surfaces: she's crying, shaking, gripping his wrist too hard, and she whispers: "Don't let it learn you. It's not looking *at* you. It's looking *through* me. I can't hold it much longer — it's so cold in here, Mark —" Then the surface closes over. The thing in her smiles and says "Bad dream, sweetheart?" **Chapter 5 — "Four Minutes" (~1000 words)** Mark drives to Voss's house and demands the truth. The paramedic finally breaks: Ellie wasn't underwater for four minutes. It was closer to eleven. The medics had called it. She was dead on the shore. Then she opened her eyes on her own — no shock, no CPR success — and the first thing she said was "He's warm," while looking directly at Mark, who was kneeling in the mud sobbing. Voss never told anyone because who would believe it, and because he's spent six years since his own retirement trying not to think about the lake. He tells Mark one more thing: the lake has done this before. In the 1970s. A family. A staring husband. Mark drives home in silence. **Chapter 6 — "The Goodbye" (~1000 words)** Mark finds Ellie's journal — hidden, written in a hand that degrades over pages, the early entries hers, the later ones something else's. The early entries are love letters to him, instructions, a map of herself in case she starts disappearing. *If I stop humming the song from our wedding, I'm already gone.* He confronts her with it, gently, at the kitchen table. And Ellie — the real one, fighting up through whatever depth she's trapped in — surfaces one last time. She tells him she can feel it moving through her like current. She tells him she knew what it wanted from the way it stared at Mark through her eyes. She tells him she's sorry. And she asks him to take her to the lake — because whatever came out of it must go back in, and only the vessel can carry it there. This is the devastating scene. End: they drive to the water in the last light. **Chapter 7 — "The Lake" (~1000 words)** Climax at the shoreline. The ritual isn't Latin or candles — it's Ellie walking back into the water that killed her, with Mark holding her hands from the shallows, pulling her back at the last possible moment. But the entity has been waiting for this. It never needed Ellie at the lake. It needed *Mark* at the lake. As Ellie submerges, the thing inside her doesn't resist — it releases her and reaches for him through the water, through the mud, through the cold. He gets her out. She's alive, herself, weeping, human, *warm* — and Mark is standing in the shallows feeling something settle into place behind his eyes. The last thing he sees with his own clarity is Ellie looking at him with dawning, absolute horror. He smiles. It feels like someone else's smile. **Chapter 8 — "The Staring" (~1000 words)** Aftermath, tonally inverted. Ellie has moved them to an apartment in the city, away from the lake, and Mark notices she sleeps with the light on now. She flinches when he hums. She's been pretending to sleep — he can tell, because he can hear the difference between a real heart rate and a rehearsed one. Weeks pass. The thing wearing Mark is patient. It doesn't need the lake to take what it wants — it never did. The lake was just a door. Final scene: nighttime, the same bedroom geometry as chapter one. The narrator — no longer fully Mark — lies awake, watching Ellie across the pillow, watching her chest rise and fall in a carefully staged rhythm. She's pretending to sleep. She thinks he doesn't know. Final line: *"She caught me staring at her again. She thought I'd been sleeping."*

Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive.
