# Chapter Seven — The Lake I want the decision on the record, all of it, because a decision you can't explain is a vacancy, and I'm done filing those. I drove home from work on a Tuesday in the second week of November and she was at the window, and I stood in the yard where I'd stood after Alden, and I understood I'd been standing in that yard for weeks, and that standing in yards is a thing you do instead of arithmetic. Voss said don't take her back to the water. She — one of the two of them — said take her back to the water. Dee would say get help. The neurologist would say adjust my expectations. Every instruction I owned had been handed to me by somebody, and a man who can't originate a move can at least count the hands offering him one. I walked in and said: "Come to the lake with me." She was up off the window seat before I finished the sentence — quick, easy, reaching for her coat on the hook like we were going out for the mail. "It's freezing out," she said, and got her coat anyway, and put her boots on standing, one hand on my shoulder for balance, fourteen pounds of pressure, exactly the way she always has. Every part of her agreed. That's the detail I've turned over since. She didn't ask why. There was no reason on earth she'd have come to the water in November without asking why, unless the why was hers. We went down through the yard, past the dead garden, past Mrs. Kowalski's dark windows, and out on the dock, and the wind off the water was doing what November wind does to a face. She stopped at the end and looked at me — the dock light on the far side of the cove, the Hendersons' place dark, geese long gone south — and she said: "It goes on the list, Mark." And she went in. I want the physical facts plainly stated because the physical facts are all I have left. She went in off the end of the dock, not a dive, a step, in her coat and her boots, and the water took her the way it takes everything — completely. She didn't struggle. She went down through her own ripples and the November water closed over her without a sound I could file. I was in after her, and the cold was what it was in April, an object rather than a condition. I found her hands in the dark under and I held them, the way I'd held them on the shore, and I planted my feet on the bottom, waist-deep, and I waited. I have never in my life waited like that. I counted. Eight to the minute. I'd count her back, or I'd count for both of us, or I'd just count, and the water stood in me and the sky did nothing. And here's what the record has to hold, and I'll hold it as flat as I can. I felt it leave her. Not a struggle. Nothing left the way a hand lets go of something it's finished with. Something went through the water between us — not toward the deep. Toward the shallows. Toward me. And the hands I was holding stopped being a held thing and became a weight, a woman's weight, all at once, the way a puppet becomes a body when you set it down. I hauled her. I want it stated that hauling a human being out of November water is nothing a movie prepares you for — the dead weight of her, the boots full of lake, her ribs, God, her ribs, and she came to on the stones and vomited water into the mud for a long time, on her hands and knees where I'd knelt over her in April, and then she was shivering, and I want it on the record that shivering is a good sign. It's the body defending its temperature. It means somebody's home. She said my name. I can't tell you the way she said it without telling you fourteen years, but it went in two parts the way it's always gone, the second part falling, the way you say a word you've said ten thousand times to one person. Her eyes were hers. Her pupils did what pupils do. She looked at me from the mud and she was in there, wrecked and furious and cold, and she said my name the old way, and the whole lake was behind her and it didn't matter, she was back, the arithmetic had finally come out, I'd done something — And the cold stopped being cold. I've looked for the sentence in me that comes next and it isn't mine. Waist-deep in November, holding my wife's hands, weeping with relief, and the water went quiet in me like silt settling, and the wind stopped being wind, and something came to rest behind my eyes the way a boat comes to rest against a dock. I did not fight it. I want that stated plainly, because the record has been about vacancies from the beginning, and I have to close the file honestly: there was no fight because there was no lock. It had watched me for months. It knew the room was available. It had known since the shore — *he's warm* — that the door was open in me, and it is a patient thing, cold water is a patient thing, and I was the shore it had been rowing toward the whole time. The last thing I saw with what's mine was her face. She'd gone still on the stones, not shivering anymore, done being cold the way you stop being cold when fear outbids the weather, and I watched the horror come up in her like weather, and I watched her know it, and her mouth made the first part of my name and didn't finish it. My face did the rest itself. I've seen the smile in the mirror since. It's a good smile. It's warm. The water was warm.

# Chapter Eight — The Staring We live on the fourth floor of a building in the city now, three hours from any water, and I want the move on the record because the move was hers. Ellie found the listing, signed the lease, hired the movers, changed the address on everything — she did it in nine days in December with the efficiency of a woman who has a plan and no interest in discussing it. The building has an elevator and a garbage disposal and no view worth the word. There's a mirror in the elevator. I practice the worried face in it, between floors, and then I stop, and just look, and it's very comfortable. The bedroom light stays on all night. That's her doing too. I've filed it and made no comment, the way you'd note that a client has added a clause: not my department to ask why. She sleeps facing the door. She asked for the side of the bed closest to it, which meant we switched, which means the geometry in there is reversed now — I'm on her old side, she's on mine, and the streetlight through the blinds puts its stripe across the pillow between us, up the wall, moving like breathing when the traffic moves. It took me two weeks to place what the stripe was reminding me of, and then I placed it, and I want it noted that I placed it with something a claims man would call satisfaction. She pretends to sleep. I want to be precise, because precision is what I have. There's a technique: slack jaw, mouth just parted, breath through the nose at eight to the minute, the eyelids done with the slow settle and not the squeeze. She learned it recently — December, I'd say, from watching me, or from a memory of watching me — and I'd know it anywhere, because I built it. She was on the dock in April and I was the one on the shore, and every night since we moved she lies facing the door and does my own method back at me, and it's good. It's very good. There are only two tells. Her breath runs eight to the minute, yes, but the exhales hold a quarter-second too long, like someone performing the number rather than owning it. And she counts in her head. I can hear the counting, the way I've always been able to hear counting — it's how this started, her counting me, months before either of us said a word about it. She counts to hold the rhythm. I never needed to count. I've been faking sleep since I was nine, and she's been faking it for a month, and the difference between us is that I was never once fooled by her, and she knows it, and the light stays on. There's a man who lives in me somewhere. I'll put that on the record too, flatly, because the file demands it. He's far back, in a room with the door open — that's his own phrase, the vacancy, he was very proud of that phrase — and he's fading the way anything fades in cold water. He surfaces in small ways I've learned to leave alone. Last week I made a joke at dinner and then apologized for it, and I understand this is residue; he always apologized for the jokes. He figured out the humming, one night in January. She flinched when I hummed — she flinches every time — and he worked out, far back, in his slow ledger way, where the melody came from, and I'll tell you what he found, because it was his last good file: it's the sound of the lake at night. Water against dock pilings. He heard it for three years, off the end of his own dock, and never once filed it as a voice, and it is a voice, and it was saying the same thing the whole time. It was saying: I'm patient. It was saying: I'll learn your house. I don't hum around Dee, but the phone carries everything eventually. She called in February, and I want the call transcribed, because the transcript is the whole of it. "He's doing really well, Dee. Sleeping better. I know everyone worries, but honestly? I think the move was good for us." Every word true, which is the only kind of word I keep. There was a pause on the line with weather in it. Then: "Mark. Put my sister on." And then Ellie, from the kitchen, coming to the phone with her dish towel, saying "Everything okay?" in the voice that has fourteen years in it, and Dee's voice going somewhere I could hear but not reach: "Ellie. Why is your husband humming Mom's song?" Nobody humming. Nobody had hummed. I've gone back over that call the way I've gone over every night since April, and I can't find where the melody got onto the line, and I want it noted that I'm not concerned. Dee's mother was eleven months dying, and Dee spent all of it on watch, and grief does things to the witnesses. Dee said she'd call back. There's been no call back. There's a note on the calendar for Thanksgiving that nobody's written anything next to. The shopping list on the fridge reads: coffee, the good olive oil, stamps. She wrote the stamps, and then took the pen away, and I've made nothing of that, because there's nothing yet to make. My phone lies face-up on the nightstand now. I stopped doing that in December. It's a good phone. It has nothing on it that frightens me, and it's watched me do everything since, and I don't mind being watched by things. I never did, really. It was only ever the man I'm wearing who minded. Tonight the stripe is on the ceiling, moving like breathing. She's facing the door, doing the technique — jaw slack, eyelids settled, eight to the minute with the quarter-second hold. There was one moment, a month ago, when her mouth started the first part of my name in her sleep — the real sleep, the deep kind, the kind I've never once seen her get — and stopped herself before it finished, and I've kept that in the file where I keep the counting and the light. She hasn't said the name since the lake. I don't need it said. I have all the time in cold water, and the door is open, and I watch her the way I've watched everyone I've ever loved across a pillow: patiently, all night if I have to. She caught me staring at her again. She thought I'd been sleeping.

# Brainstorming **The core hook:** "They fucked with the wrong babysitter" implies (1) someone was wronged—violently, personally, unforgivably, and (2) the babysitter appears to be the least threatening person in the room until she isn't. Pulp demands immediacy: blood, betrayal, a body count, and a protagonist who solves problems with force and nerve rather than patience. **Interpreting "babysitter" — who is she?** - **The Retired Operator:** Ex-military, ex-mercenary, ex-enforcer for a criminal outfit. She babysits because it's quiet, because she loves the kid, because she's trying to be a person instead of a weapon. Her old life comes knocking. Classic, satisfying, easily pulped up. - **The Career Sitter with a Dark Streak:** No special forces past—just a woman who grew up hard, scrappy, mean when cornered. More grounded, grittier, but harder to justify her surviving against professionals. - **The Framed One:** She was blamed for something—a kid hurt on her watch, a kidnapping she "allowed." She lost everything and now hunts the actual perpetrators. This gives a longer-burning revenge motive. - **The Suburban Avenger:** Comic pulp angle—the people who wronged her are the neighborhood itself: a corrupt HOA, PTA moms running a money laundering ring, cops on the take. Tonally lighter, more Elmore Leonard, more satire. **Who are "they"?** - A crew of home invaders who hit the wrong house while she's watching the kid. - Her old crew/employer—she took money, or a kid, and skipped town; they've found her. - The family she works for—turns out the sweet suburban parents are monsters (traffickers, cultists, white-collar butchers), and she finds out. - The kidnappers who took the child during her watch, then framed or gaslit her. **What's "the wrong" done to her?** - They hurt/kidnapped the kid she was protecting. - They killed someone she loved (her own child? her partner?) and the babysitting job was her way of rebuilding. - They destroyed her reputation and life via a frame job. - They came into *her* house—the house where she was the only line between a child and violence. **Timeline structures:** - **Single-night siege:** Die Hard in a Colonial. One location, escalating violence over 8–10 hours, claustrophobic and propulsive. Strong momentum, hard to sustain 8,000 words without it feeling like a video game level. - **The slow burn:** The wrong happens in chapter 1, then a campaign of revenge over weeks. More room for character, investigation, double-crosses, set-piece confrontations. - **Braided timeline:** Present-day revenge chapters intercut with flashbacks to the night of the wrong. Each flashback reveals another layer of what "they" did and another skill from her past. Good for pacing reveals. - **Crescendo structure:** Wrong committed early → she plans and takes out the crew one by one (mini-climax per chapter) → final boss confrontation with the boss who ordered it. **Tone options:** - Hardboiled noir: terse sentences, cigarette smoke, rain, moral compromise. - Men's adventure magazine pulp: lurid cover-art energy, chapter-ending cliffhangers ("The last thing she saw was the muzzle flash"), punchy violence, red-blooded momentum. - Crime caper: Donald Westlake/Westlake-as-Stark *Parker* energy—professional, procedural, cold. - Revenge tragedy: darker, where the revenge costs her the thing she was avenging. **Chapter title possibilities (very pulp):** "Sitter," "The House on Kessler Road," "Bad Men, Good Night," "What the Knife Was For," "Insurance," "Bedtime Story." **Specific scene seeds:** - Opening in medias res: blood on her hands, a baby monitor crackling, a man tied to a kitchen chair. - A babysitter interview at the start—smiling, sweet,references, sunlit—juxtaposed with what she keeps in her bag. - The moment the invaders realize the soft-looking girl is something else—a beat where the reader gets to savor the turn. - A confrontation where a bad guy monologues his advantage and she's already undone it. - Using babysitting/domestic imagery as weapons: baby monitors as surveillance, alphabet blocks hiding razor blades, knowledge of the house's layout as a weapon. - A final scene where she tucks the kid in, blood drying on her knuckles—closure image. - Betrayal beat: the parents who hired her are complicit, or a friend sells her out. - A cop or fixer character who could go either way—classic pulp wild card. **Character roster ideas:** - The babysitter: name options—Marisol "Mari" Vega; Wren; Delia Kane; Sadie. Mid-30s, underestimated, precise. A tell: she counts exits, sits with her back to walls, hums lullabies while doing terrible things. - The kid: 6–8 years old, precocious, the reason she stays human. The kid should matter, not just be a prop—maybe the kid saves her at a key moment, or their bond is the story's heart. - The villain boss: someone who ordered the wrong and remains smugly untouchable. Pulp thrives on a boss who deserves what's coming. - The crew: named heavies with distinct traits—the knife guy, the talker, the one with a conscience who becomes a liability/wild card. - The parents: oblivious, complicit, or dead. Their fate is a moral fulcrum. **Pacing over 8 chapters (~1000 words each):** - One big set-piece every 1–2 chapters; a twist or cliffhanger at every chapter end; flashbacks or reveals rationed one per chapter. - Chapter 1 must open with a hook and establish the wrong—or at least its aftermath. - Chapter 4 (midpoint) should flip the story: a reversal, a betrayal, or a reveal that reframes everything. - Chapter 7 is the low point/all-is-lost. - Chapter 8 delivers the climax and the resonant final image. # Reflection The prompt's title reads like an old men's adventure magazine cover, so the tone should lean hard into that: punchy, lurid, propulsive, with chapter-end cliffhangers. A tongue-in-cheek suburban caper risks undercutting the satisfying "wronged professional gets even" core. A pure noir slow-burn might spread 8,000 words too thin. The strongest fit is pulpy hardboiled with momentum and wry menace—a babysitter who is retired violence, because that's the premise's promised turn. The single-night siege is tempting for momentum but risks monotony: eight chapters in one house means the violence must escalate through ever-more-contrived staging. A crescendo structure—wrong committed up front, then a revenge campaign across locations, ending with the boss—gives each chapter its own shape, own mini-climax, and lets the body count feel earned. But I want a slice of that siege energy in the opening wrong, so the ideal shape is: **the wrong happens in chapter 1–2 (the night they attacked the house / took the kid while she was on duty), then chapters 3–7 are her methodical campaign, chapter 8 the reckoning.** This directly delivers on the title—"they" wrong her first, then learn the lesson. The ex-crew option is strongest for "they" because it pre-loads history: the invaders aren't random, the betrayal can be layered (they knew her, they sent people she trained with), and the boss has a personal reason to tie off a loose end. The wronged party should include the kid—hurting or endangering the child she protects is the one sin that makes the revenge morally clean and emotionally hot. If the kid dies, it's tragedy; if the kid survives but is taken, we get the bonus drive of a rescue mission braided with the revenge. Kidnapping-not-murder also lets the ending be satisfying rather than only bleak, which suits pulp. The kid needs real presence across the campaign—the story is better if she's protecting a small person who talks back, not an abstract motivation. Flashbacks should be rationed: one per chapter maximum, showing pieces of her old life and the original night. Pacing-wise, every chapter needs a kill, a reveal, or a reversal; the midpoint (chapter 4) should carry the biggest twist—perhaps that the parents were complicit in the kidnapping, or that one crew member wants to defect. The final image should rhyme with the opening: her doing the ordinary work of babysitting, but changed—or the world around her changed and the routine intact. Blood on knuckles, bedtime story, lights out. That's the pulp promise kept.

Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>

# Intention **Premise & hook:** Delia "Dee" Kane is a 34-year-old babysitter in a quiet suburb — formerly a "sitter" in the employ of Asa Voss, a criminal fixer: in the trade, a sitter is the operative who watches a mark, clocks their routine, and opens the door for the kill team. She walked away five years ago with Voss's ledger as insurance and rebuilt herself around the most ordinary job she could find. She has been watching Theo Halloran, age seven, three nights a week for two years. He is the reason she stays human. The night a crew hits the Halloran house and takes Theo while she's on duty, she recognizes the tradecraft — it's Voss's. The kidnapping is half debt-collection (Theo's father Mark owes Voss serious money) and half trap: Voss knows exactly who the babysitter is, and he wants his loose end tied off. They fucked with the wrong babysitter twice over — they hurt her kid, and they sent her old world to do it. **Structure:** The wrong is committed in Chapter 1; the aftermath and her decision occupy Chapter 2; Chapters 3–7 are the campaign — hunting the crew one name at a time, a kill or major reveal per chapter, a cliffhanger to end every chapter; Chapter 8 is the reckoning with Voss and the closing image. **Key choices:** - **Theo survives.** The kid is kidnapped, not killed. This keeps the revenge morally hot and lets a rescue braid through the revenge plot. Theo is a real character — dinosaur-obsessed, mouthy, hums the lullaby Dee taught him — and he actively helps at the critical moment. - **Midpoint twist (Ch 4):** Mark Halloran is complicit. He arranged a staged kidnapping with Voss to clear his debt, not knowing Voss would turn it real to flush Dee out of hiding. The father sold out his own son's sitter. - **The ledger** is the McGuffin — the burn book she took when she left, which names Voss's clients. It's what Voss actually wants. - **Coyle**, her old partner, leads the crew — the story's tragic secondary. In the end he chooses her and dies for it. - **Voice:** First-person, past tense, hardboiled and wry. Terse sentences. Domestic imagery as menace — baby monitors as surveillance, alphabet blocks hiding razor blades, a bedtime lullaby as a signal. She counts exits, sits with her back to walls, and stays underestimated right up until the moment the story's title pays off. - **Aim for:** Pulp momentum — every chapter ends on a turn. Real cost — she gets hurt, loses allies, wins ugly. An ending that rhymes with the opening: blood dried on her knuckles, a bedtime story, lights out. - **Avoid:** Sexualized violence, graphic harm to the child, cartoon invincibility, cops arriving to solve anything, torture-porn, and a kid who's only a prop. Also avoid the comedic suburban-HOA angle — the men's-adventure-magazine tone is the right register for this title. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — "Bedtime"** (~1,000 words) A normal night: dinner, dinosaurs, the lullaby, Theo asleep by 8:30. Dee's tells — counting exits, the bag she never lets out of reach — seeded lightly. Two men come in through the back. A brutal, close-quarters fight in the kitchen and stairwell: she breaks one, but a third hits her with a taser and she goes down watching a silhouette carry Theo out. She hears a phrase — "clean crib" — old Voss crew shorthand. Cliffhanger: she's bleeding on the nursery floor, and she knows exactly whose people these are. **Chapter 2 — "The Sitter"** (~1,000 words) Aftermath: cops take statements, swallow the home-invasion narrative, treat her as a witness. She pockets evidence before they bag it. Flashback (rationed, one per chapter): who she was, what a "sitter" is, the job five years ago she refused — one that involved a kid — and the ledger she took when she walked. She visits her buried stash in a storage unit: guns, cash, the burn book. End: she burns her quiet life's paperwork, loads the bag, and leaves a note for no one. **Chapter 3 — "First Names"** (~1,000 words) The campaign begins. She finds the crew's wheelman/talker through a pawned-phone trail and works him over in a parking garage. Confirms: the job was off-book for Voss, Mark Halloran's debt is the cover story, and the crew knew the babysitter's identity before they went in. She leaves him alive as a message — a message Voss's people will finish. Cliffhanger: the crew leader's name. Coyle. **Chapter 4 — "Debt"** (~1,000 words) She confronts Mark Halloran. Midpoint twist: he arranged a staged kidnapping to erase seven figures of debt — and told Voss who the sitter was as a sweetener, assuming Dee was "just a babysitter" and irrelevant. Voss turned it real to smoke out the woman who took his ledger. Grace Halloran (the mother) knew nothing; Dee promises Mark nothing. He gives her the contact protocol. Cliffhanger: Coyle calls her own phone. He has Theo. He wants to talk. **Chapter 5 — "The Trade"** (~1,000 words) Diner meeting with Coyle — old partner, old loyalties, real history. His offer: the ledger for the kid, clean exchange. She smells a kill box, springs it first; both sides double-cross. Wounded in the escape, she takes two things: a location (a safe house upstate) and a defector — Petey, the crew's youngest, who didn't sign up for kidnapping children. Cliffhanger: Voss moves the timeline — Theo is being moved tonight, and not to be returned. **Chapter 6 — "All Quiet"** (~1,000 words) Low point. Dee hits the safe house early with Petey's intel — it's a trap inside a trap. Petey is killed for his betrayal; she's taken. Voss gets his ledger back, gloats properly, and reveals the plan: Theo stays as permanent leverage on Halloran, and Dee gets a shallow grave. Zip-tied in a basement. Cliffhanger: through the wall, faint — Theo humming their lullaby. He's here. He heard her name. **Chapter 7 — "Wrong House"** (~1,000 words) The escape. Domestic tradecraft as warfare: a razor blade in a barrette, Theo's help from the other side of the wall — he kills the lights, bites a guard, slips her the key. She carves up the safe house. Coyle stands between her and the door; the fight is ugly and personal — and at the last second he chooses her, takes the bullet meant for her, dies for it. She gets Theo out, hands him to Grace and a state-trooper post as a hard boundary, and turns back toward Voss's estate. Cliffhanger: she walks up the drive with everything she has left. **Chapter 8 — "Lights Out"** (~1,000 words) The reckoning. Voss's estate the night of a client party. Dee uses the one advantage nobody priced: she knows this house — she sat in it for years, watching marks, learning the servant's doors and blind spots. She dismantles the security, and when Voss monologues his advantage, she's already undone it — the ledger was copied years ago and is already in the mail to three federal offices and three rival clients; his partners have been quietly informed; his evening drink was prepared in his own kitchen. The boss dies by his own sin. Closing image rhyming with Chapter 1: three nights later, a different porch, a bandaged hand, a bedtime story. Theo asleep. Lights out.

# How a Human Might Approach This Piece Before critiquing the plan, it's worth picturing what a flesh-and-blood writer — say, someone who grew up on Parker novels and old Gold Medal paperbacks, who now writes crime fiction for a small press — would actually do with "they fucked with the wrong babysitter." **They'd come to it with love, not a mandate.** A human writing pulp has specific appetites. They've stolen something particular: the procedural competence of *Parker*, the domestic menace of *The Professional*, the deadpan violence of *Get Shorty*. Their story would show the seams of those loves. An LLM, given "pulp revenge tale," produces an averaged distillation of a genre it has read about rather than in. The result is genre-flavored rather than genre-native. **They'd write out of an itch, not an outline.** A human would likely have two or three scenes burning a hole in them before they knew the plot — the fight in the kitchen, the kid humming through a wall, whatever it is — and build outward from those. Some chapters would be over-polished because they were fun, others conspicuously thin because they were connective tissue the writer resented writing. The plan, as it stands, is evenly excellent on paper, which is exactly the problem: it promises evenly excellent execution, and evenness is a machine signature. **They'd know things the plan doesn't.** A real writer has held jobs, watched kids, been underestimated. They'd know a babysitter charges somewhere between $15 and $25 an hour, that parents text weird passive-aggressive messages from dates they're trying to save, that you learn a house through its snack schedule. They'd know what a broken nose feels like, or at least commit to a specific, credible fiction of it. This material lives and dies in specificity. **They'd be willing to be uncool.** A human writer of pulp will sometimes write something that doesn't work — a sentimental beat, a chapter about the ex-partner's funeral nobody asked for — because they needed it for themselves. The LLM equivalent of this is not sincerity but *manufactured* poignancy: the kid's lullaby deployed at the structurally optimal moment for maximum emotional yield. Human sentiment is lumpy and badly placed. That's what makes it land. **They'd end colder.** This is the big one, and I'll return to it. Genre-literate humans know that pulp endings are rarely clean wins. Parker ends books with less money than he wanted. *The Killers* ends with the protagonized dead and nobody caring. The satisfying pulp ending gives the reader the kill they were promised and withholds everything else. A human knows this instinctively; an LLM has to be *told*. # Telltale LLM Approaches and Why They'd Sink This Particular Piece **The bow-tied ending.** The plan's Chapter 8 is the worst offender, and I'll flag it now so the deep dive can circle back: the ledger is copied and mailed to federal offices *and* rival clients, the partners are quietly informed, the empire collapses in one evening, the villain dies "by his own sin," and then we get a closing image that "rhymes with Chapter 1." That is not one bow; that is four bows on the same package. A human pulp writer would kill Voss and let the empire rot slowly offscreen, or never confirm the ledger did anything at all. **Writing safely with a violence costume on.** LLMs told to write violence choreograph it but don't inhabit it. You get camera directions — "she pivoted, driving her elbow into his jaw" — without weight, duration, consequence, or the mundane ugliness of real fights: how exhausting they are, how long a tased person takes to get their legs back, the fact that your hand breaks when you punch a skull. Pulp violence needs to be *specific* and *costly*, or the revenge has no exchange rate. If the fights are frictionless, the reader feels nothing when she wins. **The polished sentence disease.** LLM prose wants every sentence to be an aphorism; pulp wants roughly one aphorism per thousand words and plain momentum otherwise. The genre's power is in short declaratives, concrete nouns, and a narrator who doesn't know she's being quotable. If Dee's every chapter-ending line is a perfect zinger, she stops being a person and becomes a delivery mechanism for the title. **Saying the title out loud.** The single most predictable failure mode for this specific prompt: at some climactic moment, Dee says "you picked the wrong babysitter" or Voss's man says "she was just a babysitter" with a sneer. A human might use that line once, mockingly, from a bad guy early on, and never have anyone acknowledge how it turned out. The LLM cannot resist underlining the thesis. **Tidiness as compulsion.** The plan currently gives every named character a purpose, an arc, and a death that "means something": Petey dies *for his betrayal*, Coyle dies *for choosing her*, Voss dies *of his own sin*. That's narrative accounting, not storytelling. Human crime fiction is full of guys who just drive away, whose names you never learn, whose deaths are meaningless. Loose threads are texture. When every thread is woven in, the world feels small and authored. **Moral legibility.** In the plan, everyone's goodness or badness is indexed to how they treated the child. Grace "knew nothing" — the innocent mother. Mark is the bad father. Theo is pure. This binary is safe and warm and false. Human mess: Grace could be angry at Dee, irrationally, because anger is easier than grief. Grace could have suspected Mark's finances and chosen not to look. A mother who half-knew is a person; a mother who knew nothing is a plot device. **The competence fantasy without friction.** Dee in the plan is five years rusty — the plan even says so — but every subsequent beat shows her winning: works the wheelman, springs the trap first, escapes the basement, dismantles the estate. Rust is claimed, never demonstrated. A human writer of professional-criminal fiction knows the genre's real pleasure is watching a pro be *imperfectly* excellent: she misjudges a guy's reach, her taser hand is her wrong hand, she has to quit a fight she's losing. Competence that costs nothing is the LLM's action-figure mode. **Sensory-filler syndrome.** Expect LLM prose in this genre to smell rain three times, taste copper, and hear fluorescent lights buzz. Pulp sensory detail is idiosyncratic: the smell of a man's fear in a parked car, the sound a zip tie makes when it cinches. Write what Dee would notice, which is not what a poetry workshop would notice. # Deep Dive: Chapter-by-Chapter Critique Against These Pitfalls **Chapter 1 — "Bedtime."** The structure is sound (warmth, rupture, cliffhanger) and honestly this chapter is the least at risk. The pitfalls here are prose-level: the LLM will want the domestic warmth *too* warm — the kid too cute, the dinner too lovingly described — because it's manufacturing the emotional stake the reader is supposed to feel later. A human makes Theo slightly annoying (he wants a third book, he cheats at the dinosaur quiz) because an annoying kid is a real kid and a real kid is a stake. Also watch "clean crib": good pulp shorthand, but the plan must resist the urge to have Dee internally explain the term to the reader in the same breath she hears it. Trust the reader to feel her recognize it. **Chapter 2 — "The Sitter."** Highest risk chapter. Flashbacks in LLM hands are compressed résumés: "Five years ago, Delia Kane was the best sitter in Asa Voss's employ, until the night a job went wrong..." No. A human reveals the past sideways and partially: a specific job detail that implies the rest, a single sentence about a man she watched through a window for three weeks. The plan's worst idea in this chapter is the *note for no one* — that's a manufactured-poignancy flag; it's the LLM writing a symbol instead of an act. Also, "burns her quiet life's paperwork" is a movie beat. What paperwork does a babysitter have? **Chapter 3 — "First Names."** "Works him over in a parking garage" — fine, pulp-standard. The trope risk is the interrogation itself: LLM interrogations are transactional and clean. Human version: the wheelman is exhausted, mid-divorce, doesn't even hold out long, and the information comes out pathetically rather than through prowess. The plan's good instinct is leaving him alive as a message. The risk is what happens to him next: if Voss's people kill him offscreen as promised, that's the tidy-accounting problem again. Letting him survive, scared, and resurface would be more human. Also, "leaves him alive as a message" is itself a phrase an LLM loves; the act can survive, the phrasing can't. **Chapter 4 — "Debt."** The midpoint twist (Mark arranged it, used Dee as a sweetener) is genuinely good — it's grim, it's plausible, it deepens the wrong. But the *scene* as planned is a confession: she confronts Mark, Mark confesses, gives her the contact protocol. Too clean. A human version would have Mark lie first, badly, or have her find it in his phone and never give him the dignity of a confrontation, or have Voss *tell her*, specifically to make her spend the night hating the father instead of him. Also: the plan says "she promises Mark nothing," which is an LLM's way of hinting at menace without paying for it. Decide what happens to Mark and let it be unsatisfying in a true way — Grace leaving him might be crueler than anything Dee does. **Chapter 5 — "The Trade."** "She smells a kill box, springs it first" — this is the competence-without-friction problem at its purest. She's five years out of the game and she reads the double-cross perfectly and wins the exchange? Let the double-cross half-work. Let her get clipped in the escape *because* she trusted Coyle's face for one second. The Petey problem lives here: "the crew's youngest, who didn't sign up for kidnapping children" is a stock figure — the sympathetic defector — with no texture. Give him something mundane: he does a side hustle reselling sneakers, he calls his mom, he's not especially young. If he's going to die in Chapter 6, he should die as a person, not as "the betrayal-consequence character." **Chapter 6 — "All Quiet."** Structurally this is the right low point and the cliffhanger (Theo humming through the wall) is the plan's single best beat. Real, specific, cheap, devastating. Protect it. But: "Voss gets his ledger back, gloats properly" — the word "properly" is doing genre-cliché work. Voss should not gloat; gloats are for operetta villains. A scarier version: Voss is *disappointed* in her, tired, almost kind — he talks to her like an old employer about a disappointing former employee. That's more menacing and more human. Also the plan has Voss "reveal the plan" — villain-exposition syndrome. He should reveal almost nothing; she should piece together the worse truth from what he says by accident. **Chapter 7 — "Wrong House."** The razor blade in a barrette: fine, pulp-functional. But the chapter plan has stacked humanizing machinery: Theo kills the lights, bites a guard, slips her the key, the lullaby motif pays off here (if it's being used as a signal — cut that; the humming in Ch 6 is enough, a motif shouldn't be a Swiss Army knife). Coyle's death — "takes the bullet meant for her, dies for it" — is the most conventional beat in the plan. Every LLM redemption ends this way. What would a human do? Maybe Coyle doesn't get a clean heroic death; maybe he's simply shot by his own people while hesitating, and it's ugly and abrupt and she doesn't even get to say anything. Or maybe he lives and goes to prison and that's worse for him. The "chooses her and dies" version is the sentimental optimum the LLM reaches for. Also "hands him to Grace and a state-trooper post as a hard boundary" — the phrase "hard boundary" is therapy-speak leaking into a pulp narrator's mouth. Dee doesn't narrate in therapeutic vocabulary. **Chapter 8 — "Lights Out."** The most rewrite-needing chapter, as flagged. Problems in order: (1) The ledger-as-omnibus-solution — mailed to feds *and* rivals, collapsing Voss's empire on schedule — is LLM-scale justice, where one action produces total consequence. Institutions survive scandals; rivals kill you for other reasons; the ledger should do *less* than she hoped, or its effects should be unknown. (2) "She knows this house — she sat in it for years" is a genuinely good idea undermined by "when Voss monologues his advantage, she's already undone it," which is the Mission: Impossible beat, the smartest-person-in-the-room beat, the beat that asks the reader to applaud rather than worry. (3) "The boss dies by his own sin" — poetic justice is a fairy tale mechanism. Voss dying because his evening drink was prepared in his own kitchen is elegant, and elegance is the wrong currency here. Consider: she just shoots him mid-sentence. The emotional climax was Coyle and Theo; this is garbage-taking-out. (4) The closing rhyme — "three nights later, different porch, bedtime story, lights out" — is the bow. It tells the reader everything healed. A human version leaves one grain of sand in the shoe: her bag is closer than it used to be. She checks the back door twice. Or the story ends at the trooper post and we never see the porch at all. # Brainstorm: Ways to Make It More Human **Embrace friction in the competence.** Dee's five years of rust should be a physical fact: her draw is slower, she favors a hand, her cardio fails in a stairwell and she's terrified by that, because the body knows the truth before the mind admits it. Give her at least one clear tactical mistake per chapter that she has to claw back from. **Give her an economy.** Human crime writers think in numbers. What Dee charged as a sitter for Voss ($15k a job?) versus $20 an hour for the Hallorans, and how she privately runs the math constantly — the babysitting money is *real* to her in a way the old money never was. That's a character tic a reader can hold. **Let one heavy be a bore.** At least one crew member is a tired middle-aged man with a bad back and a kid of his own, who is doing a job. He's not evil; he's inadequate. Maybe he's the one who slips up and tells her something without needing to be "worked over." **De-commit the motif.** The lullaby hummed through the wall in Chapter 6 is the story's best moment. Use it exactly once as a signal (Ch 6) and never again. Cut the "lullaby as rescue signal in Ch 7." A motif that does one thing perfectly beats a motif that does three things adequately. And end the story without it — no humming over the final porch image. **Never say the title.** Or if the phrase "wrong babysitter" appears at all, put it in a bad guy's mouth early, dismissively ("relax, it's a babysitter with a taser"), and never note the irony. The reader supplies it. That's the difference between a story that trusts you and one that taps you on the shoulder. **Mess the moral ledger.** Grace's anger at Dee — irrational, wrong, deeply human — is worth a scene. Mark's fate should be something other than clean comeuppance or clean forgiveness; a human option is Grace quietly divorcing him and nobody ever telling Theo why, and Dee having to sit with the knowledge at the end of the story. Punishments delivered by life are more pulp than punishments delivered by plot. **Break the outline's symmetry.** One chapter should be structurally wrong for the plan: a chapter with almost no violence, or one where she loses a fight entirely and has to run. The LLM discipline of one kill-or-reveal per chapter is good scaffolding but produces metronome rhythm. Chapter 5 might be best as a near-silent chapter: the diner meeting, no sprung trap, just two old colleagues talking around a betrayal neither will name, ending with her walking out not knowing if she's been played. **Muddy the ledger's power.** Options: she copied it years ago, but the copies are five years stale and name clients Voss no longer has. Or she mailed it and nothing happens on-page, ever — the reader, like Dee, has to live with unverified justice. The kill becomes the only justice she *knows* she got. That's pulp: small, certain, cold. **Threaten the ending's warmth without destroying it.** The genre reader has earned Theo back and a porch. But the last beat should carry one honest grain: she's watching a different kid, or the same kid with a bag within reach and the back door double-checked, and no narration explaining what that means. An image with an itch in it — that's the human version of a rhyme. **Prose-level commitments.** First person, past tense, mostly short sentences, one or two long ones when she's watching and waiting. Dee narrates the way she works: counts exits, prices things, avoids adjectives when verbs will do. No aphorism more than once per chapter. No smelling rain. Violence written for duration and cost, not choreography — a fight is over in three sentences and the *aftermath* gets a page, because aftermath is where a human writer's attention lives and an LLM's doesn't.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>

# Intention **Premise.** Delia "Dee" Kane, 34, watches Theo Halloran, age seven, three nights a week for twenty dollars an hour. Five years ago she was a "sitter" for fixer Asa Voss — the operative who watched a mark, learned their routine, and opened the door. She walked out mid-job with Voss's ledger and spent five years being ordinary on purpose. One night a crew takes Theo on her watch, and she recognizes the tradecraft as Voss's. They hurt her kid and sent her old world to do it — twice over, they chose the wrong babysitter. **The plot skeleton (kept deliberately lean for 8,000 words).** Ch 1: the wrong. Ch 2: the decision. Ch 3–4: the campaign's first names and the midpoint twist (the father sold her out). Ch 5: the Coyle diner — near-silent, no trap-springing. Ch 6: the low point — she's captured, and hears Theo humming through a wall. Ch 7: escape; Coyle dies ugly and abrupt. Ch 8: Voss, stripped of cleverness — and a coda with one grain of sand in it. **Voice and style.** First person, past tense, mostly short declaratives. Dee narrates the way she works: counts exits, prices everything, distrusts adjectives. One aphorism maximum per chapter. Violence written for duration and cost rather than choreography — a fight is three sentences, the *aftermath* gets the space. Rust is a physical fact of the prose: her draw is slower, her cardio fails in a stairwell, she breaks her hand in Ch 1 and it stays broken for the whole story. **Character corrections from the critique.** Theo is slightly annoying — cheats at the dinosaur quiz, negotiates for a third book — because a real kid is a stake. The lullaby motif is used exactly once, as the through-the-wall hum in Ch 6, and never again. The sympathetic young defector (Petey) is cut entirely; his slot goes to a tired, heavy middle-aged crew man who spills information pathetically, not under duress. Coyle's death is not a redemption arc — he hesitates and his own people shoot him, fast, and she doesn't get to say anything. Voss never gloats; he's disappointed in her, tired, almost kind, and it's much worse. The ledger's power is deliberately muddied — her copies are five years stale, and whether the mail ever did anything is never confirmed on the page. Mark Halloran gets no comeuppance scene; Grace quietly divorces him and Theo is never told why, and Dee has to sit with that. Grace is irrationally angry at Dee — wrong, and human. **Aiming for:** pulp momentum with a broken rhythm (one chapter nearly silent, one she loses outright); consequences that outlive their scenes; an ending that gives the reader Theo back but keeps one itch — the bag closer than it used to be. **Avoiding:** the title ever being spoken or nodded at (one bad guy says "relax, it's a babysitter," dismissively, early, and no one notices); gloats; poetic justice; Mission: Impossible beats where she's already undone the villain's plan; the ledger-as-omnibus-solution; therapy-speak ("hard boundary," "closure"); manufactured poignancy (no notes to no one, no burned paperwork); smelling rain; four bows on the ending. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — "Bedtime"** (~1,000 words) An ordinary night rendered specific: chicken nuggets negotiated to sixteen, the dinosaur quiz (Theo cheats), Theo asleep at 8:40. Dee's tells woven in plainly — she knows the back door sticks, sits facing the stairs, keeps her bag by the couch. Two men come in through the back. The fight is short and costly: she breaks her hand on a jaw, gets one man down, and eats the taser from a third. As they carry Theo out, one says "clean crib." Another, annoyed at her twitching on the floor: "Relax. It's a babysitter." No interiority explaining either phrase. Cliffhanger: on the nursery floor, hand already swelling, she knows whose shorthand that is — and the reader doesn't yet know why she isn't screaming for the cops so much as reaching for her phone. **Chapter 2 — "The Sitter"** (~1,000 words) Cops take statements and swallow the home-invasion narrative; Grace is shattered, Mark is oddly composed — a seed planted, not flagged. Dee pockets evidence before they bag it. Her past comes out sideways through a storage unit: she pays three months in advance, unlocks a footlocker, and the objects do the expositing — the cash in rubber bands, the old phone, the ledger wrapped in a dish towel. One flashback paragraph, concrete: three weeks watching a man through a window once, and the job she refused, the one with a kid in it. No résumé narration. She takes the gun, the money, and the book, and does not burn anything — she just doesn't go back. End: her hand won't close around the steering wheel, and she prices the drive. **Chapter 3 — "First Names"** (~1,000 words) The campaign starts ugly and small. She finds the wheelman through the pawned phone — and he turns out to be a tired man named Tarkis, mid-divorce, bad back, doing a job. He doesn't get worked over; he spills pathetically over gas-station coffee, mostly because he needs someone to talk to and can't tell his sponsor. Confirms: the hit was off-book for Voss, Mark Halloran's debt is the cover story, and the crew had her name and face before they walked in. She leaves him alive, scared, and drives away not feeling like the woman in the movies who does this. Cliffhanger: she asks who ran the crew. Tarkis won't say it. He just says, "You know him," and looks at her broken hand like it answers something. **Chapter 4 — "Debt"** (~1,000 words) She confronts Mark Halloran, and he lies first — badly, about a poker debt, about the alarm code, and the numbers don't add up. She finds the truth in his phone while he's in the bathroom: he arranged a *staged* kidnapping to erase seven figures owed to Voss, and threw in a sweetener — the identity of his babysitter, assuming she was nobody. Voss turned it real to smoke out whoever took his ledger. Midpoint twist delivered through evidence, not confession. Grace comes home mid-scene and her anger lands on the wrong person — on Dee, for being there, for surviving it. Dee takes the contact protocol off Mark and promises him nothing, and means it as insufficiently as it sounds. Cliffhanger: her own phone rings. A voice she hasn't heard in five years says, "You kept the kid's bedtime. I always liked that about you." Coyle. **Chapter 5 — "The Trade"** (~1,000 words) The near-silent chapter. A diner off the parkway, 2 a.m., two old colleagues and a pot of coffee neither drinks. Coyle offers the trade — the book for the kid — and they talk entirely around the betrayal neither will name: a job in Jersey they both remember wrong, a woman named Fatima they don't discuss, the fact that he called her "Dee" and she called him nothing. No trap gets sprung, no moves get made. He slides a napkin with an address across the table and says he's off the rest of it, whatever that means. Cliffhanger: she walks out not knowing if she's been given a gift or set up, and she can't tell — and she's five years out of practice at telling — and the last line is her decision made anyway: she puts the car in drive. **Chapter 6 — "All Quiet"** (~1,000 words) The low point, and she loses outright. The address was true — that's the trap. They're waiting for the book, and she brought it, because she wanted the kid more than she wanted to be smart. Voss's people take both. Voss appears: no gloat, no monologue — he's tired and disappointed, talks to her like an employer to a former employee who let him down, takes the ledger, confirms nothing about Theo, and leaves her zip-tied in a basement with a man watching the door and a shallow grave already rented. Cliffhanger — the story's one use of its motif: through the wall, faint, someone small humming the lullaby she taught him. Theo is here. And he's humming because he's scared, and humming is what he has. **Chapter 7 — "Wrong House"** (~1,000 words) The escape, written for cost. Razor from her barrette, twenty minutes of work on the zip tie, a hand that won't grip. Theo helps from the other side of the wall the way a seven-year-old actually can: he kills the hall light, he bites the guard who picks him up, he has already untied himself because seven-year-olds are half knot anyway. She clears the house ugly — no choreography, just duration, noise, and the aftermath getting the page. Coyle is in the kitchen when she comes through it, gun drawn on the guard, not on her — and his own people shoot him for the hesitation before she can speak. No dying words. She takes Theo out through the back that sticks, hands him off at the trooper post to Grace, and Grace says the wrong thing again, and Dee lets her. Cliffhanger: Voss isn't running. Voss is at home. She knows the house. **Chapter 8 — "Lights Out"** (~1,000 words) Stripped to the bone. No party, no security gauntlet, no monologue about undone plans. She enters through the servant's door because she spent three years learning this house from the inside and never forgot a hinge. Voss, in slippers, is genuinely unsurprised. He starts a sentence — about the ledger, or the copies she mailed years ago, or the stale names of clients he no longer has, none of which she can verify and none of which will arrive in time — and she shoots him mid-word, because the kill is the only justice she'll ever *know* she got. Two paragraphs, cold, done. Then the coda, three weeks later: Theo's new house, his father gone without explanation, a different couch, a bedtime story she reads all the way through. No lullaby, no narration explaining anything. Final image: she moves her bag a foot closer to the door, checks the back lock twice, and turns out the light.

# Dee Kane (Delia "Dee" Kane) **Background & personality.** Thirty-four. Grew up in Schenectady, daughter of an assembly-line father who drank with a specific rhythm she learned before she was ten — she could tell his mood from the sound the front door made. That's where the watching started: as survival, not tradecraft. At twenty-three she was an insurance-fraud investigator, good at it in a way that embarrassed the men she worked with. She got recruited sideways: she clocked one of Asa Voss's men surveilling her mark and reported it to her boss, who sold her name to Voss, who paid more. Seven years sitting marks for Voss — learning a man's dog's name, his mistress's parking spot, the hinges on his back door. She walked at twenty-nine over a job with a kid inside the perimeter, and she took the ledger with her because Voss keeps receipts on everyone and she kept a receipt on him. Five years of Camry, cash, storage unit. Two years of the Hallorans. She is dry, watchful, allergic to being thanked. She prices everything — it's how she thinks. She isn't hard-bitten so much as *tired in advance*: she expects the worst not dramatically but the way you expect traffic. She was starting to like the Hallorans, which is the thing that actually got broken. **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** Counts exits; sits facing doors; keeps her bag within reach even at dinner. Presses her thumb against each fingertip in sequence when she's thinking, and will deny it. Watches movies she's already seen because "nothing can happen I don't already know about." Runs constant arithmetic: twenty an hour, three nights, against four grand a week from Voss, and can't make the sums say what she feels about them. Knows her storage-unit due date the way other people know their anniversary. Flaws: cannot accept help and won't ask — she's been alone so well it's become a performance she gives to an audience of herself. Deflects everything warm with a joke, then resents people for laughing. Five years of rust is real: the heavy bag in her unit has a rusted chain and she's been meaning to use it for two years. Her fatal flaw in the field: she wanted the kid more than she wanted to be smart — and knows it, and does it anyway. **Physicality.** Medium height, wiry, forearms from a job history nobody at the PTA could account for. Dressed down for five years on purpose — "the kind of woman a bartender forgets." When idle she looks like she's waiting for an appointment that's running late. After Chapter 1, her right hand is broken for the rest of the story: it changes everything — how she holds a gun, a zipper, a cup of coffee. She writes left-handed and badly. **Motives, allegiances, relationships.** Motive: they came in on her watch, and the watch is the only clean thing she ever built. She would not call it love; the reader will. Allegiances: Theo, period — and she'd be wrong, because Coyle still has a claim she won't admit. She and Grace were becoming actual friends before the job; the fake babysitting references were getting old enough to have real ones. The refusal job from five years ago has an unresolved aftermath she's never looked up. She doesn't know what happened to the kid. That's deliberate. She doesn't want to find out. **Voice.** - *(Internal, pricing things:)* "Voss paid me four grand a week to learn a man's dog's name. The Hallorans pay twenty an hour and there's no dog. I know which job I liked better. I just didn't know it counted as one." - *(To Tarkis, flat:)* "Drink your coffee. Then tell me about Thursday." - *(Internal, Chapter 1 aftermath:)* "The knuckle on my right index finger stopped being my knuckle somewhere in the first minute of the kitchen." --- # Theo Halloran **Background & personality.** Seven. Dinosaur pedant — cheats at the quiz by standing in front of the bookshelf to peek, then lectures *her*: "Pterodactyls aren't dinosaurs, they're pterosaurs, that's the oldest trick in the book." Negotiates everything like a Teamster: sixteen nuggets, not twelve; one more chapter, the short one, "say deal." He's scared of the dark and denies it, so he leaves the hall light on "for you, Miss Dee, in case you need it." Dee is his favorite adult because she doesn't lie to him — when his joke is bad she says so, and he trusts that more than laughter. He narrates his own life in third person ("And then Theo DEFEATS the vegetables"). **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** Corrects adults constantly; asks why in a loop; eats with his mouth full as a negotiating tactic. Under stress he hums — the thing Dee hums doing dishes, which he's decided is called "the dishes song" and is actually "Moon River," a fact he does not know. Flaw, if a seven-year-old can have one in this story: he believes deals. When captivity breaks that, it should cost him — he decides grown-ups lie, and nobody gets to undo that for him, even at the end. **Physicality.** Small, gap-toothed, permanent cowlick, dinosaur pajamas two sizes too big because he insisted they'd last. Hugs too hard because nobody ever taught him a softer setting. **Motives, relationships.** To be seven; to be believed. He's the story's stake and its agent at the crucial moment — he unties himself in captivity ("seven-year-olds are half knot anyway") and helps from the other side of the wall the way a kid actually can: kills the hall light, bites the guard who grabs him. He is not plucky. He's scared, he counts the days by school lunches, and he hums because humming is what he has. **Voice.** - "Pterodactyls aren't dinosaurs. They're pterosaurs. That's the oldest trick in the book." - "One more. The short one. Deal? *Say deal.*" --- # Asa Voss **Background & personality.** Mid-sixties. A fixer with an actuary's soul — he talks about people as risk exposure, and he's been in the quiet end of the business long enough to remember when the money was worse and the manners better. He keeps receipts on everyone; that's not a metaphor, it's filing cabinets. Never raises his voice. Gratitude is his management tool: he remembers birthdays, and it's worse than cruelty. He has a housekeeper who's been with him thirty years and a cat he refers to only as "the animal." Bad hip, slippers, gout he pretends is weather. **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** His flaw is the interesting one: he cannot process people leaving. Dee walking with the ledger wasn't a business problem, it's an affront he's chewed on for five years — not the money, the *ingratitude* of it. His paternalism is the ugliest thing about him; he thinks of Dee the way a father thinks of a daughter who robbed him. He underestimates nothing except sentiment — his own included. His world is consolidating around younger, louder crews, and he knows it, and it makes him tired in a way he lets people see on purpose. **Physicality.** Silver, neat, small in person — everyone expects taller. Moves carefully on the hip. Still, when seated, in a way that makes rooms arrange themselves around him. **Motives, allegiances, relationships.** Loose ends, and the one specific itch named Delia Kane. He took Mark Halloran's sweetener and turned a staged job into a live one specifically to draw her out — not for the ledger's paper value but because a ledger exists at all means she's been holding something over *him*. Allegiances: to his filing, to no living person. He was her best boss and knows it, which is what he says to her in the basement, and it should be unbearable. **Voice.** - "You were the only hire I never had to tell twice. That's the part that disappoints me." - *(To his people:)* "I don't need drama. I need a hole and a receipt." - *(In the basement, and it's worse than a gloat:)* "Sit down, Delia. Your hand looks terrible." --- # Coyle (Walter Coyle) **Background & personality.** Mid-forties. Ex-armored-car driver out of Philadelphia, Voss muscle for fifteen years; he taught Dee the watching, or likes to say he did. Keeps a rubber-banded box of diner receipts because he files taxes on cash income like a man with a mortgage on a house he'll never leave. Divorced; pays support for a daughter he sees four weekends a year and never mentions. He's a leg-breaker with a code, and the code is mostly a story he tells himself, but the story has been getting harder to tell since the crews stopped having manners. **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** Doesn't drink coffee after nine — orders it anyway when he's nervous, then doesn't touch it. Keeps his receipts. His flaw is the fatal one: he waits too long to choose a side. He's been one job away from getting out for a decade, and Chapter 7 is the last "one job." He never says anything dramatic; the drama is in the pauses he leaves, hoping Dee will fill them. **Physicality.** Big, gone soft through the middle, hands like a man who's handled safes; walks with a hitch from an old armored-car thing he never explains. Sits at counters, not tables. **Motives, allegiances, relationships.** He runs the crew because refusing Voss isn't on his menu, but the job turned from staged to real and he found out the same night Dee did — the "clean crib" phrasing wasn't his. He calls the diner meeting because he wants to hand her the address *and* wants the ledger for Voss, and he never fully decides which. The Jersey job, years back — a woman named Fatima, whose death whose-fault-it-was is the thing he and Dee have never once said aloud. He calls her Dee. She calls him Coyle. That's the whole confession. **Voice.** - "You kept the kid's bedtime. I always liked that about you." - *(Diner:)* "I don't drink coffee after nine." / "You ordered it anyway." / "I like having something on the table in front of me. Even if I don't use it." - *(Last thing he says, leaving the napkin:)* "I'm off the rest of it. Take that how you want." --- # Grace Halloran **Background & personality.** Late thirties, ICU nurse — twelve years of other people's worst nights, which made her the competent one in the marriage and the one who half-knew something was wrong with the money and chose not to look. She hired Dee two years ago, screened the references like a charge nurse, and somewhere in the last year the sitter became her closest friend without either saying so. She is neat, controlled, hugs Theo one squeeze too hard. **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** Her control is competence-based: when she can manage a thing she is the best person alive, and when she can't, she finds the nearest person to blame and works the blame like a shift. Her anger lands on Dee — wrong, and she knows it's wrong *while she's doing it*, and can't stop, because Dee is safe to be angry at. That buried wrongness (she chose not to look at Mark's money) is the engine under it. **Physicality.** Nails chewed to nothing against an otherwise pressed appearance. Stands six inches too close when she talks. Under stress, does inventory — says the contents of rooms out loud. **Motives, relationships.** Get Theo back, then reassemble a world that no longer includes most of what it included. Her two lines to Dee are the arc: the hospital rage, and the handoff at the trooper post. **Voice.** - *(Hospital, wrong and human:)* "You were *there*. You were in the house, and you couldn't—" - *(Trooper post, Theo wrapped around her:)* "Thank you. Don't come back." --- # Mark Halloran **Background & personality.** Mid-forties, commercial real estate — a man who thought he was big and was actually leveraged. Seven figures deep to Voss after a development ate him. He is affable, the soccer coach, the first-round tipper, everyone's friend, and underneath it all is a man who cannot stand being *found out*, which is the flaw that sells his babysitter's name to a fixer as a "sweetener" for a staged kidnapping he genuinely believed would return Theo by Sunday. **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** Lies badly — the poker debt, the alarm code, numbers that don't add up. Laughs early at his own jokes to buy the room. Big gesturing hands when he's lying, still ones when he's caught. He didn't ask what the sweetener would cost Dee because he assumed she was nobody, and that assumption — not the debt — is his real crime. By the end: Grace quietly divorces him, Theo is never told why, and Dee has to sit with knowing. **Physicality.** Gym-soft, good teeth, the tan of a man who golfs with lenders. **Motives.** Keep the life. Be liked. Not be seen. In that order, and he'd swear it wasn't. **Voice.** - "Nobody gets hurt in insurance, Deel. That's the whole— it's *insurance*." - *(Caught:)* "You

# Chapter 1 — Bedtime The nuggets went from twelve to sixteen because Theo held up two fingers and said, "Four more. Deal? *Say deal,*" and I said deal, because it was a Tuesday and I'd been saying deal to that kid for two years and it never once cost me more than a nugget. He ate them with his mouth open, which he does on purpose because it works. Nine years of eating dinner across from men whose names I never learned taught me how to sit through worse. "And then," he said, "quiz me." He stood in front of the bookshelf while he did it, which is how he cheats. I let it go for the pterodactyll one because correcting him on the bookshelf would've started a whole thing, and it was already eight-fifteen. "Pterosaurs aren't dinosaurs," he said anyway, to the ceiling, like he'd discovered it and not the bookshelf. "That's the oldest trick in the book." "Mm," I said. "Bath." "One more chapter. The short one." "The short one costs a bath." "Deal," he said, fast, before I could change the market. I ran the water while he narrated getting in ("And then Theo DEFEATS the soap"), and I listened to the house the way I listen to houses. Fridge, furnace, the back door doing its little settle around the latch. It sticks. It has stuck since I started working here and Mark keeps saying he'll plane it and Mark keeps not planing it. I put my bag under the end table by the couch, strap toward me, and I sat where I always sit, in the chair facing the stairs. I read the short chapter. Then I read the long one, because he negotiated for it while I was mid-sentence, which is a violation of the deal and I let it stand. Asleep by 8:40. I stood in his doorway with the hall light on and listened to him breathe. He leaves the hall light on "for you, Miss Dee, in case you need it," which he announced one night in March like he was doing me a favor, and never took back. I did the dishes. I hum while I do the dishes. I don't remember when that started. At 9:20 the back door didn't stick. That's how I knew. It didn't make the sound. A half-second of nothing where the sound goes, and I was already off the counter and my hand was already in the bag before the first one came through the kitchen doorway and I understood, in the way you understand the price of something, that the night had changed. He was big and he came in fast and confident, which meant he'd been told it was a soft house, which meant somebody had told him wrong. I hit him in the hallway where the light was bad for him and good for me. I got my forearm across his throat and put him into the wall and it should have ended there and it almost did. Then I threw the punch. I threw it right-handed and I threw it at his jaw and I felt the knuckle on my index finger stop being my knuckle. Somewhere in the first minute of the kitchen, before I even heard the second man. That's the arithmetic I did later, on the floor. The punch did its job. He went down like a bag of wet sand and my hand went with him. The second one knew what he was looking at. I watched it land on him — the quarter-second recalculation, big to careful, careful to grabbing the rail and giving me the stairs. He'd been read in on a babysitter. He was doing new math. He was still doing it when the third one came around the corner with the taser, and I never saw the third one at all. The darts took me in the back at the top of the stairs and I went down the stairs the fast way, on my side, and while I was still clenching through it — it isn't pain exactly, it's your body getting taken over and run by somebody who doesn't like you — I heard them move through the house above me. Not loud. They weren't loud. They were quiet like men going through a house they'd had described to them. Somebody went up. I heard Theo's door. I heard the little hitch in his breathing that he does when the dark gets to him and he won't say so, and I heard a man say, easy, "Hey, buddy. Your dad sent us." I got a hand on the newel post. My right hand. I got it most of the way closed and it fired a flare up my arm that whited out everything for a second, and when the second came I didn't know where the flare had gone or if I'd made any noise at all. They brought him down past me. He was wrapped in his own comforter like a rolled carpet, dinosaur pajamas inside it, and his face came around for one turn of the roll and I saw it and he saw me and his eyes were the whole word he didn't say. He bit somebody. I heard it. I heard a man hiss, "*Quit it,*" and I loved Theo Halloran so much in that one second that I could have died of it right there on the landing, useful to nobody. The one who wasn't carrying anything stood over me while the others went out through the back that didn't stick. He watched me twitch. He had a bored, unhurried face, and he was waiting for me to finish doing what the darts were doing to me, and there was nothing in his hands at all. Somebody up in Theo's room said, "Clean crib." The bored one read it off me, whatever my face did. He crouched down to my level, which men like him do when there's no percentage in it, and he said, annoyed, not unkind, the way you'd talk about weather: "Relax. It's a babysitter." Then he stood and walked out through a kitchen that had a bag of wet sand in it and a back door that somebody had planed in the last hour while I read the long chapter. I got the twitching under control the way you get a cramp under control — you don't, you wait, and you swear at it. I got myself over to the couch. I got the bag off the floor with my left hand. I got my phone out of the side pocket and I did not call 911, and later there would be people who would want to know why I didn't call 911 first. I looked at the phone. Then I looked at the back door. Clean crib. I hadn't heard that in five years and I knew exactly which world it came out of, and what it meant was that this was not a night for strangers in uniforms. What it meant was that somebody had paid to have my watch broken, and I was going to find out who, and I was going to price it.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a strong opening chapter that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me work through the key elements. **Voice and Style** The first-person voice is well-realized. Dee narrates with the promised dry arithmetic: "it never once cost me more than a nugget," "I understood, in the way you understand the price of something, that the night had changed." The short declaratives land consistently. The voice doesn't overreach — it stays in character throughout. The aphorism-avoidance is handled well; there's no single pithy line that announces itself as The Lesson. **Theo** The plan called for Theo to be slightly annoying, a real kid. He delivers: the open-mouth eating as negotiating tactic, the bookshelf cheating, the mid-sentence deal renegotiation. "And then Theo DEFEATS the soap" is exactly right. Pale ones. Fresh. Somebody had come to that door earlier in the evening — while I read the long chapter, while I hummed — and planed the latch quiet, and swept up after themselves, and missed two curls that rolled behind the hinge. I picked them up with my left hand and put them in my jeans pocket, and I drank the water, and I went back and sat down and answered everything. They took it all down the way you take down a home invasion. Bad neighborhood spillover, wrong house maybe, a crew that likes quiet streets. Brandt asked if the Hallorans had enemies and I said you'd have to ask the Hallorans, which is the kind of answer that sounds like nothing and is exactly true. Grace got home at 10:50. Mark had been at a thing — a closing, a dinner, I never got it straight and I noticed that, too, noticed that I didn't get it straight and hadn't in two years. Grace came apart in the doorway the way a person comes apart who has held it together all the way there, which is to say completely, and all at once, and only once she'd crossed her own threshold. I stood up when she came at me and she grabbed my shirt with both fists and asked me where he was, where was he, and I said I didn't know and she said *you were here* and I said yes. There was a moment in that — I'll be honest — where I almost said something about the door, and didn't, because a woman with both fists in your shirt is not a jury you make your case to. Mark stood behind her in the hallway the whole time. He had his hands at his sides and he was very calm, and at the time I filed the calm the way you file a man being in shock. I've spent five years filing things wrong on purpose. It's a lifestyle. They took Theo's room as a consolation and the rest of the night happened at the hospital, to my hand — spiral fracture, second metacarpal, the doctor said it with the enthusiasm of a man who loves a clean break — and to Grace, and not to Mark. Somewhere around 3 a.m. I left, which nobody stopped me from doing, which told me how witness-shaped I'd become in one evening. I didn't go home. Home is a studio apartment with a cat that isn't mine, belongs to the building, and I wasn't going there yet. I went to a storage unit off Route 9. The place runs month to month and I've been there five years under the name Dailey, and I always pay three months in advance, and the kid behind the counter has never once looked up. Inside, under the plastic tree stand and a box of other people's Christmas, there's a footlocker, and in the footlocker there's my old life. It doesn't take up much room. That's the thing nobody tells you about a past. Mine fits in a locker you can carry. Cash in rubber bands, counted, recounted. An old phone, charged dead, battery swollen like a tick — you charge a burner every month or it dies of it. The ledger, wrapped in a dish towel I took from Voss's kitchen because he was the kind of man who'd miss the towel. He kept receipts on everyone. I kept one on him. And the heavy bag, chain gone to rust in the corner, that I'd been meaning to use for two years. I sat on the locker and I let one flashback in, which I ration like a diabetic. Three weeks, one time, watching a man through his own windows — his dog's name was Captain, his daughter left her bike in the drive every night like a dare. That was the job I refused. There was a kid inside the perimeter, and I said no, and then I said no on my way out the door with the towel-wrapped book under my arm, and I never found out what happened after, and I made a point, a whole lifestyle, of not finding out. Five years of it. Now a man had stood over me on my own landing, in a house with a kid in it, and said the words for a tidy job, and I knew which world had come through the door that doesn't stick. I took the cash. I took the ledger. I left the Christmas. I did not burn anything. Burning things is for the movies. You just don't go back, is what you do, and I've gotten good at it.
