# Intention **The premise is honored literally, not structurally.** The prompt's nouns and verbs are the scaffolding: she is *strung up in the back* — a wagon, chains, canvas, road-noise. The wagon is the set piece for the whole first half. Her physical restraint is the relationship's barometer, loosened scene by scene: strung up (ch. 1) → down, wrists cuffed (ch. 2–3) → cuffs unlocked at the fire (ch. 4) → cuffs off at night, on her word to stay (ch. 5) → gone (ch. 6) → the thrown-open cuffs (ch. 7) → cuffs as a stolen souvenir (ch. 8). And "talk him into an early grave" is literalized as an engine: every night she pitches him a con, each more audacious, and part of the danger is that her ideas are *good* and he's tempted. Her mouth is dangerous in every register — seduction, schemes, and once or twice pure competence (talking down trouble with nothing but words). **Voice:** First person, past tense, Cade — but the noir dryness is *strained and unreliable*, not merely dry. He claims detachment while the dialogue proves otherwise; he reports her jokes as annoyances while conceding hers were better; his desire is on the page as the failure of his own restraint, occasionally pathetic, never leering in a way he'd own up to. Humor undercuts every emotional announcement. The narration is allowed to be slightly obsessive about one thing — her *hands*: what the cuffs do to them, what she does with them, the first time she touches him with both hands free. **Cade:** likable through failure, not virtue. Casual anti-tiefling prejudice in the early narration — he's complicit in how the world treats her, and the shame of wanting her is part of the heat and part of the arc. His motive is unflattering: debts to the Grey Ledger, a loan-shark guild, and a vague plan to drink himself comfortable. He loses arguments first; that's why losing other things feels inevitable. **Kess:** flawed and sovereign. She's genuinely a thief, eats more than her share, lies about small things for fun, pitches cons that would get him killed, and misreads him at least once. Her past comes in three different versions across three chapters, playful and contradictory; only one detail is independently verifiable. When he tries to hand her the hero halo in chapter 7, she refuses it. Her power in the dynamic is real — but the cuffs twist is deployed as *an act, not an absolution*: she throws the open cuffs at him mid-fight, no monologue, and the ambiguity (chosen captivity is still captivity; she stayed) is allowed to sit unresolved rather than being smoothed into a speech about choice. **The erotic approach:** committed and explicit, written at ground level — cramped wagon, cold ground, horns catching his cloak, her tail deployed for comedy and heat both, one thing going wrong per scene, interruptions, fumbling. The charge lives in small mercies: the first unlock, the first meal she eats with free hands. No safety rules stated as policy — instead, the power is negotiated messily on the page: her escalation is mixed-motive (manipulation becoming real), his restraint is a losing battle, and wanting is unmistakable from both sides in every scene. The midpoint scene precedes the moral turn so the intimacy *complicates* the choice rather than rewarding it. **The villain and the money:** Vhane is a person, not a phrase — Cade reads one of his letters at the tollhouse, and Vhane's vanity is specific (he signs his threats, he uses good ink). "Alive and unspoiled" does slow, disgusting work across the story. Cade notices the contradiction in the writ — a man who wants her unspoiled doesn't send outriders and look the other way while rival hunters roam — and that detective beat is better than exposition. Prices are concrete throughout: the 3,000-crown bounty, the 212 crowns he owes the Grey Ledger, the toll at the Blackford tollhouse, the cost of a room, the guild's cut, the horse she jokes about ruining. **Plot shape:** escort → corruption of loyalty → her scheme from chapter 2, refused then, executed in chapter 8 as the ending — an earned callback, not a bow. The chapter-6 fake-out withholds her motive: he finds the coin purse without a cute note, learns the truth third-hand at the tollhouse, and *sits in the anger*, nearly selling her out before catching himself. The chapter-7 fight is frightening rather than spectacular — her devil-blood scares him and he has to decide, in the ugly aftermath, whether he can still want her; chapter 8 resolves that, not just logistics. **Loose ends stay loose:** the Thorn brothers are scattered, not dead; Vhane is humiliated, ruined in reputation, not destroyed; she keeps more than her share of the take and dares him to object; Cade is still broke-adjacent and doesn't care. The ending is a small domestic beat, not an aphorism — the cuffs as souvenir, stolen back. **To avoid:** prompt-inverting closing lines and triple symmetry; combat choreography as spectacle; emotional announcements the prose could show; banter where every line does three jobs (let some jokes just be jokes); the itemized-bill cuteness; a hero's halo for her; a conscience that doesn't cost Cade anything on the page; flashback exposition (her history is a con she runs on *him*); neat chapter-end rhythm — vary the endings: cliffhanger, quiet beat, comic beat, mid-argument cut, and at least one chapter that barely advances plot at all. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — Three Days Out.** The wagon, the chains, the writ, the voice. Cade narrates the setup with the weariness of a man doing sums: 3,000 crowns against 212 owed to the Grey Ledger. She's strung up in the back and he has to take her down to feed her — the first loosening, played for discomfort and reluctant closeness. She's already dissected his debts and his loneliness by the second night. He insists he isn't enjoying it; the dialogue insists otherwise. End: comic beat — he catches himself answering one of her questions honestly and swears at her; off in the dark, a rider's pace matches theirs. **Chapter 2 — Coldford.** The tavern scene: she talks a wool merchant out of his boots and both of them out of a knife-fight while cuffed to a chair. The wanted-sketch on the wall has the wrong name — thread one. The innkeeper won't serve a devil in the common room; Cade lets it happen and is ashamed a beat too late — thread two. Her pitch #1: *don't deliver me — sell the writ back to him; men pay more to bury their own secrets.* He refuses; she files it away. End: quiet — he realizes he laughed tonight and cuts the thought off before it finishes. **Chapter 3 — The Thorns.** The near-miss skirmish: two Thorn brothers, road dust, ugly and short. She saves him hampered and is subtly *too* composed about the cuffs — skill on first read, choice on reread. Rough camp; wound-tending with charged hands. Pillow-talk that isn't: she tells version one of the reliquary story (heist, glory, a Magister who deserves it), and he can't tell if he believes her. She whispers the hook: "Ask why he wants me back *unspoiled*." End: mid-argument cut — he asks it, she smiles, and the chapter ends on her not answering. **Chapter 4 — The Fire.** Rain, the wagon, canvas drumming. Her instigation, mixed-motive and knowing; his restraint losing in stages. He unlocks the cuffs *first* — and it's a scene beat, not a policy: his hands shake, she notices, and doesn't let him live it down. Full explicit scene, ground-level, horns and tail and one thing going wrong. Afterward, warm and unsentimental, she tells version two of the reliquary story — it contradicts version one in one detail and one only. He chooses not to ask which is true. End: quiet, her tail across his ankle, both pretending to sleep. **Chapter 5 — The Quiet Chapter.** Barely advances plot, on purpose. A card game she cheats at, handcuffed elegance with the deck; dinner; her third and strangest version of the story. He rereads the writ by firelight and spots the contradiction — unspoiled, yet outriders and a blind eye to rival hunters — and understands the employer never expected her *unhurt*, only *usable*. Small trusts: cuffs come off at night now, on her word to stay. He catches himself doing the sums with her in them. End: cliffhanger — dawn, the fire dead, and she's gone with his coin purse and his good knife. **Chapter 6 — The Anger.** He tracks her half a day and finds nothing but the purse under his saddle blanket — no note, no joke, nothing. He sits in it. The ugliest chapter: he rides to a crossroads relay where Vhane's outriders drink, and comes within one sentence of selling her out — the actual sentence is on the page before he catches himself. He doesn't understand why she left, and the story doesn't tell him — or the reader — yet. End: comic-bleak — he buys a bad meal with her stolen coin and notices it tastes better than it should, and hates that. **Chapter 7 — The Tollhouse.** Blackford toll, dusk. Vhane's men in force — and she's already there, having intercepted the outriders days ago and bought the tollkeeper's silence; Cade learns this from the tollkeeper, third-hand, mid-ambush, not from her. The fight is frightening: something old flashes through her, the lanterns gutter, and Cade is afraid of her for one full page. Mid-fight, wordless, she throws the open cuffs at his chest — the twist shown, never explained. Aftermath: blood and quiet; he asks when; she says day two; neither knows what to do with that. He tries the hero halo; she refuses it — "I didn't want the guilt, that's all it was." End: ugly-quiet — he decides he can still want her, and the chapter doesn't celebrate it. **Chapter 8 — Irongate.** Her scheme from chapter 2, executed: forged proof of death, the reliquary's contents as leverage, Vhane paying them to say nothing — signed in his good ink, humiliated, ruined in reputation, alive and petty and vengeful someday. Costs stay real: the Thorns are still out there, she keeps the larger share and dares him to object, he's still not rich. Final scene, small and domestic: on the road *away* from Irongate, she eats with both hands free; he's kept the cuffs as a souvenir and she steals them back before he notices — or lets him notice. No aphorism. End mid-banter, like a door left open.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Cade Rennick **Background.** Forty-six. A farrier's son from Millrow, a two-cart town where the Ashen Road goes to die. Ran at fifteen — not from anything, toward the uniform — into the Iron Band of Kessel, a war company that broke eleven years later on an unpaid contract: the captains took a lord's silver and left the men standing in a field. That taught him his politics, which are: no causes, no lords, just pay. Eleven years a soldier, ten a bondsman-hunter. He is exactly as good as the job requires and no better, and he knows what that says about the job. The debt is ugly and he'd never tell it straight: his old partner Wren took a crossbow bolt meant for him outside Greyfall. He drank for a year and borrowed for the drink — the Grey Ledger, a loan-house guild, holds 640 crowns on him, carrying interest at a polite, terrible rate; the 212 crowns is this quarter's installment, the one they break legs over. He also borrowed to buy the bounty on the man who shot her and the man simply never had a price. The 3,000 for Kess clears the Ledger and buys the door out of the trade — a little house somewhere the writs don't run, a chair, a dog, and a quantity of afternoon he's never had. The stain that anchors him: three years back he delivered a deserter named Fenwick, sixteen, who cried the whole three days, and Cade delivered him anyway and drank the fee in under a week. He still does the sums on Fenwick sometimes, and they don't come out. **Personality.** Dry as a defence. He narrates losses as bookkeeping because arithmetic doesn't have feelings. He's a professional disliker of things: his tea, his tobacco, the weather, other people's festivals. Casual bigotries he's never had to examine — chapter one he thinks *devil-blood* in his own head, clean and easy, and doesn't notice it's a slur until she says it back to him with a smile in chapter two. The shame arrives a beat too late to be useful, which is the story of most of his conscience. Idiosyncrasies, with anchors: - Does sums to fall asleep. Bounty minus feed, board, tolls. He's done them wrong on purpose before, to have something to fix in the morning. - Keeps a grease-stained notebook of everything things cost — the Ledger's schedule, tolls, what a room runs in Coldford versus the shame of the common room. Writing down what things cost is how he writes down what they are. - Whetstone ritual: maintains gear when rattled. Sharpens knives that don't need it. - Talks to the horse (Copper, a rangy grey gelding bought cheap, named in a moment of optimism) in a voice he'd deny in court. - Hates being thanked. The one time she thanks him, it lands like an accusation. - Eats like a soldier — fast, hunched, folds everything in bread, wastes nothing. - His one allowed excess: her hands. He notices what the manacles do to her wrists, how she holds a cup with both hands, and he notices that he notices, and files it in the notebook he doesn't write down. - Rations his drink on the road — a nip at night, measured — and the measuring says more about him than the drinking does. **Physicality.** Big and going soft at the middle; a soldier's chest under ten years of bounty-man's laziness. Face that's been hit a lot and learned to be hit. Grey threading black at the jaw. Old pike wound in the left knee from the siege of Marle — he comes down from the wagon seat rear-first, always, and hates being caught doing it. Hands: knuckles like knots, nails trimmed flat and absurdly clean — the farrier's son in exile, his one vanity. Smells of pipe tar, leather oil, horse, and a cheap bay rum a dead woman gave him, which is why he still wears it. Sits with his back to walls. Parade-rest slouch. **Motives, allegiances, relationships.** Want: the money, and the door out. Need: to be a man rather than a hired fist — he's watched himself become a service and the notebook is how he pretends he hasn't. Allegiances: none. The Band is scattered; one friend survives, Serjeant Brann, a wheelwright now, whom Cade drinks with one day a year and never writes. Mistress Arrell of the Grey Ledger — polite, unsmiling, remembers his birthday — is less a person than weather. Wren is dead and still in the sums. Copper the horse is the last thing he's fond of that can hear his voice. And then Kess: the first person in years to hear his actual laugh, which he'd been rationing so hard he'd forgotten he owned it. **Flavour.** > "Three days out of Irongate with a devil in my cart and a devil in my debts, and only one of them was talking." > "I laughed. In Coldford. Before witnesses. A man my age, laughing at a prisoner's jokes like jokes were free, which nothing is, because I'd be paying for that laugh within the hour, and she knew the price before I did." > "The words were in my mouth before I'd decided to say them, which is where all my worst decisions live." > "She was worth three thousand crowns to the Magister and maybe forty in scrap to me if she froze on the road. I caught myself caring about the wrong number and put it in the book I don't keep." --- # Kessarah "Kess" **Background — the working core the story keeps unstable.** Twenty-six and feels older; the blood does that. Born listed: her grandmother, a tiefling matron in Irongate's Rookery district, signed a compact with something below, and the debt passes through blood. The Vhane family bought the paper generations back — bought at a discount, Kess says, because the Vanes never pay retail for anything, including people. The Magister's own collateral is coming due down below, and refinancing requires a living signatory of the line, delivered *intact and unspoiled*. Kess was that line item until she took herself off the market. She'd been Vhane's fixer for six years — retrieved things, delivered threats, unwitnessed problems. She knows where his letters sleep and can quote his hand ("he uses good ink and signs his threats; vanity like that gets people hanged"). Fourteen months running. The tail is a record of the run: the notch clipped by a manacle in Greyfall (the Thorn brothers; they'd tell it differently), the burn from a torch-happy hunter in the marshes. The three versions she tells, orbiting one truth: *(1) the righteous thief* — "he's a monster and I stole his conscience"; *(2) the back-wages* — "I robbed my employer, which is just payroll with better hours"; *(3) the strange one*, nearest true — she never stole anything, she *was* the stolen thing, the listed property, and she stole herself. The verifiable detail: version three's phrasing — *remanded property, intact and unspoiled* — matches the writ's exact legalese, which Cade can reread, and does, and sits very still about. **Personality.** Her mouth is a livelihood and a hobby and a weapon system. Teases the way other people touch. Lies recreationally — the merchant's sob story in Coldford is ninety percent invention, and the ten percent that's true is so mundane it must be real (a sugar bowl, her grandmother's, gone with the Rookery tenement). Refuses pity on pain of violence: worse than the manacles is his face going soft at her. Keeps score aloud — every kindness rendered becomes a named debt, because she'd rather be anyone's creditor than anyone's charity. Idiosyncrasies, with anchors: - Hums a Rookery lullaby when her hands are busy — locks, cards — and stops the instant she notices. - Steals sugar cubes everywhere; hoards them in her cuff. There's a system. There's always a system. - Calls him "Coins," from his arithmetic, and refuses his actual name until chapter seven — the first time she says "Cade" is mid-fight, and neither of them comments, which is how you know it cost her. - Corrects grammar mid-peril. Has corrected a man's diction while he was holding a knife to her. - Counts on her fingers, visibly, theatrically. - The tail is honest when she isn't. It gives her away at the fire in chapter four. - Claims she can't cook (lie). Claims she can't swim (lie, revealed at the worst possible comedic moment). Sleeps like she's owed all the blanket, and takes it, because she never had a room where the space was hers. - Her horns: swept, ram-curved, one cracked and capped in gold. "If it's the last thing they see, it should shine." She'd deny this at length. **Flaws.** Pride to the point of sabotage — she'd burn goodwill before she'd accept pity. Recreational lying as armour, which costs her the one conversation she can't afford to have straight. She runs from warmth: chapter six is partly tactics and partly flight from the chapter-four fire, and she will never file it as anything but tactics. She misreads people where it matters — she reads his gentleness in chapter four as technique, *softening the goods for delivery*, and is genuinely, badly thrown when it isn't; she leaves in chapter six partly because she's predicted he'll sell her out and is punishing him in advance for a betrayal he hadn't planned. Her "equal split" of the take in chapter eight is not equal, and she dares him to do the math. **Physicality.** Five feet nothing in boots and entirely unbothered by it; moves like the space is owed to her. Crimson hair, heavy and half-wild, worn like a standard. Dusky red-violet skin; gold eyes with horizontal pupils that catch lamplight like a cat's and make tavern men cross themselves. Her hands are her true face — quick, theatrical, a magician's hands; the thing he watches. Voice: low, unhurried, amused; audible even at a whisper; a voice that has talked its way out of three hangings, one of them by the Thorns. Carries herself like a duchess in a world that calls her vermin — chin up, hipshot, daring someone to say it. **Motives, allegiances, relationships.** Want: not freedom in the abstract — the specific freedom of *not being listed somewhere as an asset*. Need: to be wanted, not owned; not as vessel, not as price, not even as a job well done — and chapter four terrifies her because wanting to stay is a debt she doesn't know how to book. Allegiances: none. Auntie Nettle, Rookery

Model Output:
The sums were the first thing I did every morning and the last thing I did every night, and the middle of the day was just the part where the sums came true. Three thousand crowns on delivery. Alive and unspoiled — the writ said it twice, once in the body of it and once in the margin where a clerk had added *unspoiled* a second time as if once weren't enough for whatever the Magister had planned. Six hundred and forty owed to the Grey Ledger, two hundred twelve of it due this quarter, which was the quarter Mistress Arrell had marked in her ledger with a little red star, and I'd been on the wrong end of her red stars before. Feed for the horse, tolls, my own board. Call it forty crowns a day on the road and I was still clearing enough to buy a door and walk through it. That was the arithmetic. I'd done it every night since Greywater, and every night it came out the same, and every morning the middle of the day found a way to charge me for it. The middle of the day, in this case, was chained to a ring bolt in the back of my wagon. I'd strung her up proper, which is to say the way the guildbook tells you and the way I've always done it — wrists to the ring, high enough that she could sit or kneel but not stand, because the guildbook cares about your cargo arriving and doesn't care about anything else. I'd felt fine about it in Greywater. I felt fine about it the first day out. By the second night I had complicated feelings, and complicated feelings cost money, so I was trying not to have them. She was a tiefling. I'll be honest about the word I used in my own head, back then, because it's the one I was raised with and it rhymes with nothing I'd say to a magistrate: devil-blood. Red skin gone dusky at the joints, ram's horns off the temples, one of them cracked and capped with gold like a bad tooth, a tail that lived its own life at the end of her spine. Crimson hair on a woman the color of a struck match. You couldn't call it hiding. Taking her down to feed her was the part the guildbook doesn't cover. I had to climb into the wagon bed and unlock the ring and hold the chain short while she worked the blood back into her hands, and her hands — I'm getting ahead of myself. First the feeding, then the hands. The feeding went like this. I'd unlatch her right wrist so she could manage a cup, and she'd hold the cup with both hands, cuffed and all, and drink like a duchess at a christening, and watch me over the rim the whole time, and the whole time my thumb would be through the chain because that's how you hold chain, and I want it on the record that I never once forgot the chain. "Hm," she said, the first night. That was all. Hm. "What." "You're left-handed. You hold the chain in your right because you want the hand free. You favor the right knee getting up into the seat, which means the left one's the bad one — old, though, an old wound walks different from a new one — and you sat down on the wagon bench like the seat owed you money." She sipped. "Also you're forty-something, your horse is named Copper because you're sentimental and cheap, and you owe somebody six hundred and forty crowns and change, because you count on your fingers and your mouth moves." I sat there with the tin cup in my hand and did the only professional thing available, which was to say nothing. "Two hundred of that's due soon," she said. "That's the one that has you doing sums at night. You think nobody can hear you doing sums. You do them out loud, darling. You *narrate* them." "My name's not darling." "Your name," she said, "is Coins, until you earn a better one." Here's what I should have done. I should have re-locked the ring and climbed back up front and let the road do the talking, the way I had with every other piece of cargo these ten years. Here's what I did. I asked her how she got the six-forty figure, and she said a man who borrows at Ledger rates is a man who drinks or a man who grieves, and grieving men don't take bounty work, and I said that was rude and accurate, and she said thank you, and I caught myself meaning it. That was the first night. I'm telling it out of order, but that's how she told it to me, out of order and upside down, so it's only fair. The second night was the one I stopped feeling fine about. Rain came on toward dusk, that thin cold rain the Ashen Road gets, and the canvas drummed, and I had her down to feed her, and her wrists had gone purple in the manacles where the third day would have cracked the skin. Anybody who's done the work knows what that is. It's a cost. I sat there in the rain-noise doing the cost against the bounty, and I looked up and she was watching me do it, watching me book her wrists like a toll. "Go on," she said. Quiet, that time. Not soft. Quiet. "Tell me what I cost." "Sixty a day," I said. "Rough." "Mm. And what's the rate for taking them off?" "There isn't one. It's not in the writ." "No," she agreed. "None of me is in the writ. Not really. There's a line item where I used to be." I unlocked her left wrist to let the blood back, and held the chain, and she flexed her fingers one at a time, all ten, unhurried, like a piano player, like a woman who had done this before and knew exactly how long the feeling took to come back and had decided, somewhere in there, to be gracious about it. Then she looked at her own hands, and I looked at her hands, and I have been trying ever since not to remember that I looked at her hands the way you look at weather coming in. "Ask me," she said. "Ask you what?" "Whatever you've been not asking me for two days. You're very loud when you're not asking." So I asked her what she'd done, to be worth three thousand crowns to a Magistrate of Irongate. And she smiled at me with the gold-capped horn catching the lantern light, and she said, "Stolen goods," and she drank, and that was all I got. I re-locked the ring and climbed down off the back and up onto the seat, rear-first on account of the knee, and I sat there a while doing the sums to make myself sleepy, and I was halfway through the tolls before I noticed I'd told her about Millrow. My father shoeing horses. The whole thing, the sounds and the smell of it, told to a chained woman in the rain, and I couldn't for the life of me remember consenting to it. "Goddamn it," I said, to the canvas, to the horse, to nobody. "Mm-hm," said the wagon. She hummed something after that, while I sat out front with my pipe, some Rookery lullaby with too many notes in it, and the rain came down, and I did the sums wrong on purpose so I'd have something to fix in the morning. That's when I heard it. Out past the tree line, in the dark where the road behind us was: hoofbeats, walking pace, coming on steady. Copper flicked an ear at it before I had. The pace never changed, and it never fell behind, and I told myself it was a carrier or a pilgrim, and I did not believe me.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of opening chapter writing. Let me work through its qualities and weaknesses systematically. **Voice and Narration** The first-person voice is the chapter's greatest achievement. Cade's narration is genuinely dry without being affectless — the arithmetic conceit ("the middle of the day was just the part where the sums came true") is earned and then sustained throughout without becoming a tic. The voice has the quality the plan calls for: "noir dryness strained and unreliable." He claims detachment while the prose demonstrates otherwise. The line "I have been trying ever since not to remember that I looked at her hands the way you look at weather coming in" is excellent — it's the kind of retrospective self-awareness that makes first-person narration feel inhabited rather than performed. The plan's note about his obsession with her hands is executed beautifully here. The hands appear three times: the cup-holding, the blood-return flexing, and the weather-coming-in moment. Each escalates in emotional weight without announcement. **Dialogue** The dialogue is the chapter's second major strength. Kess's opening deductions ("You're left-handed...") could easily tip into the Sherlock Holmes parlor trick cliché, but it's saved by two things: the specificity of the details (the knee, the narrated sums) and the fact that it's immediately weaponized as intimacy rather than cleverness. "Coins" as a nickname is perfect — it's character-revealing, it's earned, and it does exactly what the plan says: her mouth is dangerous in every register. The exchange about what she cost ("Tell me what I cost" / "Sixty a day, rough") is the chapter's best moment — it's simultaneously economic, erotic, and devastating, and it's shown rather than announced. The dialogue avoids the plan's warned-against flaw of "every line doing three jobs." Some lines just land as jokes. Some are just quiet. The rhythm varies. **Character Consistency** Both characters are consistent with their profiles. Cade's casual "devil-blood" in his own narration, his rear-first dismount, his sums-as-sleep-aid, his talking to the horse (implied), his inability to remember consenting to tell her about Millrow — all of these are in the profile and rendered naturally rather than as a checklist. Kess's deductive opening, her "Coins" nickname, her humming the Rookery lullaby, her holding the cup like a duchess — all consistent. The shame arriving "a beat too late to be useful" is present in the narration's structure: he uses "devil-blood" in his head, and the chapter doesn't flag it as wrong, which is exactly right for where Cade is at chapter one. **Following the Chapter Plan** The plan calls for: the wagon, the chains, the writ, the voice; taking her down to feed her; her dissecting his debts and loneliness; him insisting he isn't enjoying it while the dialogue insists otherwise; a comic beat ending where he catches himself answering honestly; and a rider's pace matching theirs in the dark. All of these are present. The comic beat ("Goddamn it" / "Mm-hm") is well-executed — understated, not overplayed. The rider at the end is handled with appropriate restraint: no melodrama, just Copper's ear and Cade's self-deception. **Weaknesses** The chapter is not without flaws. "Like a woman who had done this before and knew exactly how long the feeling took to come back and had decided, somewhere in there, to be gracious about it" is slightly over-extended — the sentence earns its length but just barely. The "duchess at a christening" simile is good; "like a piano player" is slightly generic. The opening paragraph's density of numbers risks feeling like throat-clearing before the story starts, though it pays off thematically. The "out of order" meta-comment ("I'm telling it out of order, but that's how she told it to me") is a slight misstep — it draws attention to the narration's construction in a way that feels slightly defensive, as if the author worried the reader wouldn't follow the non-linear structure. It's the one moment where the voice becomes self-conscious in an unearned way. **Prose Quality** The prose is largely clean and controlled. There's no purple prose to speak of — the metaphors are grounded and physical. "A woman the color of a struck match" is vivid without being overwrought. The rain-noise, the canvas drumming, the lantern light on the gold-capped horn — these are sensory details that do work without calling attention to themselves. **Emotional Engagement** The chapter is emotionally engaging in a way that's unusual for an opening: it creates genuine tension not through plot but through the slow revelation of Cade's vulnerability. The moment he realizes he's told her about Millrow without consenting to it is the chapter's emotional climax, and it lands. **Plot** For a first chapter, the plot is appropriately minimal — setup, establishment, the hook of the rider. The writ's "unspoiled" detail is planted. The chapter does exactly what it needs to do without overstaying. Overall, this is a high-quality piece of genre fiction writing that executes its plan with skill and restraint. The voice is distinctive, the characters are alive, and the prose serves the story rather than performing for the reader. The sums for Coldford ran like this. Stabling three coppers with feed, two if you argued, and I can always argue. Supper two a bowl. Room eight, but I wasn't taking a room, I was taking half a stall and a hayrack and telling myself it was for the horse's sake. Add it up and Coldford was going to cost me seven coppers and whatever the town charged a man for what he'd see there, and I hadn't figured that line yet, because I hadn't met the wool merchant. But that's out of order. First the inn, because the inn came first and the inn is where I learned the first thing Coldford had to teach me. The Golden Fleece stood on the square, name painted in gold leaf that had gone the color of old butter, which tells you most of what you need to know about Coldford. I went in with her wrist cuffed to mine, thumb through the chain, because that's how you hold chain, and I'd done the arithmetic on the walk over: two bowls, eaten quick, back on the road before the light went. I got as far as the bar. "Not in my common room," the innkeeper said. He said it to me, not to her, the way you'd tell a man his dog wasn't housebroken. "You can order at the door." I want it on the record what I did, because I've had to live with it. I'd argued the stabling down from four coppers to three — I'd spent four full minutes of my voice on the innkeeper's boy about hay and the going rate of oats — and when the man told me my cargo wasn't fit to eat among honest wool, I spent none of it. I said, "Two bowls, then," I paid at the door like he asked, and I took her back out to the porch and cuffed her wrists to the crossbar of a chair, and the worst part — the part I did the sums on later, many times — is that she sat down before I'd finished reaching for the chair. She'd done this math before, in other towns, with other men, and she'd already subtracted me from it. I went back in to wait for the bowls. That's when I saw the paper. Every guild house walls its posted papers near the bar, and I read them out of habit the way you check a horse's teeth. Runaways, debts, a man from Marle who'd married twice and deserted once. And one that was her. Good likeness, actually — the artist had gotten the hair, which is most of the battle with her, and the way the chin comes up. But the name printed across it was one I hadn't heard her say and one I hadn't expected from the writ. *KESSARAH VHANE. RUNAWAY. Restore to the household of the Magister of Irongate, or his lawful agent, and receive the sum of—* I read it twice. The writ in my saddlebag said thief, said stolen goods, said three thousand crowns for return delivery, alive and unspoiled, words a magistrate uses about criminals. The paper on the wall used the words you use about property. RUNAWAY is what you post about a slave or a wife, and restore is what you do to furniture. I stood there with my thumb hooked in my belt doing the arithmetic of it — the same name as the man paying me — and I didn't ask the innkeeper a thing, because a bounty man asking questions about his own cargo is a bounty man telling the room he's thinking, and thinking is the first symptom of not delivering. That's when the boots business started, out on the porch, and I heard it through the door in pieces, the way you hear a card game you're losing. The wool merchant had come out to smoke his pipe, and I'll give him this much, he was wearing good boots — high wader-hide, the kind they make in Marle, the kind that cost more than my first horse. And she was on him like weather. I missed the opening. When I got the door open with the bowls, she had him telling her about the fleeces, about his stall at the autumn fair, about his sons, and she was laughing at everything he said like he was the funniest man in the Downs, chained to a chair in her underskirts and cold, and he was *glowing*, and I stood in the doorway with two bowls of stew and watched a master work. The trade, when it came, took under a minute. She'd turned her ankle in front of him — turned it, I'm certain, exactly the right quarter-inch — and he'd offered his sympathies, and she'd looked at his boots and said, wistful, that they must be Marle river-hide, that her grandmother had a pair once, before the tenement went, and that she'd trade her ring for them this minute, gold for good hide, just to have her feet warm in something that remembered a better house. It's not gold, the ring. I'd have bet the bounty it wasn't. He didn't check. Men don't check, when the story around the ring is the right shape. He walked back inside in his stockings, half-pleased with his own gallantry, and I set the bowls down and started figuring out what I was going to do about a prisoner in stolen boots, and I hadn't got far when his driver came back out with the ring and a knife. "You was rooked," the driver said, and put the point of it about a foot from her ribs, and here's the thing I want on the record: I had my hand on my own knife and I was three steps away, and I never got to use either. She looked at the knife the way you look at a bill you'd already budgeted for. "You *were* rooked," she said. "If we're doing this properly. And put that down, you're frightening the stew." And then, low, unhurried, in that voice that carries without ever getting loud: "Here's your morning, either way it goes. Put it away, and you're the man who watched a devil in chains take your master for his dignity — funny, free, and buying your breakfast. Put it in me and you're the man who gutted a chained woman in a wool town over a pair of boots, and my owner's magistrate will come ask you questions, and your master walks home barefoot regardless. You're not a fool. You're wearing the boots of a man who isn't a fool." The driver stood there doing sums. I knew the look; I'd been wearing it for two days. He put the knife away. He even took the boots back inside, and the merchant — and this is God's truth — told him they suited her, and to leave it, and the last I heard of the two of them was the merchant laughing at his own story with his feet under the table in his stockings. I sat down across from her with the bowls, and her tail came around and hooked one over to her, and she ate like a duchess at a christening. "You're Vhane," I said. "The name on the wall." "That's the name I was born owing," she said. She didn't look up from the stew. "Eat your supper, Coins." That night, in the stable, cuffs to the ring I set in the loft post, she made her first offer. She'd earned it, she said, and she laid it out cheap and simple, the way you lay out a hand you can't lose: don't deliver. Write to the Magister. A man pays three thousand to retrieve his property, but a man pays anything to bury his own secrets — sell the writ back, double the price, no delivery, no witnesses, no one in Irongate who's seen his paper come home in a bounty wagon with questions attached. "The last man who traded with his cargo is a hole in the Grey Road," I said. "And the last man who delivered her is going to be a rich one," she said. "I know. I've heard the offer's poor odds. I'll leave it with you. No charge tonight. I'll book it later." And she didn't push it, which frightened me more than the pitch did. Con artists push. Gardeners water what they've planted and walk away. I did my sums by lantern to make myself sleepy. Stabling, supper, the second bowl — I'd paid for two before I'd thought about it, and there's a line in the book for that if I ever fill it in. And somewhere in the middle of the column I heard myself remembering the yard, the driver's face while she worked him, and I laughed. Out loud, alone, in a stable in Coldford. I laughed tonight, I thought. In Coldford. Before witnesses, if a horse is a witness. A man my age, laughing at— No. I know what that sentence costs. I wrote down what the day had run me, every copper of it, and left the laugh off the page entirely, and I want it on the record that I knew exactly what I was doing when I did it.

I'd been doing the sums on the hoofbeats all night in Coldford, and the sums said carrier, because the pace never changed and a man with intent doesn't keep time like a mill wheel. The sums were wrong. I've said it before: the middle of the day is where they come true wrong. They came up on us at noon on the downs, where the road goes between two barrows and a fool could see the shape of an ambush a mile off, and I saw it, and I saw it was two riders, and I did the arithmetic on two riders and decided we could ride through, because two riders against a man with a writ is a conversation, not an ambush. The conversation caught us between the barrows. Thorn brothers. I knew the horses before the men — hunters keep rangy road-bred geldings like mine and these two had horses that looked like their owners, big dusty men, and the older one rode like somebody who counts, and the younger one rode like somebody who hasn't finished a thing in his life. The Thorn brothers worked the Greywater circuit. They'd been on her before. I knew that because she told me, later, and because when they came alongside the younger one looked at her the way you look at a horse that's thrown you twice. "That's our writ," the older one said. He didn't hurry it. Men who don't hurry are the ones you mind. "Paper's in my satchel," I said. "Guild seal, Greywater office, three days old. You can read it when I deliver the body that's on it." "The guild can have the paper," the younger one said. "We'll have the bounty." And here's the part I've turned over a hundred times. I was already off the seat, rear-first on account of the knee, and I had my hand on my knife, and I was working out the geometry of two mounted men and a wagon in a defile — and she spoke up from the back, chained to the ring, calm as a toll-taker. "Don't take the purse until you've seen him fight," she said. "The one who counts will circle left and wait for your brother to rush. Your brother always rushes. He rushed in Greyfall too, if it's the same brother—" and the younger one *looked at her when she said it*, looked for a full breath, and that breath cost him my knife-hand's full attention. It went ugly, which is how these things go, and short, which is the only mercy in them. The older one circled left, exactly as advertised. The younger one rushed. I gave the rusher my shoulder and the flat of a crate slat off the wagon rail, and while I did it the older one put six inches of Marle steel across my forearm, a clean cold line I didn't feel until I saw the blood doing sums of its own on the boards. She saved me while hampered. I want the manner of it on the record, because I've tried to make it sit right since and it never has. The younger one came back around the tail of the wagon for the horses' heads, and she was on him before he got there — on him, out of the wagon bed with three feet of chain paid out and both cuffed hands fisted around it, a whip with a woman on the wrong end — and she took his legs out at the ankle and put him down in the road dust, and knelt on his back with her knee between his shoulder blades, gasping, wild-haired, the gold-capped horn inches off the back of his neck. "You've had your piece of me," she said. The tail came around — I saw the notch, the old clipped place, manacle-shaped, if you know what manacles make. "Greyfall. You kept the tail. What did it fetch? I've always wanted to know what I go for by weight." He bucked under her. She stayed on like a jockey. "Give her to us and we split the three thousand," the older one said to me, across the whole tableau, mind already moving, and she laughed at that, one syllable, genuinely amused. "Coins," she said. "Tell him what you'd do to me if we split it, and watch his face when he decides the money's simpler." I didn't say it, and I didn't have to. The older one looked at her wrists, at the chain, at me leaking on the wagon boards, and did his own sums, and men who count always come out of the fight with the horse they came in on. He got his brother up. They took the north track at a trot, the younger one turning twice in the saddle with his mouth full of something I didn't stay to price. Then it was the road, the quiet, the blood. Here's the thing I did that I can't account for. I checked her cuffs before I did my arm. Guild habit, cargo first — I don't know what I told myself. The lock was sound. The wrists under it were purple and ringed and I knew what three more days of that would do to them, and I knew the writ's margin said *unspoiled*, and for the first time the two facts lay down next to each other in my head and I didn't like the bed they made. She watched me check the lock. A prisoner should sulk about a lock check. She just watched, patient, like a woman watching a man confirm something he already knew, and I filed it under *professional* and moved on. I've taken it out of the file since. It isn't *professional* in there. I don't know what it is. Camp that night was a hollow off the road and a fire I let burn small. She dressed my arm with her two hands, cuffed together, working the needle like a piano player, and I sat on a stone with my sleeve off and my mouth shut and let her sew me, because the alternative was dying of it or sewing it myself and I've done both before and she had steadier hands. She hummed while she worked. Too many notes, the same lullaby, and she stopped the second she caught me listening. "Say what you're thinking," she said. "You think loudly." "The Thorns wanted you alive," I said. "Everything wants you alive. The guild, the paper in Coldford, the Magister's margin. Alive and unspoiled. Six hundred and forty crowns of me is owed to a man who'll break my legs, and you're worth three thousand to a man who won't let you be so much as bruised. I've never in ten years carried a body everybody wanted *undamaged*, and I carried a magistrate's illegitimate daughter once." She tied off the stitch. Bit the thread. Both hands. "All right," she said, settling back, agreeable as a cat in sun. "A story, since you bled. Version one. Once there was a Magister of Irongate who trafficked in souls — bought the paper on an old compact at a discount, mind, because the Vhanes never pay retail, not for grain, not for people. And there was a woman in his household, a fixer, who fetched his letters and delivered his threats and learned where all of it slept. And she stole the one strongbox in that city that could hang him — his conscience, some men keep theirs in a reliquary — and she ran, and the writs have been chasing her ever since, because he is a monster and she robbed him blind." "True?" "Version one," she said. "I'll sell you the others." The fire ticked. My arm ached down in the sums somewhere, one more cost on the day. I watched her fold her cuffed hands in her lap, easy, like they were a muff and not iron. "Why unspoiled," I said. "You. Him. Why does he want you back exactly whole. Nobody posts *unspoiled* about a thief. They hang thieves. They don't care what condition we're hanged in." She smiled at me over the small fire, gold eyes flat and shining, and said nothing at all, and I sat there holding my own arm like something I'd carried out of a burning house, and waited, and the night filled up with the sound of her not answering.

The rain started an hour past the downs and settled in like a creditor. By the time I found a hollow with a stand of ash to break the wind, the canvas was drumming steady and the fire I built under the tailboard was more idea than warmth. I had her down to feed her — the fourth time, the wrists by now a map of everything the road had cost — and I was sitting on the crate doing the sums on the night: wet wood, cold food, the arm aching where her neat little stitches pulled. "Coins," she said. I looked up. She was watching the rain come off the canvas lip, cuffed hands quiet in her lap, and she didn't turn her head when she said it, which is how I knew I was in trouble. "You're going to Irongate," she said. "Three days more, and you deliver me to a man whose writ says *unspoiled*, and you've been very careful, and I've counted. Do you know what I haven't had in fourteen months?" "A bath," I said. "A bed. Several arguments I'd have won." "Those," she agreed. "And the rest of it." She turned her head then. Gold eyes, lantern light, the pupils gone flat and horizontal like a goat's, like a cat's, and underneath all the wreck of my good sense some old stable-boy arithmetic started running itself. "I'm not asking you to forget the chain," she said. "I'm asking you to take it off." I want the decision on the record, because I've audited it a hundred times since. The writ said unspoiled and I told myself the wrists were costing me value. I told myself she'd sit easier, sleep warmer, arrive in better condition, that it was bookkeeping. All of that was true the way a stump's a chair. My hands were on the key before I'd finished lying to myself, and here's the part she never let me live down: my hands shook. Both of them. The key chattered in the lock like a die in a cup, one cuff, then the other, and she held very still while I did it, and when the second one came off she flexed all ten fingers one at a time, unhurried, and looked at my hands, which had not stopped. "Coins," she said, gentle as a debt collector. "Your hands." "They do that in the cold," I said. "It's July," she said, "and I'm going to remember this for the rest of your life." She put both hands — both, free, the first time, and I'd been watching those hands for four days the way you watch weather — she put both of them flat on my chest and pushed me back against the wagon boards, and the boards knocked the wind half out of me, and she laughed, actually laughed, low, and said, "One thing goes wrong. It's traditional. Now hush." I'd like to tell you I was suave about the rest. The record shows otherwise. Her horn caught my cloak and held it like a coat hook while I tried to get out of it and she watched me struggle, turned out, arms crossed, providing commentary. Her tail — the tail that lies when she doesn't — the tail had opinions the whole while, wrapping my wrist, nudging my hip, once knocking the lantern so the whole tableau swung across the canvas like a shadow play, and when I finally got my mouth on her throat she made a sound I'd never heard from a chained woman, which was no sound at all, just the tail going rigid against my arm like a struck string. She touched me then. Both hands free. She'd touched me before, cuffed — dressing my arm, ten-fingered, a piano player — but this was different in kind, and she knew it was, and she was unhurried about it, criminal, the way she does everything, like the time was owed to her. And when she'd had enough of my breathing she took my hand and put it where she wanted it and said, clear as a toll-taker, "There. Yes. I'll book it, you needn't keep asking with your face." I'll spare us both the full itemized account, though Lord knows I itemize. Some lines shouldn't go in the book. What I'll enter is this: rain on canvas, her knees against my ribs, the gold-capped horn snagging the lantern light every time she tipped her head back, the lullaby humming starting up in her and dying when she caught it, dying twice, not dying the third time. The boards complained. She didn't. Afterward she sat up in the wreck of my cloak with her hair down her back like a banner taken in battle and inventoried her own wrists, turning them in the light. "They'll fade," I said. Stupidly. "Yes," she said. "That's generally what happens to things, Coins." And then, before I could decide whether it had been cruel, she leaned over and bit my shoulder, brief, proprietary, and settled back down against me with her back to my chest like a woman climbing into her own bed, in her own house, in a life she'd owned for years. We lay there while the rain did its work on the canvas. "Version two," she said, into the dark, some time later. "Since you paid." "I paid nothing. You've ruined my cloak." "You've paid all night, one way or the other, don't fish for the figure. Version two. Once there was a Magister of Irongate, and he had a fixer, and she kept his books and buried his bodies, metaphorical and otherwise, and he paid her in room and board and the privilege of being listed on his household rolls as *remanded property* — that's the phrase, it's his father's phrase, it's in the writ, you've read it. And one day she went into his counting room at noon, first-class, walked out the front door, and took the noon coach. First class, Coins, because you never run. Running is what they expect. Writs have chased her ever since, and she has never once been in a hurry." "Version one," I said, "you ran." "Did I," she said. "Hm." One detail. Changed. Sitting there in the dark with her ribs rising against mine, I did the arithmetic on it — one lie in two tellings, or two lies and one truth, and no way to price which — and she felt me doing it, I know she did, because the tail came around, slow, and laid itself across my ankle, warm as anything, and stayed. "Ask me," she said, sleep-voiced, whether it was an offer or a dare. "Later," I said. "Mm," she said, which is what she says instead of yes. The rain kept on. We both pretended to sleep, and did not, and then, sometime past the middle of the night, did.

That night the rain quit and the sky came out clear and cold, and she asked — asked, which was its own event — if I played cards. "I play to win," I said, which was a lie in both directions. I play to pass time. She had no cards. She had, produced from somewhere in the lining of her coat that I'd have sworn the guild searchers emptied, a worn deck, and while I got the fire built up she shuffled — cuffed, wrists still locked together, the cards rippling through her two hands like water through a lock gate, bridges and fans, and the manacles never once interrupting the flow, and I sat there watching her hands do it and forgot to say anything about the deck being contraband. Her hands. I've tried to stop reporting on her hands. The record is what it is. We played for sugar cubes, because it was that or coppers and she had cleaned me of small change by other means already. She'd stolen sugar all day — I'd watched her do it twice at the noon stop, off the counter at a waystation, into her cuff, and I'd said nothing because she wasn't escaping, she was *shopping* — and she set her hoard up in a pile like a bank. She cheated. I want it understood that I knew she was cheating, roughly from the third hand, and I kept playing, which is a fact about me the book doesn't have a column for. She cheated with the cuffs on, which is the part I still don't fully believe. Palms that should have been too hampered to pour water without spilling it, and the cards went where she wanted them. She lost four hands in a row first, careful, so I'd get confident, and then she took nine straight and did it lazily, narrating. "Coins, you hold your losses the way you hold the chain. Nobody's impressed by either." "I'm not paying out sugar I watched you steal from me in the first place." "Then you've learned something about interest," she said, and swept the pile, and sorted her hoard, and there was a system to the sorting — I never got to the bottom of the system — and she hummed while she did it, the too-many-notes lullaby, and this time I let her catch me listening, and this time she didn't stop, and that felt like being given something, which is exactly the con, and I took it anyway. Dinner. She cooked. I want that on the record because it took me the whole meal to be sure of it: she'd told me in Coldford she couldn't cook, told me with her chin up, daring me to test it, and here was a rabbit done with road herbs and a heel of bacon fat, better than anything I'd eaten since Greywater, and when I looked at her over it she said, "I can't cook. This is magic," and ate like a siege survivor. Then version three, and I didn't even ask for it. She just gave it to me, watching the fire, hands quiet in her lap, and it was strange the way the others hadn't been, because it wasn't a caper. It was an inventory. "Once there was a compact," she said. "Signed by a grandmother I never met, in a room I never saw, and the paper on it passes through blood, which is the only inheritance I'm clear on. And the Vhanes bought the paper — at a discount, because they never pay retail — and the debt comes due in Irongate in their lifetimes if the line stays in the city. But a contract needs a signatory, Coins. It needs a warm body that the blood runs in, and there's a clause about condition of collateral. *Remanded property, intact and unspoiled, restoration of the line.* That's the writ. Not the wall-poster. The writ. You've read it — you've read it a hundred times, you do sums on it at night. The legalese you thought was a clerk's fussiness." I got the writ out of the satchel. I've made a lot of motions in my life that I knew were mistakes while my hands were doing them, and this was one: unfolding the guild copy by firelight, running my eye down the clerk's hand, past *thief*, past *restoration of goods*, to the margin, to the added phrase, and reading it the way she'd just taught me to read it. *Remanded property, intact and unspoiled.* Coldford's wall said RUNAWAY and restore. The writ said property and remanded and unspoiled. Three documents, one grammar, and it was the grammar you use for things, not people, and I sat there with the paper in my hands feeling the whole bounty do what a bad coin does in your palm — the weight suddenly wrong. And then the other thing arrived, the thing I've turned over since and never got to sit right. Unspoiled. And yet outriders shadowing the road, per the hoofbeats I'd been telling myself were a carrier's. And yet the guild letting the Thorn brothers take their shot at a writ that specified condition — because guilds don't discipline their own until the fee's claimed, and if the Thorns had dragged her in with the tail clipped and the wrists broken, who was going to testify about the condition of the goods? The Magister's agent takes delivery. The Magister's agent writes the report. Nobody else ever sees the paper. He never expected me to bring her unspoiled. He expected her *usable*, and the writ was worded for the event of her not being perfect, because there are rituals for minor damage and none for a dead signatory. "You've gone quiet," she said. "You do sums loudly when you go quiet." "Two days," I said. "Blackford toll, then Irongate. My six hundred and forty crowns, her three thousand, and every word on this paper is what a man writes about a thing he owns." "Mm," she said. And then, easily, like the price of milk: "Take the cuffs off at night now. On my word I'll stay. You've the writ, I've got nowhere the writ isn't, and you sleep better without doing the arithmetic on my wrists every hour. You've been doing it. You narrate it." I want to explain what I did, and I can't. I took them off. She folded her hands, free, and gave me her word, which I couldn't bank or audit, and we both slept, and I'd love to report that I lay awake worrying about it, but the record shows I slept like a paid man. We were two days out of Blackford. I did the sums to make myself sleepy and they came out strange, because somewhere in the column there were two bowls, and a deck, and sugar I hadn't bought, and I didn't take the lines out. Dawn, then. Fire dead. Cold in the way that means it died hours ago, which means I slept hours past my own habit, which had never once happened on a job. Her bedroll was flat. Her boots were gone from the line. The coin purse — gone, out of my satchel, the satchel I sleep with. My good knife, the Marle one, gone with it. cuffs and all? No. The cuffs lay on my chest, folded, tidy, where a person would put them to be found. And the horse was still there, and the wagon, and the writ. I've told this part to nobody, because it's the part where I ran to the road and there was nothing on the road in either direction, and I stood there in first light doing sums, and I couldn't make them come out. Three days out from Irongate, the sums had said. Three thousand crowns. The sums had never once said what to do if she kept her word and left anyway.

The boot prints went a quarter mile north up the verge and then the ground stopped keeping her secrets. I read them twice, on my knees in the wet grass like a man at prayer, which the Lord would have recognized as sarcasm. Even stride. Unhurried. No skelping, no running — she'd walked out of my camp the way she'd walked out of everything, at a duchess's pace, and that was the insult I couldn't get past all day: not the theft, the *stroll*. She'd told me once you never run, running is what they expect, and I'd thought it was philosophy. It was method. It had been method the whole time, all four days, and I'd been writing it in my book under *character* like a man with hay for brains. I rode the road half the morning and the verges half the afternoon. I asked at a crofter's — no woman on the road, no, nor a devil neither, no coach had stopped since the Greywater mail, would I like milk. I would not like milk. The road stayed empty in both directions, which in a fugitive is one thing, and in a woman who wants not to be found is just professional. It was saddling Copper that I found the purse. Under the saddle blanket, where it would ride soft and not shift, laid flat the way a man lays tools he means to come back to. I stood there with the blanket in one hand longer than I'll admit. The coin was all there. All but one silver and four coppers. No note. I want that on the record, because I've been audited by the Grey Ledger and by worse, and I have never in my life had a document tell me so much by saying nothing. I turned the purse over twice. I checked the seams. I was waiting for the joke — a list, a rate, *your rates were reasonable, t. K.* — because that's what she does, she books everything, she'd rather be your creditor than your charity, and the joke didn't come, and the absence of the joke from that woman is itself a letter, and I couldn't read it, and I stood there in first light getting angrier by the minute about a *system* I could see the edge of and not the shape of. One silver, four. I found out at the relay what a seat on the north coach costs. That evening was Waymeet, the crossroads relay, one fire, one pot, three strangers with good horses. I clocked the horses before the men — road-bred, matched bays, expensive the way nothing on the Ashen Road is expensive on purpose, no livery and none needed. I'd heard that walking pace behind me three nights running. It didn't take a magistrate. I took a bench with my back to the wall and did the sums while the stew came. Here they are. Six hundred and forty owed. Two hundred twelve due this quarter, red-starred. Copper, worth eleven, maybe fourteen to the right fool. The wagon, eight as scrap, and it was my home besides. Add it all up, every way I ran it, and I came out short of the Ledger's patience with a great deal left over of nothing. She was three thousand crowns and I'd been carrying her the way you carry your last winter, and now the back of the wagon held a folded pair of cuffs laid on my chest like a receipt, and the writ was kindling that wouldn't burn right. And there sat three of the Magister's men with their boots by the fire. I want the sentence on the record, because I've never told it to anyone and it ought to be somewhere, sworn, like a deposition. I had it worded before I stood up. Costed, even. *Gentlemen. I hold the Greywater writ on the Magister's property. I can put you on her for fifty crowns and a clean walk-away, day's ride west, the Ashen Road, and you never heard my name.* That's it. That's the whole of it. I stood up with it in my mouth like a coin I'd already counted. The ale jug was in my hand when their talk carried across the room, the way talk does in a place with one fire. "—and the wagon man?" the younger one said. "There's no wagon man past Blackford," the older one said. He said it the way you'd say there's no weather past morning. "He's paid at the gate if the goods are behind him, and he's *seen to* after if he's seen anything at all. Hart's bought on the toll. Nobody crosses that bridge that we don't count." I set the jug down on the bar without drinking from it. Paid for it anyway. Some money you spend to keep from making change in other coin. They'd been going to pay me. That was the plan, the whole road — deliver the cargo, take the fee at the gate, and somewhere past Blackford a bridge and a quiet man and a wage I'd never live to spend. Three thousand for her, and my passage thrown in at no charge. And I'd walked the length of a relay floor ready to sell them the one thing they were already planning to take from me for free. I got my back to the wall and my stew came, and it was bad — the kind of bad that's a decision, flour and scrag and no salt — and I ate it with her coin, the one silver and four coppers' worth running through my fingers down to the last of it, and it tasted better than anything I'd had since Greywater, and I hated that. I did. Hunger and salt and spite, that's all it was, and I sat there hating a bowl of stew for tasting like her cooking and knowing exactly how she'd laugh at that sentence, and hating that I knew. I did the sums that night to make myself sleepy, the way I have for ten years. Two days to Blackford. One road. No cargo, no fee, and men at the toll counting every soul that crosses, mine included. The sums came out wrong all night. Every one of them. Not wrong like arithmetic — wrong like a ledger with a line gone out of it that I'd stopped being able to price, and the empty line cost more than the full ones, and I've been in this trade thirty years and I never once heard of a man losing money on what a woman left behind in coin and took in everything else.

The sums said go around. There's a ford at Tarbrook, two days south — no bridge, no toll, no men counting souls — and at every milestone out of Waymeet the sums said it again, reasonable as a magistrate. I rode straight on at Blackford, because I'd stopped trusting my own arithmetic the morning it came out with her gone from it. I told myself Copper wanted shoeing. That's what I'd have said at an inquest. The truth — put it in the book, seal the page — is that she was somewhere ahead of me on a road with men on it who *saw to* witnesses, and a man my age can ride all day on an undelivered debt. It's the delivered ones that tire you. Blackford at dusk: the gate across the bridge, the chain, lanterns lit early and too many of them. Horses at the tollhouse rail — I counted eight and quit, because counting past eight would have made it real. The older one from the relay stood at the gate post like he'd grown there, and he looked at Copper, and he looked at me, and he said, comfortable as a landlord: "The wagon man." Two came off the wall behind me. The sums on that were simple and I'd already done them, and I'd just got my hand on my knife when a small man with a ring of keys came out of the tollhouse at a scuttle, dodging, hands up, and put himself under my arm like a ferret going to ground, and everything I learned that night I learned in the next ten seconds from a tollkeeper named Hart, who was bought on the toll and knew it: "She outbid them! Two days back, gold down on my counter, asked after a big man on a grey horse, told me keep the gate lit and my mouth shut and no matter what I see, *stay inside* — I'm bought, I stay bought, only she paid more, do you understand, she paid *more*—" Then the tollhouse door came open behind them all, and the lanterns went out. All of them. Every flame on that bridge, one breath, like the night drawing in for a word with somebody, and the cold came off the river wrong — cold like a cellar, cold like below — and she stood in the doorway with the last light dying around her and her eyes flat and gold and open, pupils gone sideways, and I want it entered in the record that I have been in three actions and a dozen arrests and I have never once been afraid like I was in the next minute, because something looked out of her face that was wearing her face, and her voice, when it came, wasn't raised, it just arrived everywhere at once, a chord underneath the words, and a grown man crossed himself with a sword in his hand, and another ran onto the bridge and kept running, and the one who swung at her — the swing went *wrong*, in the air, like the light bent and took his arm with it, and I did the only thing I've ever learned to do with sums I can't run, which was hold still and pray they come out kind. "Cade. Down." I went down before I'd decided anything. Something went over me — the cold and then her, and then the sound of a man's arm doing what arms don't. I came up in the dark with the irons in my face. The one who counts had them out — the Magister's own delivery irons, for remanded property, I'd bet the bounty on the crest on them — and he was fast and unhurried and he got one wrist, and she *let* him. I saw it. She stood still and let him clap the second wrist, and the bridge went quiet as a courtroom, and then she turned her hands over like a piano player and opened them. One flick. The other. And she tossed the irons underhand across the dark at my chest, and I caught them the way you catch anything that's yours coming back — before you've asked yourself why it would be. Wordless. The whole thing, wordless. It took me until the river stopped sounding wrong to run the arithmetic, and then it ran itself: the irons, three seconds, in the dark. My cuffs. Silver, guild-issue, on her wrists since Greywater. Day one, day two, day three, day four. The fight was over by then, or the part of it I could follow. Two down the road not stopping. One in the river, deciding to stay there. One dead by the wagon, and one alive on his knees, begging — he'd gone down when the lanterns did and he was still telling her things, names, amounts, where the strongbox in the tollhouse was. She stood in front of him with her hands loose at her sides and listened like a banker. Quiet, after. The river. My own breath doing sums. I was on the far side of the gate from her and I stayed there one beat too long, and her tail — the tail that lies when she doesn't — the tail went dead still at the end of her spine, and I knew she'd clocked it, and it cost me, and it was the truth, and I paid it. "The cuffs," I said. "The lock. When." "Day two," she said. Day two. Every night strung to the ring post. The Thorns, hampered, performing hampered. The fire, the rain, the key chattering in my shaking hands like a die in a cup while she held still and let me be a fool. None of it was ever holding her. All of it was her, staying, and neither of us said one word about what to do with that, and the river kept on not helping. "You came back to keep me off their list," I said. "Ahead of them. Buying the toll. That's what the gold—" "Don't." Quiet, the dangerous register. "I've been bought and I've been sold and priced and posted, and I know exactly what I am in a man's ledger. I didn't buy your life, I bought mine *clean*. I've carried bodies out of Irongate on my own two shoulders. I know how heavy they come back. That's all it was." She was watching my face to see which line I'd credit, and I understood she didn't know, either, which frightened me worse than the lanterns. "Now," she said, after a while. "About that offer I made you in Coldford." I had two pairs of cuffs in my coat by then — hers and the Magister's — and a man my age ought to know what that says about him. I'd made the decision somewhere in the middle of the fight, around the part with the lanterns, at the moment I was most afraid of her. I put the receipt away and didn't celebrate it.

The metaphor system is consistent and earns its moments. The emotional beats are shown rather than told. The darkness is well-earned. We rode into Irongate two abreast, her on Copper's saddle and me on the seat driving, which arrangement she announced as the natural order of things — "I ride, you narrate, it's what we're each suited for" — and I did the sums on the whole enterprise out loud, because I'd given up pretending she couldn't hear them. They came out insane. They came out: walk up to the man who'd put a bridge between me and my own wages, and sell him his secrets back at a markup. Coldford rates. I'd heard the pitch once from a chained woman in a stable, and refused it, and here I was two days later wearing it as a plan, and the worst of it was the arithmetic was *good*, it always had been good, that was the whole trouble with her. First the gate office, where I filed my last writ. That's a cost I want entered while I'm being honest: the clerk read my return — *cargo lost in transit, affray at Blackford bridge, body unrecovered* — and looked at me a long moment and stamped it and said, "You're done, Rennick. You know that." A man who loses cargo doesn't get written again. I paid the filing and thanked him, and I want it noted that thanking him didn't cost me anything, which frightened me more than the stamp did. Ten years I'd wanted the door out of the trade. It arrived by way of a bridge and a dead man, and I held it open. Then Vhane. I'll keep the scene short because she'd keep it short. He received us in a study with a good fire and better ink — I clocked the inkstand from the door, gold-mounted, the kind a man buys when he wants to be noticed signing things. Soft hands. A voice that never rose. They were two of a trade, those two, and I stood by the door and was plausible, as instructed, and put nothing on the record but this: I have never seen a man out-negotiated in his own study before breakfast, and I've seen some things. She laid it out like a hand she'd been keeping since Greywater. The guild return, filed and stamped: his property lost under his own bridge, in an affray his own men started, unrecovered. The courier who survived it, living, chatty, willing to be produced. The letters — "You never changed the locks, Alden. A fixer who can't reach your counting room is a fixer you shouldn't have kept" — copies of every one, in a strongbox she named, and she named the strongbox right, and I watched his face when she did. Her terms. The compact paper — the original, the grandmother's signature, the clause with the line in it — surrendered. A fee for silence, her figure, which she didn't dignify by saying twice. And a settlement signed, in his own ink, saying plainly what it said, which was that he paid what he paid for what he was buying, and a magistrate's signature on a purchase like that is a thing you keep in a strongbox of your own. He signs his threats, she'd told me once. Now he'd signed a receipt with the same nib. He called her *it*, twice, on his way to signing. The second time she let the word sit in the room, and then she said, pleasant as a toll-taker, "Say the next one as *who*, and we'll take four percent off for accuracy," and he didn't, and that was the whole humiliation, the whole of it, a man who deals in legalese made to feel one word cost him four percent. I've known men killed for less and I'd never seen a cleaner robbery. At the door he got his last word in, because his kind always does. "Bought at a discount," he said. "The pair of you." "I've never once been retail," she said, and shut his own door on him. The split she handed me that evening, out past the walls, on the road away — a purse, counted. I counted it in front of her; we're professionals. It came out eight hundred fifty-two crowns exactly, plus one silver and four coppers, plus one sugar cube. "The Ledger figure," I said. "To the crown." "You do your sums out loud," she said. "You've been broadcasting your debts since Greywater. The rest is mine. I was the cargo; cargo rates apply. Object." I did the sums. Six hundred forty plus the quarter's two hundred twelve cleared it to the copper, first time in seven years the book came out flat, and I stood there trying to construct an objection and my own arithmetic wouldn't provide one. "You'd rather be my creditor," I said, "than my charity." "Mm," she said, which is what she says instead of yes. The rest of the take rode in her coat, majority and unapologetic, and I want it on the record that I didn't argue, and that not arguing was the easiest money I never made. The guild voided the writ by week's end; the wall-posters came down in Coldford and stayed up in two other towns I could name, because paper travels slower than truth. The Thorns were seen riding north with a grudge and a poor grasp of arithmetic. Some other day. Everything on this road has a cost and most of it invoices later. We made Coldford in three days — out of Irongate, mind, away from it, the direction I hadn't planned and preferred — and the last night she cooked, which she can't, magnificently, and ate with both hands free, fast and total, a siege survivor at a christening, and I watched her hands work and I've stopped pretending the watching isn't on the record. The fire was good. The lullaby started up and died when she caught me at it, and started again anyway, which I entered nowhere but here. I'd kept the cuffs. Guild silver, sentimental, cheap — I'd have told you souvenir, if you'd asked, and lied by half. I reached into my coat for them at bedtime, to set them by the fire where I could see them, and my hand found the pocket empty. She had them on. Both of them, loose, dangling off two fingers like a woman wearing her own history to bed. "Those are mine," I said. "They were never yours," she said. "They were mine the whole time, Coins. You were just holding them." I opened my mouth to run the objection, and she raised one finger off the cuff, unhurried. "Ask me," she said, "where we're going." "Later," I said. "Mm," she said, which is what she says instead of yes.
