# Intention **Plot spine.** I will build the story on the "Trust Gambit" engine, fusing the three strongest brainstorm ideas: (1) the *vein-as-hostage* — Arthur's deposit is so vast that crude extraction or an orbital strike during a war over it could trigger a cascade decay reaction in Mars's crust, making the find simultaneously treasure and planetary hostage; (2) the *knowledge-lock* — the vein is unusable without Arthur's own engineering (his forgotten thesis on harmonic induction damping, the only technique that moderates Azra's decay cascades), so the real prize is not the land but the man; and (3) the *status-quo twist* — Antares's true motive is preserving scarcity, since abundance would collapse the balance of power and force a war, which makes Vosk's polite menace rational rather than villainous. The resolution: Arthur deeds the subsurface to a neutral trust administered by the Kaol Institute — equal licenses to all powers, proceeds funding settler land rights and the buyout of the indenture system — with a dead-man fail-safe that entombs the vein against any seizure. He resolves the story by negotiation and arithmetic, not force, per the Asimov tradition. **Protagonist.** Arthur Neegan, 34, first-generation settler and mining engineer: plain-spoken, dry, an active rational actor rather than a swept-along everyman. His parents were Halloran leaseholders; his education was bonded to the corporation, giving Halloran legal claws and giving the indenture theme personal stakes. His competence — not luck — is what everyone wants. **Cast economy.** One face per faction: Commissioner Vosk (Antares, courteous precision, the story's best-drawn antagonist), Undersecretary Elias Crane (Earth Federation, statute and menace), Director Renata Hallowes (Halloran Extraction, legal strangulation via Arthur's bond), Dr. Ilsa Renn (Kaol Institute, Arthur's old professor, technical exposition and conscience), and Sela Okafor (indentured tunneler whose lease Arthur buys out, the human cost made specific). No more named characters than these. **Voice & style.** Third-person past, limited to Arthur, with occasional authoritative narrator paragraphs for the wide-lens history (the discovery of Azra, the economics of indenture, the arms race) — the trademark big-and-small-picture weaving. Dialogue is the engine; characters reason at each other; elites speak without contractions, Arthur plainly. Retrofuturism played straight, without irony: punch-card surveys, assay chits, visi-plates, tape spools, atomic clocks presented as cutting-edge. Ring structure: the story opens with Arthur aboard a vessel wondering what he's involved in, and closes with him on his own land wondering how long the balance holds — crisis solved, history still in motion, wry and faintly ominous. **Aims.** Chapter 2 must be primarily dialogue per the prompt, structured as a strict escalation ladder with a physical throughline. Every element of the final gambit must be foreshadowed by chapters 4–5 so the resolution feels earned. The indenture thread must be planted in chapter 3 and paid off structurally in the Trust and the coda. **Avoidances.** No alien artefacts, no cosmic horror, no slow-poison melodrama, no tragic sellout ending, no ironic retrofuturism, no gunplay resolution. Mars must be revisited — no court-intrigue-only version. No episodic drift in the middle chapters: each faction's move must escalate and intersect with the others. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — "Outbound" (~1000 words)** Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, Mars shrinking in the viewport, replaying the armed retinue's descent on his homestead: the Antares diplomatic insignia, the polite, forceful "invitation," the sealed orders. Memory-as-exposition: the anomalous assay chit from a routine survey, what Azra is and why it matters (drives and weapons, gold rush and arms race), his parents' indenture, his own education bond, and the dawning suspicion that he never reported the find — yet someone knows anyway. Retrofuturistic texture throughout. Ends with the vessel docking against the Antares flagship *Courser*. **Chapter 2 — "The Courtesy Call" (~1000 words)** Primarily dialogue. Commissioner Vosk's chamber: tea, a viewport of stars, a dossier on the desk. Escalation ladder: gracious welcome → the offer (staggering buyout, relocation, "wardship") → a probing question revealing Arthur has been surveilled for weeks → the counter-offer when he demurs → the courteous threat → the revelation that his vein exceeds all known Azra reserves combined. Sown hints: Earth agents shadowing him, Halloran lawyers circling, Antares's monopoly anxiety, and one deliberate ambiguity — why Antares wants the vein *controlled* rather than simply mined. Vosk sends him home "to think," which is its own threat. **Chapter 3 — "The Paper" (~1000 words)** Return to Mars; the claim and the counter-move. Hallowes arrives with Arthur's education bond and dusts off his father's old lease — Halloran can tie the land up in litigation for a decade. Indentured crews are diverted to survey the plot; Arthur meets Sela Okafor and quietly begins buying out leases. Dr. Renn arrives from Kaol Institute with the technical problem: the vein's density makes it cascade-unstable; crude extraction could crack the planet's crust. The damping problem is named — and Renn recalls Arthur's forgotten thesis. **Chapter 4 — "Three Visits" (~1000 words)** The tug-of-war triangulated. Undersecretary Crane arrives with Earth's position: emergency war powers can conscript both the land and the man. Arthur assembles the board and asks Renn the load-bearing question — what happens if a war is fought *over* the vein? Answer: any orbital strike cracks it; the planet goes. The mutually-assured-destruction logic seeds itself. Arthur begins, quietly, keeping notes of what each faction fears rather than what each wants. **Chapter 5 — "Cascade" (~1000 words)** The story's one burst of physical danger. Halloran (plausibly deniable) pushes a bribed crew into a crude core sampling; a partial cascade scare — the vein's response described in loving retro-technical detail — and Arthur's damping technique quells it, publicly proving that only he can make Azra usable. The knowledge-lock locks. Meanwhile: survey evidence surfaces suggesting Antares has secretly mapped the vein from orbit — a card Arthur pockets for later. His lease buyouts accelerate. **Chapter 6 — "The Closing Fist" (~1000 words)** The deadline chapter. Vosk and Crane converge with convergent ultimatums: sign away or be declared an enemy asset / conscripted under war powers. The clock runs out; Arthur sends invitations of his own. The quiet heart of the story: Arthur, Renn, and Sela at his kitchen table, working out the gambit — the Trust's structure, the fail-safe, and the moral logic that freedom has to be load-bearing, not decoration. End on Arthur composing the invitation list with dry satisfaction. **Chapter 7 — "The Azra Gambit" (~1000 words)** The council scene: Vosk, Crane, Hallowes, Renn, Institute observers, and a broadcast feed. Arthur lays the cascade hazard bare for the public record (the planet as mutual hostage), demonstrates the damping method, reveals Antares's secret orbital survey (mutual embarrassment as equalizer), and presents the Azra Trust: neutral stewardship, equal licenses, proceeds to settler land rights and the abolition of indenture — and the dead-man fail-safe entombing the vein against any seizure. Resolution by arithmetic, not force: he lets the wolves work out that peace is cheaper than war. The signatures come grudgingly. **Chapter 8 — "Load-Bearing" (~1000 words)** Coda, months later. Mars: the Trust functioning, the Institute licensed, Sela enrolled in engineering, Hallowes fighting a small war of tariffs and lawyers instead of atomics. Mirror of Chapter 1: Arthur on his own porch, sitting atop the largest treasure in the system, drinking tea — a deliberate echo of Vosk. The wry closing beat: a visitor arriving with a new insignia, and Arthur reflecting that the balance holds only so long as everyone can still do the arithmetic. Faintly ominous last line; the crisis is solved, the history is not.

Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Model Output:
# How a Human Would Approach This Piece **They'd have read Asimov, not summarized him.** A human pastiche writer has the *feel* in their bones: Asimov's prose is famously lean and unornamented — he's almost anti-atmospheric. No hissing airlocks, no "the stars were cold and indifferent." His descriptions are functional and confident, his digressions have *spin* and opinion ("It is a curious feature of human history that..."), his dialogue is chess between smart people, and crucially — he's funny. Dry, pun-adjacent, cheeky. A human would steal his actual moves: the fictional encyclopedia excerpt done satirically, the invented-but-plausible physics gag (plutonium-186 in *The Gods Themselves*), the ending that lands on a wry reversal rather than a shudder. LLM "classic sci-fi" pastiche tends toward solemn Bradbury-atmosphere wearing an Asimov name tag — that's the first thing a human would get right that the plan doesn't yet guarantee. **They'd bring a private obsession.** A human writer working on indentured leases on Mars would have read about company towns, scrip, coal wars, the Homestead Act, nuclear secrecy, *Atoms for Peace* — and one of these would become the story's load-bearing interest, warping the shape around it. Asimov was a history buff; *Foundation* is Gibbon with robots. The plan gestures at history but doesn't yet *use* it. A human would know the actual legal texture of debt peonage — how it feels to owe your schooling to the mine — and would write from inside that grievance. **They'd spend unevenly.** A human overwrites the scene they're excited about and underwrites the connective tissue. They'd give Vosk 1,300 words because she's the fun one, and compress Chapter 4 into a single phone call. The plan's even 8×1000 distribution is a spec compliance thing, not a writerly thing — the prose should *feel* uneven in weight even if the word counts match. **They'd leave things out.** Humans trust readers. They'd plant a hint and never resolve it. They'd let the fail-safe have a hole and let Arthur *notice the hole* without patching it. They'd leave the Antares Combine's whole political history as a suggestive smear rather than a paragraph. **They'd commit to the era, costs included.** "Retrofuturism played straight" is stated in the plan but not interrogated. Playing it straight means period social attitudes, smoking, UN-style Earth government, "atomic" as an adjective for everything, American-culture-writ-large. A human makes that choice consciously and lives with its awkwardness (or deliberately plants a couple of period-era assumptions and lets the reader squirm). An LLM plays "straight" only visually — the gadgets — while modernizing all the sensibilities invisibly. That's the tell. # Telltale LLM Approaches & How They'd Fail This Piece **Writing safely.** The most dangerous one here. The tell in the current plan: the Chapter 5 "cascade scare" resolves harmlessly. Nobody dies. Sela's buyout is frictionless. The Trust works. Asimov himself was an optimist, but his wins *cost* — even *Foundation*'s victories come with erosion and aftermath. A bloodless scare in a story about a metal that accelerates death is a safety reflex, and a human would let the sabotage kill someone we've met. **The bow.** LLMs resolve every planted seed, mirror every opening, and symmetrize the ending. The plan currently does this *by design*: "mirror of Chapter 1," "deliberate echo of Vosk's tea," "faintly ominous last line," every Chapter 2 hint paid off by Chapter 7. Some ring structure is fine — it's even period-appropriate — but the plan as written closes every loop with a click. A human would leave at least one thread deliberately hanging, and would resist explaining the tea echo. **Writing impressively.** In Asimov-pastiche this manifests as: solemn, "elevated" narration, portentous chapter titles, sensory saturation ("the stars stretched like cold fire"), characters who are always articulate, feelings named and italicized ("dread settled over him"). Asimov's actual register is closer to good science journalism with jokes. The prose should be *plainer than the plan implies*. **Mechanical structure applied as formula.** The plan's "strict escalation ladder" and "physical throughline (the tea, the viewport, the dossier)" are good instincts that become LLM tells in execution — the tea appears exactly three times, each time Doing Work. Real dialogue scenes breathe, misfire, contain people not answering the question asked. Asimov's menace-scenes include *tedium* — the bureaucrat drones, and the droning is the menace. **Antagonists who explain themselves.** LLM fiction loves the full-disclosure confession. The plan's Vosk has a secret motive (scarcity-stability); the LLM version has her *state* it. A human lets Arthur infer it from a slip — one sentence that only makes sense if Antares doesn't actually want the vein mined. **The competent-savior protagonist.** The plan's Arthur plays every card exactly when planned and no one ever lands a blow on him. Even the "gambit" title is unearned as written: a *gambit* sacrifices something. The current plan sacrifices nothing — the Trust costs Arthur no real pain, no concession, no loss. This is the deepest structural critique below. **Character-as-function.** "One face per faction" is chess-piece tidiness. Worse, Sela is described as "the human cost made specific" — which is a description of a *prop*. The noble poor woman who gets rescued and enrolled in engineering is pure LLM savior-fantasy bow-tie. **Checklist compliance with the prompt.** Hitting every requested element visibly — the dialogue chapter that *reads* like a dialogue exercise, the worldbuilding digression that reads like a Wikipedia insert. A human satisfies the brief without making the seams show. # Deep Dive: Auditing the Intention & Plan **The gambit with no sacrifice (Ch. 6–7).** The biggest pitfall. In chess a gambit gives up material for position. Arthur's Trust, as planned, is a wish-fulfillment device: he keeps the land, frees the indentured, outmaneuvers three great powers, and loses nothing. A human would make at least one real concession — e.g., to get Antares to sign, Arthur must grant the Combine short-term exclusivity on the damping licenses, a concession he has to defend to Sela and the settlers; or the Trust requires giving up the *surface* homestead — the thing his parents suffered for — to neutral stewardship, and the story lets that wound stay unhealed. The "gambit" should have a price the reader can tally. **Vosk, Crane, Hallowes: three articulates.** As planned, all three are polished menace-figures — interchangeable LLM villains in different suits. A human gives them *speech textures*: Vosk wins arguments by quoting your own words back to you; Crane speaks in statute citations and is genuinely boring, and the boring is the threat; Hallowes should be *nice* — grandmotherly, warm, talks about amortization schedules the way someone talks about grandchildren. Three menaces, three registers. Also: at least one faction's visit should come off-page or in a garbled form (via a drunk foreman, via a document) to break the episodic arrival-offer-refusal rhythm of Chapters 3–5. **Chapter 7's venue is a phone book.** "The council scene" staged as a conference is Asimov's actual weakness inherited uncritically — Foundation is full of speech-symposiums and only Asimov's charm saves them. A human would stage it *in the shaft* — everyone in damp-suits, the damping rigs audibly humming, the vein's instability tickable in the ear of every delegate. The stakes become sensory. The demonstration happens *next to the thing*. **The bloodless cascade (Ch. 5).** The sabotage beat is currently an engineering set-piece with no human toll. A human kills someone — probably someone from the indentured crew, which complicates everything: the crew was coerced or bribed, so the death indicts the whole lease system, and the Trust's indenture-abolition clause stops being sentiment and becomes *reparations*. It also gives the coda a shadow: the peace is bought with that death. **Sela as prop.** "Human cost made specific" — no. Options: she doesn't want to be bought out *that way* (agency, resentment); she's the one coerced into the sabotage (dilemma, guilt); she takes the buyout and is *grateful* in a way that's uncomfortable for the reader. Or she wants the vein sealed forever and becomes Arthur's internal opposition in Chapter 6 — the person who argues the moral position he's tempted to abandon for pragmatism. Any of these beats "rescued and enrolled." **The ring structure is too exact.** Opening vessel / closing porch is fine. But "drinking tea — a deliberate echo of Vosk" plus "a visitor arriving with a new insignia" is bow-stacking. The new-insignia visitor re-opens the cycle artificially for resonance — a very LLM "faintly ominous" move. A human ends smaller and more sideways: Arthur back down the shaft, fixing a pump, and one unhealed detail from the cost of the gambit. **Wikipedia digressions.** "Authoritative narrator paragraphs for wide-lens history" will read as infodump if executed as neutral summary. Asimov's digressions are argumentative, opinionated, occasionally funny. The fix is voice, not placement. **Every hint resolves.** The prompt asks to sow hints of "larger intrigue, stakes & dangers." The LLM will sow hints and then cash every one. Keep one forever unexplained — e.g., why the Antares survey team's roster includes a name Arthur's father mentioned once. One loose thread makes the world feel bigger than the plot. **The fail-safe is frictionless MAD.** The dead-man switch works as planned. A human acknowledges the hole — who maintains the fail-safe? Who guards the guardians? — and lets Arthur knowingly accept an imperfect device, maybe even has Hallowes *spot the flaw* in Chapter 7 and extract her best terms because of it. A loser who fights the frame skillfully is more human than wolves out-argued. **"Dry satisfaction," "faintly ominous."** The plan's emotional stage directions are all summary tags. In prose, these become "he allowed himself a thin smile" — a top-tier LLM tell. Behavior carries it; cut the labels. # Brainstorming: Making It More Human - **Steal Asimov's actual comic register.** Azra's physics is a joke machine: a metal that makes everything hurry up and die. Half-life jokes write themselves. Vosk should be *witty*; politeness-as-menace is funnier when it's actually funny. - **Bureaucratic documents instead of encyclopedia epigraphs.** A Halloran induction pamphlet ("Welcome to the Halloran Family!"), a lease contract excerpt, a leaked memo — satire documents, period-flavored, cheap in wordcount, huge in texture. - **Give Arthur one non-plot obsession** — hydroponic tomatoes, his father's broken pocket watch, chess-by-mail with someone on Earth (very period). Let it recur *without becoming a symbol*. The LLM instinct is to make the watch thematic; the human move is to let it just be a watch he never fixed. - **Mars texture economy:** pick two or three specific settler textures (company store prices, hydroponic smell, ration chits, pump-noise) and *repeat* them across chapters. Repetition builds a place; a list of fresh details builds a set. - **Crane bores us on purpose.** Stage one Earth Federation communication as an actual tedious memo read aloud — the tedium of power, done deliberately. - **Vosk's motive stays silent.** Arthur deduces it; she never confirms. If pressed, she says something deflecting that is itself a confirmation. - **Chapter 5's death** ripples forward: the Trust's signing includes a memorial clause no one dares object to; the coda carries the unhealed detail. - **One faction visit off-page,** one as a document, one as an ambush — varying delivery kills the procedural rhythm. - **The gamble has a price tag the reader can tally**, and at least one party (Hallowes) sees the gambit coming and negotiates *inside* it, coming away with something real — making the win feel contested, not conjured. - **Mislabeled feelings.** When Arthur is afraid, let him think it's the coffee ration. Show somatics, let him misread himself once — and let the belated recognition about his parents' suffering for this land arrive in Chapter 8, half-thought, unresolved. - **Under-write one chapter deliberately** for rhythm; let Vosk's chapter run fat. **What to keep, because it's not an LLM tell:** the MAD logic, engineering-knowledge-as-leverage, the refusal to resolve with gunplay, the clean causality of the plot. Asimov's structures *are* airtight — the mistake is confusing tidiness of structure (good, period-appropriate) with tidiness of *outcome* (the actual flaw). The humanity belongs in the texture, the cost, the comedy, and the voice — not in plot shagginess.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Plot spine.** The Trust Gambit, revised to earn its name. Arthur's vein is simultaneously treasure and planetary hostage: so vast and dense that crude extraction — or an orbital strike in a war fought over it — risks a cascade decay reaction in the Martian crust. It is also unusable without Arthur's own engineering: his forgotten thesis on harmonic induction damping, the only technique that moderates Azra's cascades. The resolution is negotiation and arithmetic: the subsurface deeded to a neutral trust under the Kaol Institute — equal licenses to all powers, proceeds funding settler land rights and the buyout of the indenture system — sealed by a dead-man fail-safe. Crucially, it is a *gambit*: it costs Arthur the surface homestead his parents' indenture paid for, and the damping method itself, which he signs over to the Trust — surrendering the very leverage that made him untouchable. He ends as salaried warden of land he no longer owns. The win is contested, not conjured: Hallowes spots the fail-safe's maintenance flaw and extracts the extraction-services contracts; Crane takes a guarantor seat to save Federation face; Vosk signs last, her motive never stated. **Vosk's secret — never spoken.** Antares's true interest is stable scarcity; abundance would force the war it dreads. Arthur deduces this from a tell, not a confession: the buyout offer is oddly *low* for the greatest Azra find in history. He misreads it as a bargaining gambit in Chapter 2 and does the arithmetic days later. Vosk confirms nothing; her parting line in Chapter 7 confirms everything by confirming nothing. **Cast, with distinct registers.** Arthur Neegan, 34 — plain, dry, competent, an engineer not a lottery ticket; keeps his father's broken pocket watch, meaning to fix it, never doing so (never symbolized). Commissioner Vosk — witty, precise, wins arguments by quoting your own words back to you; tea and ruin in the same breath. Undersecretary Crane — speaks in statute citations and is genuinely, deliberately boring; the tedium *is* the menace; his Federation move arrives as a memo read aloud. Director Hallowes — grandmotherly warmth, discusses amortization schedules the way others discuss grandchildren; the friendliest predator in the room. Dr. Ilsa Renn — Arthur's old professor, technical conscience. Sela Okafor — indentured tunneler with agency: she risks penal reassignment to warn Arthur of the sabotage, refuses his charity, argues to seal the vein forever, and takes the memorial commission instead of an education he offered. Tam — an older indentured foreman, coffee-sharer, who follows Halloran's fatal order because the lease system leaves him no choice. He dies in Chapter 5; his death indicts the lease system and makes the Trust's indenture clause *reparations*, not sentiment. **Delivery variety (killing episodic rhythm).** Halloran's move arrives as paper — a process server and a warm letter; Earth's as a tedious memo; Antares's as messages and, finally, the council. Faction beats intersect and escalate rather than arriving on a conveyor. **Voice.** Lean Asimov prose: functional, confident description; digressions that are *opinionated* ("It is a curious feature of human history that…") rather than encyclopedic; dialogue-forward, characters reasoning at each other; dry comedy — half-life jokes, bureaucratic satire. No emotional labels, no "thin smiles," no solemnity. Elite characters avoid contractions; Arthur doesn't. Retrofuturism played straight: assay chits, punch-card surveys, visi-plates, tape spools, "atomic" as an adjective, a UN-flavored Earth Federation. Three Mars textures repeated across chapters to build a place rather than a set: pump-noise, ration chits and company store prices, the hydroponic smell. Two or three in-world documents (a Halloran lease clause, a Federation memo, the Trust charter's first clause) used as satire, sparingly. **Structure.** Eight chapters, uneven in felt weight: Chapter 2 fat with dialogue, Chapter 4 deliberately lean. Ring structure loose, not exact — vessel to porch, but no tea-echo label, no new-insignia visitor. One loose thread (a name on the stolen Antares survey roster that Arthur's father mentioned once) planted in Chapter 5, touched once in Chapter 8, never resolved. Ending small and sideways: warden's paperwork, an unfixed watch, the unhealed detail of Tam's plaque, and a wry last line — the crisis solved, the history in motion. **Avoid.** Bloodless resolution; self-explaining villains; the noble rescued poor; competent-savior perfection; solemn atmospheric pastiche mislabeled as Asimov; encyclopedia infodumps; resolved every hint; the bow. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — "Outbound" (~1000 words)** Aboard the transfer vessel, Mars shrinking in the viewport, Arthur replaying the armed descent on his homestead: the Antares diplomatic insignia, the polite, forceful invitation, the sealed orders. Exposition through memory and one opinionated narrator digression: what Azra is (a metal that hurries everything toward its half-life), why it matters (drives, weapons, gold rush, arms race), his parents' indenture, his Halloran education bond, the routine assay chit that started it all. The pocket watch introduced, unemphasized. Ends docking against the *Courser*. **Chapter 2 — "The Courtesy Call" (~1100 words — the fat chapter)** Primarily dialogue. Vosk's chamber: tea, stars, a dossier. Escalation ladder — gracious welcome; the offer, oddly modest per-acre; her quoting his own survey notes back at him (the surveillance reveal); the courteous threat wrapped in a favor; the revelation that his plot sits on more Azra than all known reserves combined. Arthur asks for time; she grants it like a warning. He pockets the lowball oddness and misreads it. Tea and dossier recur naturally, not symbolically. Hints sown: Earth agents, Halloran lawyers, and one question of hers that only matters if Antares doesn't want it mined. **Chapter 3 — "The Paper" (~1000 words)** Return to Mars; the counter-move arrives on paper. Halloran's process server, his education bond, his father's old lease, and Hallowes's warm letter — amortization discussed like grandchildren. Indentured survey crews diverted to his claim; Arthur meets Sela and Tam over coffee rations. Renn arrives from Kaol with the cascade-instability problem — crude extraction could crack the crust — and remembers Arthur's forgotten thesis. Epigraph: a Halloran lease clause. Mars textures begin their repetitions. **Chapter 4 — "Terms" (~900 words — deliberately lean)** The Federation memo, read aloud, tedious, menacing: conscription of "Asset 7-A" under emergency war powers. Then Arthur and Renn at the assay table with the load-bearing question: what happens in a war fought *over* the vein? Any orbital strike cracks it; the planet goes. The MAD logic seeds itself. Arthur finally does the arithmetic on Vosk's lowball and realizes what it means — she'd rather it never be mined. He starts keeping notes on what each faction *fears*, not wants. Ends at the shaft door, the idea half-formed. **Chapter 5 — "Cascade" (~1100 words)** The one burst of physical danger. Halloran orders the indentured survey crew deeper — coercion via lease; refusal means penal reassignment. Sela warns Arthur, risking exactly that. Too late: a partial cascade — meters singing, the hum in the teeth — and Arthur improvises his damping technique from thesis memory and rig components to quell it. Tam, who followed the order, dies. The brutal detail: Halloran deducts his funeral from his accrued credit. Arthur pockets a survey card proving Antares secretly mapped the vein from orbit — its roster includes a name his father mentioned once (the loose thread). The knowledge-lock locks publicly: only Arthur can work Azra here. **Chapter 6 — "The Kitchen Table" (~1000 words)** Convergent ultimatums from Vosk and Crane: sign or be declared an enemy asset / conscripted. The quiet heart: Arthur, Renn, and Sela at the homestead kitchen table. Sela argues to seal the vein forever — that is Tam's argument. Arthur's counter: sealed, it remains a target; working, it funds the lease buyouts — reparations, not charity. The gambit's cost is decided knowingly: the surface deed and the damping method both go into the Trust; the fail-safe is designed, its maintenance flaw acknowledged and accepted (who guards the guardians — unsolved). A half-thought about his parents, unresolved. He sends invitations: the shaft, three days, all parties. **Chapter 7 — "Downshaft" (~1100 words)** The council in damp-suits, the vein audibly unstable in every delegate's ears, broadcast running. Arthur lays out the cascade hazard for the record (MAD made public), demonstrates damping beside the vein itself, and produces the Antares orbital survey card — mutual embarrassment as equalizer; Vosk unruffled, almost approving. The Azra Trust presented: neutral Institute stewardship, equal licenses, proceeds to land rights and lease buyouts, the memorial clause for Tam (no one dares object), the dead-man fail-safe. Hallowes spots the fail-safe's maintenance hole and extracts the extraction-services contracts — her real win. Crane takes a guarantor seat. Vosk signs last, saying something that confirms nothing and everything. Contested arithmetic, not force. **Chapter 8 — "Warden" (~1000 words)** Coda, months later. A small war of tariffs and lawyers instead of atomics. Arthur as salaried warden of the land he no longer owns, grumbling at paperwork. Sela on the settler council — she refused his education offer and took the memorial commission; they argue pleasantly about pump schedules. Hallowes profitable and cheerful. The watch still unfixed. He almost asks about the roster name and doesn't. Ends small and sideways: Tam's plaque on his way down the shaft, the pump noise, a half-life joke, and the wry recognition that the balance holds only so long as everyone can still do the arithmetic.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Arthur Neegan **Background.** Born in Cydonia Fields Settlement, third year of the Halloran lease era on Mars. His parents, Declan and Marta, were indentured from Earth under a fifteen-year lease; Arthur's childhood was spent doing arithmetic for them — hours worked against debt accrued, scribbling on the backs of assay chits. The education bond was the family's one gamble: Halloran paid his engineering schooling at Kaol Institute in exchange for twelve years of his labor, of which nine are served. He was never precocious, only *careful* — the kind of student who re-derives a formula rather than trust the card deck. His thesis on harmonic induction damping earned a single line of praise from Renn ("competent, and perhaps more, if he ever needed it") and was then forgotten by everyone, including Arthur, because it solved a problem nobody had. Then Azra existed, and the problem existed. **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Dry, economical with words, allergic to being thanked. He grumbles as a form of affection. He keeps his father's pocket watch — stopped at the hour of the depressurization accident that killed Declan — meaning to fix it for nine years. He means to fix it every winter. He grows hydroponic tomatoes badly and blames the seed stock, never himself, and gives the mealy results away rather than eat them. He reads lease contracts for pleasure the way other men read mysteries, hunting the flaw. He plays correspondence chess with an Earth engineer named Ponti who takes six weeks per move, and Arthur suspects Ponti has lost the board. **Flaws.** He is slow to trust and slower to forgive, and he files grievances instead of speaking them — a habit inherited from his mother. He underestimates his own leverage because his whole life has trained him to think of himself as collateral. He can be unkind about sentiment; his first instinct after Tam's death is to start calculating funeral deductions, and it takes him an ugly beat to hear himself. **Physicality.** Slight, big-eared, with the settler's long economy of movement — he never hurries in low gravity because hurrying wastes air and dignity. Carries himself like a man perpetually entering a room he's paying rent on. Smiles rarely and crookedly; when he's worried, he taps two fingers against his thigh in a damping cadence. **Motives & relationships.** He wants, in order he'd never admit: his land safe, the lease system dead, and the watch fixed. His allegiance is to arithmetic — he'd say that himself — but it's really to the people arithmetic is done *to*. Renn is the nearest thing to family; Sela becomes the colleague who argues with him; Hallowes he despises with a purity he finds almost restful. **Voice.** *"The watch works fine. It's right twice a day, which is more than I can say for the Federation."* — and, watching Vosk pour tea, thinking: *Lowball. Per acre. She's not cheap, she's not stupid, so what am I missing.* # Commissioner Vosk **Background.** Saro Vosk, born on Antares Station II to a tug pilot and a customs auditor; she grew up fluent in two languages, navigational and contractual. Rose through the Combine's trade delegation because she could lose an argument gracefully and win the clause. Twenty years of negotiating for a polity that exists *because* of Azra drives — she has watched her civilization go from orbital drums to a starfaring power in a single generation, and she is one of maybe six people alive who understands the whole structure rests on scarcity. Appointed to the Diplomatic Corps ("diplomatic" being the Combine's oldest joke) with one standing instruction regarding Martian Azra: *nothing changes quickly.* **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Witty in a way that leaves no fingerprints; wins arguments by quoting your own words back to you with slight improvements. Pours tea obsessively, badly — over-steeped, and she knows it, and serving it anyway is a small test of who will say so. She collects physical books because they can't be quietly edited, which she considers the only honest format. She is courteous to servants and lethal to peers, and never the reverse. Her one visible tic: when she has decided to tell you nothing, she becomes *more* helpful. **Flaws.** She believes stability is a kindness, which lets her rationalize almost anything, including poverty maintained at scale. She's lonely in the way of people who have made themselves into instruments; her personal life is a period of leave every four years, spent Earthside, about which she makes jokes that are entirely true. She underestimates people she has successfully read once — Arthur's slow arithmetic will be the recurring surprise of her year. **Physicality.** Small, silver-haired, dressed in Combine gray so plain it reads as a uniform for people too senior to wear uniforms. Sits very still; her stillness makes other people fidget productively. Hands express everything her face refuses — she turns her teacup a quarter-rotation before delivering a threat. **Motives & relationships.** Serve the Combine's survival, which she genuinely equates with preventing the war that abundance would force. To Antares she is loyal; to the idea of the balance of power she is *devout*. She regards Hallowes as a competent animal, Crane as furniture, and Arthur, by the end, as the most interesting thing to happen to her portfolio in a decade. **Voice.** *"You'll forgive the tea. The Combine's ambitions are limitless; its leaves are not."* — and, at signing: *"Mr. Neegan, I never doubted you'd do something. I merely hoped it would be something we could all survive."* # Director Renata Hallowes **Background.** Third-generation extraction aristocracy — her grandfather hauled the first assay rig to Mars and the family has been amortizing it ever since. Renata did a hard decade in shaft operations before headquarters, and it's the source of her power: she has crewed, so crews can't condescend to her, and she has buried men, so she can discuss death with the fluency of an actuary. Runs Halloran's Martian operations from an office with a wall of framed lease contracts she calls "the family photographs." **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Grandmotherly warmth deployed with total cynicism — she remembers everyone's mother's name, including Sela's, especially Sela's. Discusses amortization schedules the way others discuss grandchildren, with pride and endless patience. Sends handwritten letters, actual ink, because ink reads as sincere and she finds that useful. Drinks real coffee, imported, and offers visitors the cup she's poured and then takes it back if negotiations go poorly — the politest hostage-taking in the system. **Flaws.** She has spent so long inside the lease system's logic that she genuinely cannot see it as cruelty; to her it is *structure*, and structure is the only mercy the universe offers. Her warmth is real, which is worse than if it were fake. She is incapable of imagining that Arthur might not want to be rich. **Physicality.** Wide, comfortable, unhurried; sits like she owns the chair and everything the chair is thinking about. Laughs easily and exactly on schedule. Wears a crew badge from her shaft years, tarnished, prominently — the only dishonest thing about her person, because she's never once wanted to go back down. **Motives & relationships.** Halloran's share price, first, last, and always — she'd call it "the families we feed," and she could produce the payroll to prove it. She respects Arthur the way one chess player respects another across a handicap. Her Chapter 5 order — the deep core sample — is coercion laundered through the lease, and she will grieve Tam sincerely, deduct the funeral from his credit, and see no contradiction, ever. **Voice.** *"Everyone thinks the contract is how we own you. Nonsense, Arthur. The contract is how we count you."* — and, spotting the fail-safe's flaw: *"A dead-man's switch wants a mortician, dear. I happen to employ several."* # Undersecretary Elias Crane **Background.** Earthborn, Luna-schooled, a career Federation civil servant who has never personally visited a mine and considers that a strength — "distance is objectivity." Rose through the Bureau of Strategic Assets by writing memoranda so unimpeachable they became precedent. He is the *author* of the Emergency War Powers Protocol 44, the very instrument now aimed at Arthur's land, and being deployed to Mars to wave his own paperwork at someone is, quietly, the proudest week of his life. **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Speaks exclusively in statute citations and clause numbers; the tedium is not an accident, it is his weapon — men agree to things while trying to escape a recitation. Corrects terminology reflexively: "It is not an ultimatum; it is an administrative determination with coercive effect." Keeps a pocket edition of the Federation Charter he actually reads. Genuinely believes the Federation is the only adult in a room full of adolescents with atomic matches. **Flaws.** Mistakes procedure for ethics. He has the imagination to foresee what a war over the vein would mean and the training to file the foreknowledge away. He is also, underneath the gray, vain — the memo he reads aloud in Chapter 4 is his own prose, and he is a little bit in love with its balance of clauses. **Physicality.** Tall, narrow, gray-suited to the point of camouflage; moves like a document passing through a building. Voice pitched at the exact register that makes listeners lean in and then regret it. His single human tell: he takes his coffee with two sugars and is embarrassed about it. **Motives & relationships.** Federation supremacy dressed as Federation stewardship. He reports to a committee that does not exist yet and will convene the moment the vein is resolved — his real audience throughout is a quorum. He views Hallowes as a provincial obstacle, Vosk as the principal threat, and Arthur as "Asset 7-A," and the story's quiet joke on him is how long it takes his own paperwork to recognize Arthur as a person. **Voice.** *"I am authorized to inform you that you are authorized to comply."* — and, at the signing, almost wistfully: *"This would have made a very good memo, Mr. Neegan."* # Sela Okafor **Background.** Earthborn in the Lagos arcologies, indentured at nineteen on a seven-year Halloran lease — the contract she signed to pay her brother's medical debt, a debt which, by the fine print, survives the indenture and now accrues to *her*. Fifth year served. Crew lead on survey detail, which is how she met Arthur — correcting his assay math within an hour of meeting him, correctly. She is the best tunneler on the diverted crew and knows it, and knows exactly what that's worth under a lease system: nothing. **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Prickly, direct, allergic to rescue. She keeps a ledger of her own debt more ruthless than Halloran's, and the first thing she does with wages is pay principle, never interest — a small doomed discipline she refuses to abandon. She drinks her coffee ration in one swallow, black, as a matter of policy against pleasure. She names the tunnel borers after dead crew members, which the crews find macabre and she finds accurate. **Flaws.** Her pride is armor and she knows it and wears it anyway; she'd rather lose standing up than win owing someone. Her moral clarity makes her slow to accept half-measures — she argues to seal the vein forever with a purist's fire that the gambit can't afford. The memorial commission she takes in place of Arthur's education offer is a compromise that will cost her nights for years, and she'd make it again. **Physicality.** Compact, deliberate, hands callused in the specific patterns of a tunneler's trade; she carries herself with the economy of someone who has done years of hard labor on short rations and refuses to make it look easy. Meets eyes and holds them a half-beat longer than is comfortable. **Motives & relationships.** Her brother's debt, then Tam's memory, then — a distant third she won't name yet — a life that belongs to her. Her warning to Arthur before the sabotage costs her a penal reassignment threat and she never mentions the cost. With Arthur she builds a working relationship of pleasant friction: they argue about pump schedules like an old married crew. Her grief for Tam is the story's unhealed detail. **Voice.** *"Don't buy my lease, Neegan. Buy the ledger it came out of."* — and, in the shaft at the signing: *"You want to know what's down there under all that metal? The hours. Mine and everyone's. It remembers them even if you people don't."* # Tam Ores **Background.** Tomar Ores, twenty-two years indentured across three contracts — so deep in the lease system he's almost geological. An Earth-generation settler who came out young, signed to pay a gambling debt he's regretted with his whole heart and mentioned never. Foreman of the survey detail; he taught half the crew their jobs, including Sela, and does his accounting with a stub of pencil behind his ear. **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Genial, phlegmatic, constitutionally unsuited to rebellion; his small dignities are coffee — he shares his ration with Arthur on the survey shifts, pouring it out with ceremony — and a stubborn belief that the Company keeps a promise eventually, the way weather eventually comes. He has been ordered into unsafe ground before and has always come out, which is his fatal theology. **Flaws.** His decency is passive; the lease system has trained him to believe refusal is a luxury other people can afford. He knows the deep core order is dangerous and follows it anyway because refusal means penal reassignment and his contract has two years left and he is tired in the marrow. His last words to Sela are an order to stay clear of it, and she obeys them, and that obedience is part of her grief. **Physicality.** Big, stooped, gray-templed, moving like a man conserving himself for a shift that's been going for two decades. Whistles one tune, badly, when checking the rig bearings. Smells of coffee and lubricant; everyone will remember that. **Motives & relationships.** Two years. Get to the end of the two years, go Earthside, see whether the trees are as green as the postcards. That's the whole ambition, and it's the lease system's cruelest joke that it's precisely the modesty of it that kills him. He likes Arthur without reservation — the first free man he's ever worked beside who poured his own ration. **Voice.** *"Company's never once killed me yet, lad. That's a better record than most doctors."* — and the final one, reaching for the pencil behind his ear: *"Just the one sample, then. Then we're all up for coffee."* # Dr. Ilsa Renn **Background.** Sixty, Earthborn, one of the founding physicists of Kaol Institute's Mars campus — she came out during the first Azra rush to answer the only interesting question of the century and has resented the interruption of her career by politics ever since. Author of the standard text on decay-modulation; the person who wrote "competent, and perhaps more, if he ever needed it" under Arthur's thesis and has thought of that sentence, on and off, for years, with mild professional guilt. **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Sardonic, quick, runs her institute like a small weather system. Chews mint leaves against pipe-smoking, having been forbidden the pipe in three buildings. Lectures everyone, including commissioners and undersecretaries, including at dinner. Her loyalty is to the physics — she'd hand the damping method to a saint or a tyrant if the derivation were sound, which is precisely why she's the only party everyone will trust to hold the Trust. **Flaws.** Moral clarity of the ivory tower: she can be slow to see the human machinery under the equations, and her instinct in any crisis is to reach for a formula. She underestimates Hallowes for years — "the woman is an accountant with a smile" — and it costs them at the fail-safe clause. She is also, privately, delighted by the cascade crisis, and being delighted appalls her, and she's honest enough to say so. **Physicality.** Small, white-braided, kinetic; talks with chalk in hand and will diagram on any surface, including Vosk's table, once. Coats with pockets that clink with sample vials and mint. **Motives & relationships.** The safe deployment of the physics, full stop. Her arc is the story's quiet reconciliation of the small picture with the big one: she starts believing the knowledge is the thing and ends knowing the trust is the thing the knowledge requires. She is Arthur's nearest family, and says so exactly once, off-screen, in a letter he doesn't answer. **Voice.** *"The universe has no opinion, Arthur. That's what makes it trustworthy. Never confuse it with the people quoting it."* — and, about the fail-safe's flaw: *"Every lock wants a locksmith, and every locksmith wants to eat. I'll take the one who eats in daylight."*

# Chapter 1 — Outbound Arthur Neegan had never been fond of ships, for the same reason he had never been fond of hospitals: they were places where other people's competence governed his continued existence. The transfer vessel was a stubby, functional thing, all pipe and rivet, and through its single viewport Mars was shrinking with the unhurried patience of a creditor. He watched it go and did the arithmetic he had been doing since the airlock closed: forty hours to the Antares flagship, however long the meeting lasted after that, forty hours back, and somewhere behind him a claim marker standing over more Azra than anyone had ever pulled out of the ground in one place, unguarded except by distance and a fence he'd built himself. He had built the fence himself, too. He found himself thinking about the fence. It was a stupid thing to think about, and he thought about it anyway. They had come at breakfast, which he considered a meaningful choice. Six of them in the yard — a shuttle had set down on his lettuce bed, and no one had apologized for it — and they carried arms in the open, slung, in the manner of men who wanted you to understand that the arms were furniture. Their commander wore a sidearm she clearly never expected to draw and an insignia Arthur had only ever seen in newsfax: the triple-star of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. Diplomatic, in the Combine's vocabulary, was the oldest joke in the language. "Arthur Neegan," the commander had said, consulting nothing. "Holder of Claim 7, Cydonia Fields District. We'd like a word with you." "I get a word?" he'd said. "Which one?" She had not smiled, but something in her posture had conceded the point. "We'd like several, aboard the *Courser*. My principal will explain." "And if I've got a pump schedule to keep?" "Your pumps are running, Mr. Neegan. We checked." That was when he should have understood the size of it. Instead he had noted the shuttle's landing struts — unnecessary weight on Mars, vanity engineering — and asked for twenty minutes to pack. They gave him ten and stood in his yard while he took down his father's watch from the shelf, put on his good boots, and looked at the tomato vines with the guilt of a man leaving animals. The tomatoes were mealy and bad, and he'd have defended them to anyone, and there was no one to defend them to. The orders were sealed, actual wax on actual paper — Combine theater, like the struts — and informed him, in language of great courtesy, that Claim 7 had been designated "a matter of interstellar concern" and its holder "respectfully requested" to attend a consultation. There was a statute cited at the bottom. There always was. It is a curious feature of the past thirty years that the whole shape of human civilization came to depend on a metal nobody had heard of in 2147. Azra does not, of itself, do anything. It is a gray, disagreeable substance, dull as a committee, and its single property is that it hurries other things along: place it near anything radioactive and the decay runs not faster by a percentage but by factors of thousands, tame, tuneable, on command. The atomists had spent a century dreaming of controlled decay. Azra was the key dropped in the street. A drive small enough to push a ship to Antares in three years. A warhead that made the old fission bombs look like fireworks, and — the part the newsfax liked less — made them look like fireworks *cheaply*. Every power on Earth and three off it wanted Azra the way a starving man wants bread, and Mars, it turned out, had the bakery. The rush had been on for a decade, and the leases with it. Arthur's parents had come out under one of the early ones — fifteen years' bound labor to Halloran Extraction in exchange for passage, a bunk, and the promise that Mars was the sort of place where a man with a strong back and a stronger stomach could end up owning dirt. Both halves of the Neegan family had now paid for dirt: his father with twenty-two years of shifts, his mother with the asthma the mines gave her as a parting gift, Arthur himself with an education bond — Halloran had sent him to the Kaol Institute and owned, by contract, twelve years of his labor. He was nine years in. He had done the arithmetic on that contract so many times the numbers had worn smooth. Nine years in, on a Tuesday, a routine punch-card survey of his own claim — his own, free and clear, the one thing he had that wasn't mortgaged to somebody — had come back with an assay chit that he'd read four times, run twice on the old spectrometer, and then sat with for an hour in the pump noise, feeling the way a man feels when a door he's leaned on all his life turns out not to be locked so much as not to exist. He had told no one. He hadn't decided anything yet. He'd wanted a week to think, and he'd had six days, and then the Combine had come to breakfast. That was the part he kept chewing on, forty hours out, tapping two fingers against his thigh in the damping cadence he'd never noticed himself doing until Renn had pointed it out years ago and he'd kept doing it anyway. He had told no one. The assay chit was in his safe behind the seed stock. And yet the *Courser* had known, the commander had known his pump schedule, and the size of the escort suggested they'd known before he ran the second confirmation. Someone had been reading his instruments. Or someone had been reading his ground. The stars through the viewport meant nothing to him; he was a man who had spent his whole life under one thin sky and preferred it. But a ship was a place where other people's competence governed his existence, and he spent the hours doing the only useful thing an engineer can do in transit, which is to imagine every way the meeting could go wrong, in order, with estimates. The *Courser* came up out of the dark the way Antares ships always did in the newsfax — vast, silent, lit like a city — and the pilot announced docking with the modest pride of a man parking a continent. Arthur took the watch out of his breast pocket to check it, remembered it hadn't run in nine years, and put it back. Then he stood, straightened a collar nobody would look at, and walked to the airlock.

# Chapter 3 — The Paper *"Subsoil resources of every kind, whether known or hereafter discovered, remain the property of the Company in perpetuity, the Settler retaining such rights as attach to the surface to a depth of one (1) meter, together with the improvement thereon."* — Standard Halloran Lease, Schedule F, Clause 12(c) The man was waiting at Arthur's fence when the cab let him off, which meant Halloran had known his travel schedule before he did. He was young, clean, and polite, and he held his documents the way a priest holds a reliquary. "Mr. Neegan. I'm instructed to serve you with notice of the Company's interest in Claim 7. I'm sorry about the lettuce." "Don't be," said Arthur. "It was bad lettuce." The papers ran nine pages. Halloran Extraction, acting under rights assigned from the original lease of one D. Neegan, asserted title to the subsoil of Claim 7, together with — and this was the clause he read four times — "all discoveries, surveys, assays, and improvements in technique made by the bondee during the term of his education bond." Nine years in, three to run. His survey, his assay chit, his find: Halloran was claiming the arithmetic itself. The letter came separately, by private pouch, in ink. He recognized the hand before the signature. *My dear Arthur,* it began, which was impressive, since they had met twice. *Congratulations on your remarkable news — and it is remarkable; I have seen the harmonics, and in thirty years of extraction I have seen nothing like them. The Company can make this easy for you, and I do hope you will let us. My colleagues want to be difficult, and I have told them the Neegans have always been sensible people. Your mother's asthma, by the way — has it improved? I have taken the liberty of enclosing an amortization schedule which I think you will find genuinely interesting reading. Do note the compounding line. People always skip the compounding line, and it is my favorite.* *Yours, Renata Hallowes* Arthur read lease contracts for pleasure the way other men read mysteries — for the flaw — and he sat up half the night with Schedule F looking for one. He found it at two in the morning, and it was no flaw at all: whoever had drafted his father's lease had been paid well and had earned it. The top meter of Mars was his. Everything below it was theirs. Twenty-two years of his father's shifts had bought one meter of dirt, and the Company had kept the rest of the planet. The crews arrived with the morning cab: a survey detail, fourteen of them, Halloran badges and gray Company coveralls, ordered onto his land under the same notice. "Confirmatory survey," the crew manifest said. He couldn't impede them without triggering the bond clause, so he did the next best thing, which was to stand on his own meter of dirt drinking coffee and watching them work badly. They weren't working badly for long. Their foreman was a big, stooped, gray-templed man who introduced himself as Ores — "Tam, if we're going to be neighbors" — and their crew lead was a compact woman his own age who did not introduce herself until she'd looked over his shoulder at his portable spectrometer and said: "Your calibration's off. Point-seven percent on the long range. You've been reading hot for weeks." He checked. She was right. "Okafor," she said. "Sela." They drank the mid-shift ration together by the pump housing, because Tam insisted on ceremony, and Tam poured Arthur's cup with both hands like a man pouring for a superior officer. The pump noise ran under everything, the way it ran under his whole life, and Tam talked about the Company the way other men talked about weather. "They want a core sample to bedrock," Tam said, cheerful. "Deep one. I told the office the harmonics down there sing a note I don't care for. The office says the numbers are fine." He shrugged largely. "The Company's never once killed me yet, lad. That's a better record than most doctors." Sela said nothing at all, but she looked at the claim marker and the fence and Arthur standing on his meter of dirt, and there was a ledger behind her eyes, and Arthur recognized the arithmetic because he had grown up watching his mother do it. Dr. Renn arrived two days later, uninvited and unannounced, in an Institute flitter she had parked on the lettuce bed, which made it official: everyone knew but him. She came in talking. "The Halloran filings crossed my desk Tuesday — we certify their extraction safety, the one thing in the system nobody has bought. Neegan, your harmonics are the loudest numbers I have read in thirty years, and I am including the war years." She had chalk in her hand before she was through the door, and she diagrammed on his kitchen table without asking. "Do you know what happens if someone cuts a working gallery into that vein at standard spacing?" "I assume it's bad." "Crude extraction in a formation that dense doesn't mine the decay, it *starts* it. A cascade. The vein goes critical in sympathy with itself, and the crust of this planet —" she drew a line under the diagram, hard enough to snap the chalk, "— remembers it was never very solid to begin with. Anyone who works that vein with a shovel and a prayer cracks Mars open to the mantle. Everyone can see the money. Nobody has run the resonance." She stopped, and looked at him, and something changed in her face. "Or," she said slowly, "someone has. Twelve years ago. A thesis on harmonic induction damping that I read as a bound typescript and reviewed in one line, and I have thought about that sentence on and off ever since, with guilt, because I wrote *competent, and perhaps more, if he ever needed it.*" She put her hand flat on the diagram. "Well. Do you need it?" Arthur went to the shelf and took down the typescript, still in its faded Institute binding. The problem nobody had. "It's the only copy," he said. "I never needed it." Renn opened it to the third page and began, as he'd known she would, to correct his notation.

# Chapter 4 — Terms Undersecretary Elias Crane arrived on a Thursday, with two aides and no escort, which was its own kind of message: the Federation did not need armed men to be frightening. He stood in Arthur's yard in a gray suit, surveyed the fence, the marker, the tomato vines, and said, "Claim 7. Hm. Adequate." He declined coffee, then accepted it, then took two sugars, then appeared to feel the sugars were a confidence he had been robbed of. Arthur filed that away too. "I am here in an administrative capacity," Crane said, producing a folder. "I have prepared a statement. I will read it. You may wish to sit." "I'll stand, thanks." "As you prefer." He put on the half-glasses of a man who had worn them since they were young. "*Pursuant to Emergency War Powers Protocol 44, ratified by joint session, to which instrument your attention is invited: subsoil resource formations within the Martian Protectorate exceeding strategic thresholds, as certified by the Bureau, are designated matters of Federal concern. The formation underlying Claim 7, Cydonia Fields District, having been so certified, is hereby designated Federal Asset 7-A. The holder of record is entitled to compensation at Bureau rates, to appeal before a Federal examiner, and to such continuing enjoyment of the surface as is consistent with Federal use.*" Arthur let the pump noise stand in for a reply. "You will notice," Crane said, "that the statement does not require your signature. That is not an oversight. It is, if I may say, the statement's principal elegance. Federal acts do not ask. They announce, and then they are." "Bureau rates," said Arthur. "What are Bureau rates?" "Four percent of certified value, paid over twenty years, in Earth instruments." "Certified by the Bureau." "Naturally. One cannot have the fox auditing the henhouse." He removed the glasses and polished them, and for one moment looked almost human. "Mr. Neegan, between ourselves, and speaking now in no capacity whatsoever: you have a Combine commissioner on one flank and a company like Halloran on the other, and you are a bonded engineer with three years to run. The Federation is the only party in this matter that does not intend to cheat you. We intend merely to *have* you. There is a difference, and in my experience the difference is survivable." "And the appeal?" "You may appeal. The examiner is appointed by the Bureau. I mention in passing that I wrote Protocol 44, and I would ask you not to enjoy that fact as much as most people seem to." He left the folder on the kitchen table, thanked Arthur for the coffee in a tone that conveyed the sugars had never happened, and departed. Arthur read the whole thing that night, cover to cover, including the annexes. Crane wrote well. The annexes were beautiful. That was somehow the most menacing part: somewhere on Earth a man had enjoyed drafting the sentence *such continuing enjoyment of the surface as is consistent with Federal use.* Renn came over at dawn and found him at the assay table with the punch-cards spread out like a card game he was losing. "Federal Asset 7-A," she said, reading the folder. "You've been promoted from a man to an asset. Congratulations. It's more than the lease system ever gave you." "Renn. Say we sign. Say one of them signs — Combine, Federation, Halloran, any of them, and starts cutting a gallery. You said it cascades. How big?" "With damping, at proper spacing, with a crew that reads the harmonics every shift?" She chalked a quick sketch on the table, the way she sketched on everything. "Bearable. Local. Like any mine, it will kill its percentage of men and the rest will get paid." "And without damping?" "Neegan, the vein's resonance is the loudest in the system. Cut it raw and the cascade fronts will feed each other. You wouldn't lose a mine. You'd lose a district, and the dust would glow." "Now the one you won't like," Arthur said. "Say nobody signs. Say nobody mines it. Say the Combine buys it and sits on it, or the Federation designates it and a war starts over who holds the designation. What happens when the shooting comes here?" Renn stopped with the chalk in the air. He watched her do it — watched her arrive where he'd been living for two days. "An orbital strike," she said slowly, "even a conventional penetrator, even a miss, cracks the formation. And the formation doesn't care whose war it is." "The planet goes." "The planet goes." She sat down. "Thirty years I've said the physics was the interesting part. The interesting part was always the people." After she left he got out the Combine draft and read Clause Nine again. *The right of non-development, in perpetuity, at the Combine's sole discretion.* He read the price again. Fifty thousand the acre. Farmland pricing, and Vosk had all but told him so, and he'd been too busy being insulted by the number to read it. The Combine was one generation old, built on Azra drives, holding its edge because Azra was scarce. He'd asked her why they'd buy high and sit, and she'd answered with a confession and then denied making it. Now he did the arithmetic at the kitchen table, the way his mother had done it on the backs of chits. She wasn't buying a mine. She was buying a *burial*. Sixteen million to put the vein under the Combine's sole discretion forever, so the drives stayed scarce, so the balance held, so nobody had to find out what the next war did to Mars. She'd pay that out of petty cash and call it defense. He took a fresh notebook and, at the top of the first page, wrote *WANTS* and crossed it out and wrote *FEARS*: *Combine — fears abundance. Federation — fears the Combine getting it. Halloran — fears being cut out. Nobody fears the vein itself.* He read the last line twice, then underlined it, and sat for a long while with the pump noise going and the watch in his breast pocket not going. Then he got up, put on his boots, and walked out to the shaft door of the claim marker and stood looking down the dark of it, at all that metal under his meter of dirt, doing the only thing that had ever come easily to him: the load-bearing question, arriving before the answer.

Arthur got to the phone at the shaft office and got Halloran's night duty man and got a statute number in reply. He got to the cage as it was leaving and saw Tam's face in the light, and Tam raised a hand — not a wave, a *staying* gesture, the flat palm of a foreman: stay clear of it. "Company's never once killed me yet, lad," Tam called up, cheerful as weather. "Just the one sample, then. Then we're all up for coffee." The cage dropped. Sela made a sound Arthur filed away and never mentioned, then or after. He took the auxiliary cage down with Renn's emergency kit and his own toolbox, and he was two galleries from the core head when the note started. You could feel it before you could hear it. The hum came up through the rock and into the teeth, into the fillings, into the boots, one long organ note that the instruments had been trying to describe for weeks and the body understood in a second. The survey meters went off their pins. Somewhere behind him a pump began to sing in sympathy, its bearings taking up the harmonic like a choir joining late. In the core gallery the trace minerals in the cut rock were hurrying toward their half-lives all at once, and the air had the taste of ozone and lightning, and the core head was ringing like a struck anvil that would not stop being struck. The crew was running. Tam was not; Tam was at the head, hauling the sample chit out of the socket with both hands, because the order said bring up a sample, and because two years remained and he was tired in the marrow. Arthur had read his own thesis once, twelve years ago, and had never needed it. The cascade was a resonance, the loudest in the system; resonance can be drowned. The survey rig carried induction coil sets for sensing; sensing coils are driving coils with the polarity reversed; the pump gallery above had alternating motors enough to light a town. He heard the harmonic in his teeth and tapped it out against his own thigh without meaning to — two fingers, the damping cadence — and by that beat he reversed the rig's coil bank into the drive circuit and began feeding the vein its own note, upside down. It should not have worked. It worked to eleven percent, then to forty, then the hum broke into two hums arguing, and then the meters came off their pins the other way, falling, and the choir of pumps lost its note one by one, and the silence afterward was the loudest thing Arthur ever heard. He was lying in the cut, someone's coffee ration soaking his sleeve, and Renn was already running in with her kit, screaming certification language like an oath. Tam walked out of the gallery on his own legs, sample chit in hand, cheerful, complaining mildly that his coffee had gone over. He was dead by noon. The dose had been a front passing over a man with his hands full of order. He went the way the walked-away dose goes: talking, thirsty, asking whether the coffee was fresh, and then not asking anything. Arthur's first act, before he had washed the rock dust off, was to sit down with the crew's pay ledger and begin calculating the funeral. He heard himself doing it — heard the pencil, heard the accrued-credit line, heard his own father in it — and put the pencil down and was sick in the gravel, and that is all there is to say about that hour. The card came to light in the cleanup. A Combine "certification observer" had been embedded with the detail since Tuesday, and in the evacuation he had left his field kit behind. Arthur went through it because it was on his ground, and the top card of the deck was an orbital survey punch, Antares format, precision his own instruments couldn't dream of: his vein, mapped from orbit, in harmony lines, in far better resolution than anything the Company had. They had known before his spectrometer did. On the roster line, in the Combine's tidy annotation, was a survey team of five names, and the second name was one his father had mentioned exactly once, twenty years ago, at the kitchen table, in a voice Arthur had never had the sense to ask about. He put the card in his breast pocket, behind the watch, and told no one, including Renn, including himself on alternate days. The rest arranged itself without his help. Fourteen crew had watched the meters die while one man with a rig and a reversed polarity held the planet's crust on. Renn certified the incident — the Institute's language, "demonstration of the sole known damping methodology" — and the newsfax did the rest. Within a week, three governments' engineers and one company's lawyers had all quietly arrived at the same figure: the vein was worth nothing without the man. The knowledge-lock locked, in public, in ink. Hallowes' letter came on the ninth day, in ink, in her hand. *My dear Arthur — a tragedy, and I grieve with you; Tam Ores was one of mine, and one of the best of mine. I have made provision. You will find, per Schedule D, that funeral costs are an advance against accrued credit, so the burden falls lightest on those who earned it. I know you will see the sense of that, because you have always read the schedules more closely than anyone. Do note also: your crew's hearings are suspended in light of the demonstration. The Company takes care of its own.* *Your mother's asthma — has it improved?* Arthur read it standing in the yard, in the pump noise, over the ground that had killed Tam, and then he went inside and took out the notebook with *FEARS* at the top of the page, and added a line underneath everything else, in a hand that was almost steady: *Add: everyone thinks the vein is the weapon. The final annex named the escort that would arrive on the twentieth. It was beautifully drafted. He was a little surprised the man hadn't signed it in iambic. He read both twice, set them on the table, and went to make the coffee himself, since Tam wasn't there to do it with ceremony. Renn arrived at noon and Sela at dusk, and they sat at the kitchen table with the pump noise under everything, and Arthur laid out the cards the way he'd laid out punch-cards for Renn weeks ago. "Here's the ground," he said. "Everyone wants it. Nobody can safely touch it without me. If I sign with any one of them, the other two start planning, and the planning is what kills the planet. If I sit still, the twentieth happens." He looked at the two of them. "So." "Seal it," Sela said, immediately, flatly. "Cap the shaft, certify the formation untouchable, publish the cascade numbers to every newsfax on two worlds. Let it sit in the ground like a mine field with a fence around it. Forever." "Sela—" "That's Tam's argument, Neegan, so you'll hear it out." She didn't raise her voice; she never did. "He's down there because everyone could see the money and nobody could be bothered to run the resonance. You want to fix that with *licenses*? You want to fix it with paperwork from the same species that wrote Schedule F?" She put her hand on the table. "The planet doesn't need the money. Seal it, and nobody has a reason to come, and no one else stands where Tam stood." Renn, who had been diagramming on the tablecloth, said: "It's defensible, Arthur. A sealed vein under a published hazard certification is the cheapest safety in the system. I could defend it at the Institute in one paragraph." "And in ten years," Arthur said, "somebody's the third generation on from the ones who signed, and the hazard numbers are a legend, and somebody's short on drives and long on confidence. A tomb is only safe while everyone remembers it's a tomb." He tapped the table. "And there are fourteen people in that crew whose leases have years left, and thousands more behind them, and the system that killed Tam keeps killing at the standard rate, on schedule, forever. The vein's worth more than all of us, times ten. That's the one fact nobody at this table can afford to be polite about." "So we sell it," said Sela, "and everyone gets their share of the thing that killed him." "No. We *rent* it. Nobody owns it." His father's shifts. Everything they'd overpaid for the dirt, every year of it, and the whole idea of it had been that the meter was *paid for*, free and clear, his. He heard the pump. He didn't finish the sentence, and Renn, uncharacteristically, did not fill the silence. "It goes in," he said. "The whole works. It came up through the boots and into the teeth, into the fillings, into the suits' own bones. The survey meters ticked visibly on every hip. Hallowes's face did not change; she had done her decade. The silence afterward worked on everyone differently. "An orator would have used a map," Vosk said. "This was better." "You've all been planning around that formation for a month," Arthur said. Crane, recovering his voice's register: "You are describing a strategic hostage situation, Mr. Neegan." "Antares orbital survey of Claim 7, precision anything on Mars is proud of, dated before my own survey. The Combine has known what's under my fence longer than I have. I'm showing it to you so nobody here has to guess anyone's cards anymore. Everyone has a deck. I've put mine on the table." Crane looked at Vosk. Vosk looked at the card with what Arthur could only call professional appreciation. "The Combine surveys everything," she said mildly. "We are a curious polity. Nobody objected. Hallowes signed that page first, and sincerely; that was the unsettling part. Sela watched them all do it from the cage door, and her face said she was keeping the ledger. Then Hallowes did what Hallowes had flown three hours to do. "Clause Eleven," she said pleasantly. "The dead-man rig. Institute maintenance, in daylight. Very fine, dear. But a dead-man's switch wants a mortician, and I happen to employ several." She let that sit. "The flaw is published, the locksmith eats in daylight, everyone watches — all well and good. But the rig wants inspecting by someone with a *balance sheet*, not a conscience. Consciences are cheap to audit and dear to maintain. Halloran takes the inspection, annually, on the record — and while we're contracting, Halloran has the only crews on Mars who've worked ground this mean. You'll want extraction services. We give very good value." "That's the company that caused the ninth," Sela said, flatly, from the door. "That's the company that did," Hallowes agreed, "under my order, and I'll wear it to the funeral of anyone you care to name. Which is why we'll follow your charter's spacing to the card, Mrs. Okafor, because I've buried my own and I read the schedules now." She looked back at Arthur. Arthur did the arithmetic where everyone could watch him do it. "Extraction services at published rates. Inspection joint — Institute and Halloran, both signing each year." "Joint," said Hallowes, "with my name first." She held out her hand.
