# Chapter 8 — Warden The war, when it finally came, was fought with tariffs, and it was, everyone agreed, an improvement. The Federation had opened hostilities in the spring with a duty on Combine drive licenses. The Combine had replied with a filing of magnificent, malicious precision. Halloran had sued everyone at once, on principle, the way other powers conducted naval exercises. Arthur followed it in the newsfax with the detached interest of a man whose planet was no longer the object under dispute, merely the venue, and took a mild, uncharitable pride in the fact that the casualty list so far ran to two attorneys and one ambassador's career. He was a salaried man now. Warden of Claim 7, Kaol Institute Trust, at a wage he had set himself and the board had doubled, and he'd been grumbling about the paperwork ever since — license logs, crew certifications, the annual rig inspection with Halloran's name first on the report and Renn's directly under it, both signatures crooked with mutual dislike. The Trust had forty-one licensees from three polities, and each of them believed the published rates were secretly unfair to them, which Arthur considered the engine's normal sound. The house and the meter of dirt had gone into the Trust with everything else, so the charter leased them back to him at one credit per annum, and he paid it on the first of every year with visible resentment, a leaseholder like his father before him, with the difference that he now sat on both sides of the contract. Renn said this made him the only man on Mars who could audit himself and did, which he let pass, because she was the trustee and could dock him. The tomatoes were bad again. He blamed the seed stock and gave them away to the crews, and Renn, who took a bag every visit and had never once eaten one, said they were improving, which was the single most obvious lie she had told him in twenty years. Sela ran the Ores Fund. She had refused the education he'd offered — "Don't buy my lease, Neegan; buy the ledger it came out of" had only partly been about the Fund, and when he'd offered again she'd looked at him with the flat, priced expression and said, "I take the memorial commission. Somebody keeps the ledger, and it's going to be someone who was in it." She took it, and she was merciless with it, contract by contract at actuarial rates, and the settlement councils had elected her to the board within a season because Mars had learned what she was and wanted her pointed outward. They argued about pump schedules at the monthly inspection, pleasantly, at length, in front of witnesses. It was the best argument on the planet. The second borer was named *Tam*, which the crews found macabre and she found accurate, and every shift going down poured the first swallow of the coffee ration against the shaft gate, and if anyone thought that was macabre too, nobody had ever said so within Arthur's hearing. Hallowes wrote twice a quarter, in ink, warm as ever, and enclosed schedules he genuinely found interesting: extraction was up, the charter spacing was being kept to the card, the Fund's buyouts had cleared the Cydonia district ledger entirely and were working east. *You will be pleased to know,* her autumn letter ran, *that we have taken our first colonel's pension in settlement of a third-generation contract, and he cried, and I signed, and my name went first on that too. I have decided to enjoy being good, Arthur; you may tell anyone you like that it was cheaper than the alternative.* He did tell, as it happened. She'd have been unbearable if he hadn't. The watch stayed on the shelf, not fixed. He had taken it down twice this winter and put it back. The punch-card stayed in the drawer behind it, and four times now he had drafted the letter to Vosk — *a point of curiosity, Commissioner, regarding the second name on your survey roster* — and four times he had not sent it. His father had said the name once, at the table, in a voice with the sense not yet asked about, and Arthur had spent his whole professional life distrusting numbers he couldn't verify, and he put the draft in the drawer with the watch and left them both unfixed together. There are things a man is allowed not to do the arithmetic on. He had decided this was one of them, and re-decided it every week. His shift ran at dawn. He walked out across his meter — the Trust's meter — in the cold and the pump noise, checked the cage, checked the license board, and went down the way he'd gone down for years, only now salaried. The plaque was at the hundred-meter station, where the passage turned. *TOMAR "TAM" ORES, FOREMAN. HE KEPT THE NUMBERS FOR HIS OWN.* Bronze, modest, and it had gone up without a ceremony, because Sela had decided ceremonies were for people who needed them. He touched the brim of his cap at it every descent, a gesture he'd stolen from Tam without ever asking him about it, the way you learn things from a man and discover it only after he isn't there to be told. Below, the vein hummed at a whisper, tuned, milked at the physics' own rate, no faster no matter what any navy wanted, which was the whole treaty in one number. A settler kid on rotation duty had asked him last week how long the vein would last at current rates, and he had worked it out on the back of a chit to keep his hand in. "Longer than the paperwork," he'd said. The kid, who was bright, asked what would happen after that. "Everything has a half-life," Arthur said. "You just keep measuring it." He tapped two fingers against his thigh, the damping cadence, the only inheritance he'd ever want, and stepped into the gallery where the licenses hung and the meters sat on their pins and everyone's fear and everyone's want had been written down and indexed. The balance held as long as every party could still do the arithmetic. He walked down into the hum to go and do his.
